speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of fhe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MUNICIPALITIES-EXEMPTION OF PURCHASES FROM SALES AND EXCISE TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the
accepted practice I propose to take this opportunity to rise on a question which is assuming increasing importance throughout the whole of Canada. The same subject has been discussed on earlier occasions, but new emphasis has been placed upon the need of the municipalities for a thorough re-examination of their position as a result of many of the new demands which are being imposed upon them. There seems to be some tendency to accept a satisfactory surplus in the federal financial position or in the provincial position in any province without due regard to the fact that there are many municipalities in Canada today, at a time of high earnings and high revenues, that simply cannot make ends meet.
This is borne out by resolutions presented by the municipalities themselves and by the repeated resolutions of meetings of mayors and reeves in their various organizations throughout Canada. The fact is that the municipalities, which, after all, provide that form of local government closest to the people, and which give many of our most important services to the people, find themselves caught between the millstones of rapidly mounting costs on the one hand and limited tax resources on the other.
There is a particular reason why the federal government should seek the support of parliament to ease the burden upon municipalities in every way it can. It is sometimes forgotten that when the provincial governments entered into the tax arrangements in 1942, under which they gave up certain taxing powers, many municipalities gave up their taxing powers at the same time. This was recited in the statute which approved of the agreement signed at that time. They have never been restored to their position in relation to those taxes, nor has their taxing power been restored in any corresponding field.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MUNICIPALITIES-EXEMPTION OF PURCHASES FROM SALES AND EXCISE TAXES
speechtext:
Order. May I interrupt the Leader of the Opposition at this point? If he does not relate his subject very shortly to
[Mr. Claxton.l

one which is covered by the scope of federal affairs I will have to inform him that it is not in order, even on a motion to go into supply, to bring forward as a grievance a matter with which this parliament has nothing to do. The municipalities are creatures of the provinces. There may be a relationship between the provinces and the federal parliament but I do not see a direct link between the parliament of Canada and the taxing powers of the municipalities. It may be that my remarks are inopportune or premature, but I should like the Leader of the Opposition to know that if he is going to continue with the subject that he has introduced, without linking it specifically to affairs over which this parliament has jurisdiction, I will have to tell him that he is not in order.
I am informed that there is on the order paper a resolution having to do with a measure to be introduced to extend the benefits of the Municipal Grants Act and to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act. I am going to discuss the urgent need for reconsideration of the position of the government in relation to the sales and excise taxes charged on purchases by municipalities throughout Canada. This is in no way covered by the resolution to which Your Honour has referred.

subtopic: MUNICIPALITIES-EXEMPTION OF PURCHASES FROM SALES AND EXCISE TAXES

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MUNICIPALITIES-EXEMPTION OF PURCHASES FROM SALES AND EXCISE TAXES
speechtext:
The subject matter I am raising is not covered by the resolution that has been mentioned. That resolution relates to a very limited proposal. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is proper to place before the house considerations which should be borne

in mind in dealing with any matter that has not already been disposed of and is not covered by a motion before the house. There is no proposal before the house that the municipalities be exempted in whole from the sales and excise taxes on their purchases of machinery, equipment and things of that kind which they need. It is to that very urgent requirement that my remarks are directed.
The need for consideration of this subject has received new emphasis in recent weeks because of the discussions which have taken place with respect to the problem of equipping the municipalities to meet such plans as are prepared for the civil defence of this country. I raise this point by way of illustration only. I would point out that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), under whose department civil defence has been placed, has emphasized the vital importance of preparing to meet this situation. If his advice is accepted, then there are many new requirements which must be purchased by the municipalities and which will in no way be covered by such limited exemption as will be afforded by the resolution referred to by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) if it should be the will of parliament to adopt it. I would also point out that right across Canada there is increasing evidence of the need for revenue, a need that is not covered by local taxation or by any compensating grants made by the provincial governments to the municipalities. At the point where His Honour asserted that I had not yet clearly indicated the purpose of my remarks, I had intended to point out that there has been some compensation to the municipalities in respect of the taxing rights which they were called upon to forgo under the agreements of 1942. Nevertheless it is only necessary to ask any mayor, any reeve, or the member of any urban or municipal council across Canada whether or not the present situation is satisfactory to find out that today the municipalities are unable to continue to meet the increasing demands for those vitally important local needs unless some new method of taxation is found.
I do not intend to embark today upon a discussion of the need for a conference between the various levels of government in this country. I have already made that request to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who is the only person who could call such a conference. I have emphasized my reasons for believing it should be done. I leave that where it stands because the Prime Minister has indicated he is not prepared to accept that proposal. I do strongly urge, Mr. Speaker, in the absence of any immediate
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases discussion of a general readjustment of the taxing position as between the national, provincial and local authorities, that this tremendously important relief could be granted, and should be granted having regard to the practice that is already being followed.
It need not be pointed out that the whole strength of our society, and in fact the real foundation of our democracy, rests upon municipal government. It is there our whole democratic system begins; that is where the concept of personal representation is first made evident to the people of our country; that is where the relationship between the government and the elected representative is most effective; that is where we see the real supervision of the business of the people themselves. I suggest that at this particular time we have reason in this House of Commons to realize that the plans for housing, the plans for the general improvement of our country and the plans for the development of Canada, initiated in this House of Commons and approved by the parliament of Canada, in themselves impose new burdens upon the municipalities. Unless the municipalities are able to meet them, then many of the plans are rendered ineffective or hindered by difficulty in finding the appropriate conditions in which those plans can be advanced.
In no single case is this more evident than in the case of housing where the burden of the municipalities is to provide adequate services, not only such services as sewers, roads, water works and things of that kind, but educational facilities, health facilities and everything of that nature, which form an essential part of any particular program of development for the advancement of our society which may be contemplated. There is another reason, Mr. Speaker, why it seems to me that action along these lines is long overdue. The municipalities, as Your Honour pointed out a short time ago, are the legal creatures of the provincial legislatures. I hope that no member of any municipal council will feel that I am using any term that does not recognize the full dignity of the municipalities when I make that simple and unchallengeable statement.
Under our constitution, the municipalities take form under the municipal acts of the various provinces. The way in which they elect their local governments, the way in which those governments serve the people and the way in which their many activities are carried out, are defined and supervised by the provincial government. There is, therefore, a close, intimate and continuous association between the municipalities and the provincial authorities. In fact, in many cases the municipal councils are an integrated part
4774	HOUSE OF
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases of the general provincial activities. For that reason it has been difficult for many of us to understand why it is appropriate that the provincial governments should be able to buy exactly the same things that are bought by the municipal councils, and yet they should pay no sales or excise tax while the municipal councils are called upon to do so.
I sometimes wonder why a device has not been employed which could, in some substantial measure, overcome this difficulty. I think it might be one that perhaps might commend itself. If the provincial governments created a purchasing organization for the municipalities, it would seem quite evident that a provincial organization of that kind would be free of sales tax and excise tax, and could pass on that benefit to the municipalities. Nevertheless, that is a cumbersome procedure that should not become necessary, and certainly will not become necessary, unless this parliament fails to carry out the obviously necessary reform.
In saying all this, it is not my intention to discuss the motion which has been referred to by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), beyond saying its effect is so limited it offers little or no relief to the municipalities, and particularly in regard to those purchases which are of the greatest importance and cost. However, this subject is one that has been presented to the government by resolution on many occasions. The municipalities find themselves more and more reduced to taxes on real estate for their increasing needs. The very things done by this parliament throw a burden on the home owner, the farm owner and the owner of small business properties in the municipality. This is something that should be borne in mind. This is not an act of mere generosity we are suggesting, but a practical reciprocal recognition of the fact that the municipalities are called upon to do many things that, in themselves, are essential if the programs initiated here are to be carried out.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the figures in themselves are interesting and revealing. We find, for instance, that last year the mayor of the city of Edmonton stated that if the dominion had paid its share of the general obligations that the municipalities have been asking the dominion to bear, there would be a saving of approximately $600,000 in that city. That is certainly a substantial figure for any city. Whether that be the right amount or whether it should be a lesser amount, we do know what this amount of sales tax is for the city of Montreal. For the financial year 1951-52, the city of Montreal, on materials and equipment purchased either by the city itself or


by contractors, paid $382,000. Mr. Speaker, I repeat these are only amounts that illustrate what is happening in varying degress across this country. These payments are largely due to things that must be done in order to carry out programs initiated on behalf of our people by the government of Canada and by provincial governments in the general advancement of our society.
I believe that there is no single reform in taxation more greatly needed today than a readjustment of taxes which would relieve home owners, farm owners, owners of businesses and property, of the present burden of taxation. Nothing would, of itself, encourage more greatly a still more extensive building of homes and farm buildings and things of that nature, when reason suggests that it should be done. When this very thing is being done for provincial governments in relation to the very same things, then I submit that the municipalities, which are brought into existence as corporate bodies under the laws of the provinces, should have the same right and courtesy extended to them.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation which would provide for the exemption of all municipal councils and school boards from the payment of dominion excise taxes including the 10 per cent sales tax."

As I had occasion to inform the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) earlier, an amendment to the motion to go into supply should not involve legislation placed on the order paper. The very effect of this amendment is that legislation be introduced similar to that contemplated in a budget resolution.
I hold in my hand May's fifteenth edition in which, at page 706, I find this:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion.
That is, on a question for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair. It continues:
For instance, a matter which should be considered upon a substantive motion, or which would anticipate a more effective form of proceeding of which notice has been given cannot be discussed. A subject, or matter of detail which should be discussed in the committee, has been held to be out of order. The rule which prohibits reference to matters involving legislation-
Then there is a reference to page 717, to which I shall refer later. It continues:
-having been found too rigid, was relaxed, on the recommendation of the select committee on procedure of 1946.

Well, so far as we are concerned, that rule was not relaxed by any committee of procedure of this house.
And then, if hon. members will look at the reference to page 717, which is mentioned here in brackets, they will find this under the heading "General Restrictions on Debate in Committee of Supply":
Regarding the general conduct of debate in the committee of supply, it may be observed that remarks on the conduct of a servant of the state, made on the grant containing his salary, must be restricted to his official conduct. The committee of supply does not afford the proper opportunity for discussing from which house of parliament a minister should be chosen, or whether he should be in the cabinet or not, or which minister should represent the government in respect of the estimates under consideration. The administrative action of a department is open to debate, but the necessity for legislation and matters involving legislation cannot be discussed in committee of supply.
It has also been a rule in this house that if an hon. member wishes to introduce legislation or to amend legislation there is a definite form of procedure. The Leader of the Opposition may say, "Well, if it involves the expenditure of money or the imposition of a tax, I cannot move it. It has to be moved by a minister of the crown." That is the very basis upon which our parliamentary procedure is founded. Matters having to do with the spending of money or the imposition of taxation have to be introduced by the executive. The opposition has the right to criticize and to censure by amendment or by motion. But in this particular instance, on a motion to go into supply, what has to be heard is a grievance, but not a motion involving legislative matters which are to be dealt with later as they appear on the order paper.
Of course I am prepared to hear comments on the ruling. However, in view of what I have said, which is fully explained in May, I would be inclined to declare that the amendment cannot be received.

I submit further that, over and over again, in every session, the procedure I have suggested has been followed

And, so far as the second point is concerned, if the fact that some resolution dealing with a particular aspect of a problem is to deny the opportunity to propose consideration of a general approach to the problem, then I would point out that a very effective blocking device could be employed simply by introducing a series of resolutions dealing with very limited aspects of every question that might come before the House of Commons. The hands of the house would be tied in that hon. members would not be in a position to present this kind of resolution which in the past, both here and at Westminster, has over and over again formed the basis for positive and effective discussion- discussion which, in many cases, has had satisfactory results and received the acquiescence of the government. Even within the last two or three years we have had encouragement in that we have seen certain of these proposals actually accepted.
I would point out that if a resolution of this kind-which, I might add, has been introduced every year for several years, in a somewhat similar form-is to be withheld from discussion by something dealing with a limited part of it, we would have a serious situation. How could this be done? Well, certainly the government could anticipate that such a resolution would be brought forward, in view of the fact that this argument has been presented before. Under such a ruling it would only be necessary to introduce a motion that the sales tax on school rulers be removed, and there could be no discussion on the broad subject of the relief of municipalities in regard to purchases of machinery and equipment either for municipalities or for schools. Surely the intention of the rules and the rulings made in this house should not be to restrict the opportunity to place positive proposals before the house. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that on the contrary, the rules should be so interpreted as to encourage positive recommendations dealing with those matters that are obviously of considerable concern to the people of Canada, and particularly the municipal taxpayers of this country.

It is true, however, that in the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did provide for some relief to the municipalities by granting exemption from sales tax on the purchase of road building machinery. Now, that went only part way towards meeting the requests that have been made so often by members in this house. In the budget debate I expressed disappointment that the minister had not gone farther and exempted the purchases of buses and that sort of thing by school boards.
At the moment, I am not too familiar with the situations in the cities of Canada. I know they are having their troubles, of course, but they cannot be having nearly the trouble the rural municipalities are having because
[Mr. ColdwellJ

in the cities there are large concentrations of industries that are subject to taxation. You do not find this concentration of industry in the rural municipalities. Consequently, the only source of revenue the rural municipality has is the taxation applied against the farms and the homes of the people. This places a heavy burden on the rural municipalities. Federal policies dictate that on every purchase of road building machinery or equipment to transport children to school, things of that sort, a municipality has to pay a 10 per cent sales tax, and in addition certain other excise taxes.
I have calculated that on the purchase of an ordinary standard model Chevrolet car from the factory the purchaser must pay this government nearly $500 in excise and sales taxes combined; that is more than the labourers receive to build the car. I do not believe it is to the credit of the government of Canada that a situation like that exists. The ordinary, standard model Chevrolet car sells at the factory for around $2,200 or $2,300. What would a school division out in the country have to pay in sales taxes at 10 per cent on the purchase of a school bus, let us say, with which they transport the children to school, costing in the neighbourhood of $12,000 or $15,000? I shall let hon. members make the calculation themselves. It becomes a substantial sum, especially when it is recognized that the sales tax of 10 per cent is applied at the manufacturer's level and is often pyramided into a much greater percentage by the time the school division buys the bus from the retail distributor.
It is because of the extra burden on the school divisions and municipalities that I have spoken on a number of occasions in favour of having this tax abolished, and for that reason amongst others I welcome the opportunity to say something about it this afternoon and to ask the government to give some serious consideration to the extension of the good work they began in the budget this year. It must be remembered that these things are not purchased for resale. They are not bought by municipalities and school boards for the purpose of making money. The stringent nature of the revenue sources available to municipal governments constitutes a very real national problem. The finance-taxation problems of local governments have been recognized in varying degrees by the provincial governments of Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest to the house that consideration be given to the vicious nature of this tax, which can be seen if we take a moment to follow it through. Under the terms of the amendment


which is now before the house, we are discussing the payment of dominion excise taxes and the general sales tax by municipalities, school boards, and so on. As has just been pointed out by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), about 85 per cent of the revenues of municipal corporations are obtained through the medium of real estate taxes. Hon. members are fully aware of the nature of the sales tax. As we have pointed out on many occasions it is not a tax levied on the basis of ability to pay, which we think should be the principle underlying any fair taxation program. Here you have a tax which is levied on something other than the ability-to-pay basis, which the municipality has to pass on, again on a basis which is not strictly according to ability to pay. This unfair sales tax which municipalities have to pay is in turn levied on the holders of real estate within the municipalities. In other words, it seems to me you have here the case of a tax, which is not on an ability-to-pay basis, being compounded into another tax which is not on an ability-to-pay basis, and in that vein to me it is most unfair.
It means in effect that educational supplies, equipment, and all the things necessary for providing a multitude of services to our people in our cities and municipalities across this country result in a land tax having to be paid so that the municipalities can pay a sales tax. Again I would emphasize the fact that both these taxes depart from the fairest principle in taxation, namely, that taxes should be levied according to the ability to pay.
In some instances this sales tax, which a city or municipality has to pass on in the form of a real estate tax, is a tax on rented property, and in some of those instances the landlord effects a mark-up on that tax which he collects from the tenant. I realize we are discussing a very small proportion of the taxes paid by the owners of real estate in our municipalities, or a very small proportion of the taxes paid indirectly by those who rent homes in our municipalities. But nevertheless the principle is surely quite evident, namely that we are compounding one unfair tax on another, and in some instances providing for a mark-up on that tax. Surely the fairest thing all round would be for the federal government to cease collecting excise and sales tax from our municipalities so that the passing on of tax in this unfair way could be avoided.
It is sometimes put forward as an argument by members on the government side, when they feel it is necessary to defend a tax of this kind, that the money has to be found

somewhere. It is always very interesting, of course, to hear government supporters defend the status quo while it exists, then boast of the fact that the situation has been changed when the government some day sees the light. At any rate, it is a fair question. If this sales tax on municipal purchases could be suspended and the exact amount of money lost in that way had to be made up, where could the government get that money? Well, even if it meant collecting more money by means of income taxes or corporation taxes, and even if government supporters were to argue that that means collecting money from the same people, namely the citizens in our cities and municipalities across the country, then I would emphasize the point that in that instance the government would be collecting the money on a fairer basis to the extent that the money which is collected directly in income tax from our people would be paid on a graduated basis, a basis of ability to pay. That is a much fairer method than this vicious sales tax which is collected by means of real estate taxes, and mark-ups in the case of rents where those real estate taxes are paid on owners' rented property. On all counts a graduated income tax is much fairer than the method now in effect.
I certainly hope, whatever happens in regard to the procedural aspect of the amendment we now have the privilege of discussing, that the government will one of these days pay attention to this very justifiable plea made so often by the municipalities of this country, this justifiable plea which is being made from the opposition side of the house today, and that they will do away with the business of requiring municipalities and school boards to pay these unfair excise and general sales taxes.
As the government knows, and as people generally know, some of us feel the time has come to take a much broader crack at the whole question of sales taxes. We feel they should be reduced across the board. However, as Your Honour has pointed out that the subject before the house at the moment is limited in scope, I have risen for just these few moments to emphasize the vicious nature of the sales tax when it is applied to municipal and school board purchases, and to urge the government to accept the principle set out in the amendment which is now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I have not been more convinced at any time of the value of service in some municipal capacity before entering parliament than on the occasion of a debate of this kind. Members of this house who have 83276-303J
17, 1954	4787
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases had municipal experience, whether in municipal councils or school boards or both, will have a fundamental appreciation of the problem that may not strike others quite so forcibly.
The fact of the matter is that the municipalities in this country-and this applies to the municipalities in all provinces-are sorely in need of a better deal than that which they now enjoy under existing constitutional arrangements. Since 1867 there has been virtually no change in the constitutional formulas as applied to the municipalities, whether on the side of their responsibilities on the one hand or on the side of their revenues on the other. But while these constitutional formulas have remained virtually unchanged for 87 years, there has been not simply a steady increase in municipal responsibilities but a mounting multiplication of them and the attendant financial burden.
I do not propose to review the ground that has been amply covered in this debate, particularly in the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell), as to the specific responsibilities of the municipalities. I suppose no one of those responsibilities has increased more rapidly in cost than has the responsibility of providing schools. It repays anyone holding public office at any level of government to sit down and examine the rise in school costs over the period of the last 30 years. These costs have mounted literally by leaps and bounds. The public requires and is demanding newer and better schools. On every hand, with the development of the country, increase in population and shifts in population, new schools are being built in response to public demand and to necessity, at a rapid rate. The cost of construction today has outstripped anything that has been known in our past.
In the province of Ontario I suggest there is not a school that is being built today or extended of which the cost runs much less than $30,000 a room. In addition to that cost, there is the great burden of providing maintenance of school buildings and of paying the salaries of those who are employed in the school system. This burden has fallen on the municipalities with increasing weight. It is quite true that in some provinces, like Ontario, for instance, the provincial government has come to the assistance of the municipalities in helping them to meet their costs of providing schools and school facilities. But, Mr. Speaker, in the whole field of education in Canada, the burden the municipalities are carrying is one that is entirely disproportionate to their means.
Just in the last generation there has been the whole problem of providing for those
4788	HOUSE OF
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases who are said to be unemployable. Then there are those who are today the employable unemployed for whom no provision is being made except at the expense of the municipalities. Time and again appeals have been made to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and to the government to face up to this increasing problem, which is quite acute in the larger areas, of providing for the employable unemployed. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the federal government continues to deny any responsibility. These unemployed are on the doorstep of the municipality and they cannot be allowed to starve. The municipality therefore makes provision for them.
There are also the problems of those social agencies which are connected with the municipal government and which have helped so much to provide relief in these cases to which I have referred. There is the increasing burden of providing hospitalization. Although the provinces have increased their contributions to the building of hospitals and also to the per diem costs of providing for patients, nevertheless the municipalities continue to bear a too heavy share of this increasing burden. Mention has been made of the cost of constructing roads. I need not repeat what has been said on that matter.
All of us will have in mind, I know, the extent to which the housing problem has for many years now been thrown in large measure on the municipalities. Particularly in the metropolitan areas where growth has been extremely rapid and the housing problem has been most acute, the burden of providing municipal services has been cast largely on those municipalities. In some of them the problem has become so acute that the municipalities have virtually been obliged to discourage house construction and land subdivision because they could not cope with the problem of providing costly municipal services for the land.
On every hand, Mr. Speaker, the experience of the municipalities has been one of confronting rising costs. If one measures the scale of increase over the past 30 years, one can only describe it as a multiplication. At the same time within that existing constitutional formula to which I have referred there has been no increase of assured revenues to the municipalities. The municipalities are functioning today with the same tax base as that which existed in 1867, and virtually with land taxes as the only source of revenue. There are some minor sources such as licence fees and that sort of thing but they are not material in relation to the total.
The hon. member for Greenwood has stressed the undesirability of providing subsidies. There is much to be said on that


subject, Mr. Speaker. Here, however, we are dealing with an aspect of the problem which is pressing and urgent and which illustrates the utter unfairness of the way in which the federal government is proceeding to exercise its taxing powers. For the municipalities-and this applies alike to the municipal councils and the boards of education which must levy through the municipal councils-the base remains virtually the same as it was 87 years ago. The taxes that the federal government applies to the municipalities are hidden taxes. It is a thousand pities that those taxes are hidden. If the citizens of the municipalities were fully aware of the way in which they are being taxed by the federal government there would be an uprising of an outraged public opinion. But as in so many other respects, the federal government applies its taxes in this subtle manner. They are hidden. The taxpayer does not realize or is not conscious of the full weight and the unfairness of them. Every sales and excise tax that the federal government is today collecting from the municipalities is hidden. That is one of the fundamental curses of these anomalies in the constitutional powers of taxing that are being exercised in this country.
The federal government, with its abundant sources, should be devising ways of helping the municipalities to meet these urgent demands for necessary but costly services which they are financially unable to provide. On the contrary, the federal government is not only not helping the municipalities but it is actually levying taxes upon the municipalities.
How can it be said that there is anything inherently wrong in the principle for which I am contending or that there is any insuperable administrative difficulty in applying it when we see in existing federal legislation provision for exemption of purchases made by provinces? If you will have regard, Mr. Speaker, to the provisions of the Excise Tax ' Act you will see that in sections 45 and 46 clear provision is made for the exemption of goods imported by Her Majesty in the right of any province of Canada for certain purposes, with the exception of three. These three exceptions to the general rule of exemption of provincial purchases are in respect of goods purchased for these purposes:
(a)	resale;
(b)	to be used by any board, commission, railway, public utility, university, manufactory, company or agency owned, controlled or operated by the government of the province or under the authority of the legislature or the lieutenant governor in council; or
(c)	to be used by Her Majesty or by her agents or servants in connection with the manufacture or production of goods or to be used for other commercial or mercantile purposes.

There is a strong case to be made out for treating municipal corporations and commissions which are engaged in any commercial enterprise on the same basis in respect of federal taxation as similar organizations operating under private ownership. But, Mr. Speaker, as to the fundamental principle here,
I say that we have in the sections to which I have referred a clear recognition of a principle that the federal government ought not to levy the sales and excise taxes provided for in the Excise Tax Act upon provincial governments. Why is the line drawn there? If it is sound that provincial governments be exempted from federal sales and excise taxes upon their purchases, why should the principle not have equal application at that municipal level of government where the need is very great, where financial pressure is stringent today?
The same principle is not recognized in the Excise Act but there, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the act applies to the products of distilleries and breweries, tobacco and alcohol in various forms, things which municipalities are not normally purchasing. But in the sections of the Excise Tax Act that I have read we have the recognition of a principle, a recognition that emanates from a sense of fairness and a realistic appreciation of the needs of the provincial governments. At the municipal level the need is even more acute today.
What is the extent of the problem? How much is the federal government collecting today in taxes from municipalities, from municipal councils, school boards and boards of education? 1 do not believe anybody knows. I do not believe any attempt has been made to ascertain the total that is being collected year by year in this way. Some municipalities have made calculations. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) referred to a calculation made by the municipal authorities of the city of Montreal. Their estimate was that through these taxes the municipal corporation is paying into the federal treasury year by year a sum of about $300,000 annually. I may add that the city treasurer of my own city of Toronto has estimated that the city, through purchases made by the municipal council and by the board of education and separate school board, is paying a total of approximately $500,000 a year in taxes into the federal treasury. It is a shocking state of affairs that this federal government, with all the ample sources of revenue open to it, far from assisting municipalities, handicapped as they are by meagre resources, rising costs and multiplying
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases demands for services, should actually be levying vast amounts in taxes from these municipal treasuries.
Let us not have offered to us today the hoary excuse, the hoary pretext of administrative difficulties. If administrative difficulties were not permitted to stand in the way of the exemption of provincial purchases from federal sales and excise taxes, then certainly there is no case to be made out to justify any refusal to extend that exemption to purchases made by municipalities.
This is an urgent problem. Municipalities from one end of the country to the other are crying for assistance in the form of a realistic approach to their constitutional difficulties. There must be, in my submission, an opening of the eyes of the federal government to the way in which they are increasing the burdens and the difficulties of the municipalities. The time has come for action. Among all the anomalies, among all the injustices in the federal tax structure today that are crying out for reform, none is more pressing than the one we have been discussing this afternoon and which is the subject matter of the amendment, the iniquitous imposition by the federal government of taxes upon our municipal governments in the form of municipal councils, school boards, boards of education and other municipal organizations.

Mr. Speaker, regardless of what the ultimate disposition of the amendment before us may be, I think this is a matter that is worthy of discussion. The preceding speaker has mentioned that those members of the house who have had municipal experience will perhaps realize the difficulties of the municipalities better than those who have not had such experience. I am in the fortunate position of having had experience on both a school board and a city council. Because of that experience I seldom fail to read items in the daily papers that have reference to municipal and school board matters. In that way I think I keep fairly well in touch. In addition, when I get my city tax notice considerable information is sent with it as to the taxes collected and what is done with them.
I agree with those who have spoken that the plight of the municipalities is a real one. Of the three levels of government, municipal government in its various aspects is the one that is closest to the people. It is the one that has to deal with the people's problems first.
For instance, I see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) doing me
4790	HOUSE OF
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases the honour of paying attention, so I shall just take an example that touches on his department. His department brings in a family of immigrants, a husband, a wife and three or four children. They settle in a city. If the husband is able to find employment, the minister is well pleased as that is one difficulty that has been met so far as his department is concerned. However, it is really then that the problems of the school board, for instance, commences because they have to find school accommodation for three or four new pupils. While ultimately these immigrants are going to be an asset to the country, at this time they become a real problem to the school boards across Canada.
Then let us consider the matter of health for a moment. If the immigrant to whom I referred becomes ill, the first duty of looking after him falls upon the municipal authorities. The minister shakes his head, but despite anything else that may be done for the immigrant, it takes a little time and during that time lag the city has to provide certain services. Then, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) referred to the matter of housing.
After mentioning school accommodation and health requirements, there is this question that has been mentioned, unemployment, and here again the municipality has had to pay out considerable funds this year to look after those who have been affected by the unemployment situation. These are things the municipalities have to do, because if they do not provide for the people in one way they may have to provide for them in another. If they do not provide schools, hospitals and housing, they will have to provide jail accommodation, juvenile courts and that sort of thing. The problem of our increasing population falls, therefore, first on our municipal councils.
In the matter of education, the situation is becoming extremely serious. I know that is the case in my own province of British Columbia. We believe we have as good a school system as any that can be found in Canada. As a matter of fact, we are quite proud of it. During the last several years the incidence of taxation on property owners for school purposes has reached the point where the property taxpayer cannot do any more. There is grave danger now that our educational standards will have to be lowered. Perhaps all these things have been said by others during this debate, and if I am repeating them now it is merely for emphasis.
I feel the time has arrived when the representatives of the three governments should sit down together and decide upon 

some more equitable distribution of the taxes that are paid by the people of Canada, whether in their capacity as municipal taxpayers, provincial taxpayers or federal taxpayers. They are the same people. At the moment I do not wish to take perhaps the extreme position that was taken by the hon. member for Eglinton, but I cannot believe that the federal government can say that education is a provincial matter and is no concern of theirs. I do not think it is enough either to say that the municipalities are the creatures of the province, and consequently, are not a federal responsibility.
The point that we must get over is that we are dealing with the problems of the same people, whether they pay their taxes or require services as residents of a municipality, residents of a province, or citizens of this Dominion of Canada. Who is to say, "well, it is too bad if you cannot find the taxes for education; it is too bad if you cannot find the taxes for hospital services or for looking after the unemployed, but that is really not our problem". These are problems of the people of Canada, and the people of Canada are represented in this parliament. Every problem that is a problem of the people of Canada is a problem of this parliament, whether under our constitutional set-up at the moment we have direct responsibility for looking after it or whether responsibility has been given to some other governmental organization that we have created.
I am sure that ultimately the people will not take it for granted nothing can be done about their problems because the government with the largest amount of resources is not going to look after this problem. There will be a demand that this government take a look at the picture as a whole, and leave to each level of government sufficient funds to enable it to discharge the responsibilities it has been given. If there are not sufficient funds to do everything we want to do, then we shall have to establish some system of priorities and decide which are the more essential things. The people of Canada, discussing these matters through their various governments, will decide how these taxes are to be allocated and what services are to be provided. Perhaps this is a situation for which no one in particular is responsible. It has grown and developed within our system of government, but we should endeavour to ascertain our collective responsibilities and then discharge them.

Mr. Speaker, there are one or two comments I should like to make at this time. The last speaker made much of the oft-repeated statement that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces. I suggest however that we must take into consideration the great changes that have taken place since the time of confederation. I do not think anyone would suggest that the conditions existing in 1867 were those of today. While it was quite true that in all their wisdom at that time the fathers of confederation saw fit to place certain responsibilities in certain quarters, anyone who wishes to view objectively the changes that have taken place since that time must realize that some of the responsibilities cannot be met adequately with the taxing and fiscal powers possessed by the junior governments.
I believe it is recognized today that many of the problems which formerly were looked upon as municipal or provincial are now considered national in their scope. I do not think anyone can view education as being the problem of any particular part of Canada. We have a very serious shortage of teachers in this country, from one end of Canada to the other. I do not think the shortage is confined peculiarly to any one province.
Then the health needs of Canadians are national in their scope. We do not find any particular part of Canada in a position to take care of those health needs. I suggest therefore it is absurd to dismiss the suggestions made simply by saying that after all under the British North America Act the provinces were made responsible for municipal government within their boundaries. To take that view one would have to ignore completely the developments that have taken place in Canada in recent years.
I know that in my own province one of the most onerous responsibilities of municipal government is the construction of market roads, just as it is the great job of any provincial government to build the highways. We know that the federal government derives a great amount of revenue from the taxation levied against new automobiles. Were it not for the fact that the provincial governments are building highways and the municipal government are building the market roads, no automobiles would be purchased. And if it seems logical that provincial and municipal governments should take care of their roadbuilding problems, then by the same token the federal government should be prepared to leave to those junior governments the full revenue that might be derived from the automobile industry. It seems somewhat inconsistent to be told that certain responsibilities
4792	HOUSE OF
Municipalities-Taxes on Purchases should be borne by the municipal governments when at the same time the federal government is deriving a great deal of revenue from taxes on the sale of automobiles, when such revenue would not be available were it not for the expenditures made by the junior governments.
I believe it is recognized that Canada's health needs are nation-wide. We cannot expect that our junior governments will be able to bear the full burden in these matters.
I am thinking of our medical college now being completed in Saskatchewan. It has been estimated that when we begin graduating doctors from that college, in addition to the sums of money paid by way of fees by the students it will cost the provincial government somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10,000 for every doctor who graduates. In many cases those doctors will serve in various parts of Canada. The fact that in a time of war their services are urgently needed by the armed forces indicates that the federal government has a direct responsibility in this field. Consequently any relief it can provide to the municipal and provincial governments is to be desired on that account.
Then, as to education. As a teacher I am fully aware of the great need for granting some assistance for the educational authorities in Canada. I repeat that when in 1867 the fathers of confederation, in their wisdom, set up a certain relationship of powers and responsibilities as between the provincial and the federal governments they could not foresee the great need in future years for an extended educational program. Certainly no one can argue today that if we are going to have the type of educational program across Canada we feel we should have it would not require the co-operation of all governments.
How is this going to be done? For some years in this group we have argued in support of some form of federal aid for education. We feel that if the problem is going to be met and if we are going to provide an adequate number of teachers at proper salaries, and if we are going to have adequate plant equipment and more extended educational opportunities, there will have to be federal participation in a manner such as to leave no suggestion of any attempt on the part of the federal government to encroach upon the rights of provincial governments to provide education in their respective provinces. We do feel however that this can be done, and that the federal government could provide some measure of aid to the provinces in the matter of education.
Now, what we have been talking about this afternoon is not something direct. We are simply suggesting that this is certainly one 

manner in which some assistance can be given education without in any way encroaching upon the rights of the provinces to control and manage their own educational system. Because if the federal government grants a proper and adequate measure of relief in so far as taxes are concerned to school boards, then I suggest that it will indirectly be making a contribution, small as it may be in scope, toward education in Canada. Therefore, I am suggesting that in the light of the arguments that have been advanced this afternoon a case has certainly been made for the government to give consideration to granting some measure of tax relief to school boards and to municipal governments in Canada in order that they might more effectively carry out the duties that we expect of them in Canada at the present time.

The plight of agriculture is a matter which concerns not only my own riding but all of Canada, but on this occasion I propose to confine my remarks chiefly to the problems confronting livestock producers. I would like to refer to two briefs which were presented, one to the government and the other to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), by the Interprovincial Farm Union Council of Canada in regard to what has taken place in our livestock industry during the past two years, and both of which cast serious doubts on the efficiency and justice of the present marketing system.
One brief points out that the prices paid for cattle in Montreal in 1951 amounted to $24.82 compared with $14.31 in 1953. In Toronto the price dropped from $29.70 in 1951 to $17.34 in 1953, and in Winnipeg the price dropped over the same period from $27.40 to $14.70. These figures underline the decrease which took place over a period of 24 months.
Hurrah!

I am sorry to hear an hon. member say "Hurrah" because this is a matter which concerns his constituents and

all hon. members must, I think, be concerned about the drop in the return earned by any group of primary producers, particularly to the extent of 43 per cent over a two-year period. If one takes into account the increase in the cost of living for farmers during that period then the drop is more in the nature of 50 per cent.
One of these briefs points out that in Canada we consume about 95 per cent of our meat production, and it would not seem reasonable that the five per cent we export should be responsible for the ups and downs in the price of meat products we have experienced over the last few years.
The brief also points out that at the beginning of the century we had 1,278 cattle per thousand population in Canada, compared with 784 in 1953. It is very difficult to understand why we should find it impossible to produce as many cattle per thousand people in this day and age, especially in view of all the experimental work being done in our agricultural colleges. I believe we should be able to increase our production until it meets the levels attained at the beginning of the century. Of course the explanation was that the government of the day thought that it was good for the Canadian people to consume more milk, and so milk consumption and production were subsidized. In a little booklet I have here entitled "The Story of FAO" there are some passages that I think are appropriate in the light of the figures I have given. They read as follows:
A real surplus of food has never existed in the world. There have always been great numbers of undernourished people. Yet governments of the highly developed agricultural countries have sometimes found it necessary to limit their production in order to keep farm prices high enough to provide a good living for rural families....
The farmers of the world can produce enough food to rid the world of hunger-if they can use the best agricultural methods we know now. The hungry people can get plenty of the right kinds of food-if they have some means of earning money to buy food and other necessities. . . .
This is the job of the food and agriculture organization as stated in its constitution: "raising levels of nutrition and standards of living of the peoples, securing improvements in the efficiency of the production and distribution of all food and agricultural products, bettering the condition of rural populations, and thus contributing toward an expanding world economy".
Then it is pointed out that it should be guaranteed that producing nations will be able to sell their commodities, that buying nations will be able to get as much of the commodities as they need, and that prices will be fair to both. We in Canada cannot control the prices of these things outside of Canada, but if we were able during the war years to organize our own economy so that we not only maintained but increased our production and consumption of milk then I submit that we can certainly work out a program so that our farmers will have an incentive to produce and sell whole milk and so that the people of the country who want milk supplies for their children will have adequate supplies. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to have this opportunity to enter the debate which began prior to the dinner recess. The amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), is as follows:
In the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951, to December 31, 1953.
During the introductory remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie I was surprised to hear a member of the Liberal party interject by shouting "Hurrah" when the hon. member had stated that agricultural livestock prices had dropped drastically. I would want to be as kind as possible to the hon. member who interjected because I should think he must have made that comment in a jovial frame of mind.
On the other hand, if there be anyone in the house who would gainsay the importance of what the hon. member for Mackenzie was saying when he quoted figures showing the very serious drop in the prices of agricultural commodities, I would hasten to say to him that there can be no more important subject for discussion in the House of Commons, and certainly no subject which would affect more every single citizen in Canada than does the prosperity of those who are engaged in agriculture.
The hon. member should be congratulated upon having moved the amendment because already during this session of parliament we have seen delegations coming to Ottawa asking for federal assistance. We know that the ramifications of the situation extend into every home in Canada. It is well understood by all people that unless we have a healthy and prosperous agriculture we will have a serious economic condition among all other industries in Canada.
Livestock-Floor Prices It is with this in mind that I appeal to hon. members this evening to bear with me when I present the case for agriculture, in its relation to the marketing of livestock. It is now some twenty years-I believe it was 1934-since the price spreads commission indicated that at that time there was a necessity for a national livestock board. That position was taken because it was felt that at that time the producers of livestock in Canada were not getting their proper share from the sale of their commodities. An investigation into the prices farmers were receiving during the depression period indicates this quite clearly.
Since that time however we have come a long way. We know that during the period of the war and in the post-war years livestock producers in Canada have enjoyed somewhat better conditions for the marketing of their product. Under the present system however the marketing of livestock is a precarious procedure, and one with which I can assure hon. members most farmers are not satisfied.
Hon. members will have noticed that in the amendment we ask for two things, namely the establishment of the principle of national livestock marketing and also an announcement by the government in respect of floor prices for cattle and hogs at a price level not less than that obtained in the period of time indicated in the amendment. The farmer is not so much concerned with the income he receives from the marketing of his livestock as with the relationship that income bears to the cost of production.
I say the present government, and former Liberal governments, must accept a great deal of responsibility for the present position in which farmers find themselves so far as livestock prices are concerned. From 1945 on members of this group pleaded with the government to maintain some sort of peacetime price controls. If one were to look into the findings of the royal commission that sat in 1949 he would find that while they did not indicate their belief that a wartime price control policy would be feasible in peacetime, or in a post-war period, yet they did indicate that some peacetime method of price control could have been maintained. As a matter of fact the government did keep for a little while the promise it gave to the people of Canada in the days of war. In other words, it did maintain some of the price controls. One after the other, however, those controls were thrown out the window, and of course prices began to rise.
That is the key reason why today we in agriculture find ourselves in a position where our costs have mounted to such an extent that, taken alongside falling prices, we have

Livestock-Floor Prices been caught in a price squeeze. One should of course look at a farmer's income in relation to his costs. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and other government spokesmen are prone to quote figures of gross national income in respect of agriculture. That of course does not show the true picture of income in agriculture.
In this connection I should like to quote in full an article which appeared in the Co-operator for January 1954. On this occasion the Canadian Federation of Agriculture takes up the cudgel with the Minister of Agriculture and the leader of the government in the Senate, when it says:
Agriculture Minister Gardiner, in the annual agricultural conference at Ottawa on November 24, and Senate leader Ross Macdonald a day later, in the Senate, deliberately set out to soften the general warning issued by provincial government delegations and leaders of the federation of agriculture alike that the farming industry of Canada was facing a serious situation economically because of continually rising farm costs and declining farm prices.
For this purpose both the minister and the Senate leader quoted figures respecting the cash farm income and the net farm income of Canadian agriculture in 1953 as compared to 1949. It was quite easy for them to show that the net farm income of Canadian agriculture in 1953 will be about five per cent above that of 1949, although the bureau of statistics has announced that there will be a reduction of 12 per cent in 1953 from 1952.
But what the honourable gentleman failed to do was to co-relate the net farm income figures with costs of both farm operations and farm living. Therefore, without such co-relation, it is unfair to leave the impression that Canadian agriculture is as prosperous, from the farmer's own standpoint, as it was in 1949, for such is by no means the case.
The fact of the matter is that, when all factors of farm operations and farm living have been taken into account, the net result is that, even with the increase in net farm income mentioned, the purchasing power of this income will be 10 per cent less in 1953 than it was in 1949, because of increased farm costs.
In other words, while there may be no more dollars in income on farms, in mere terms of dollars, those dollars have 10 per cent less value in purchasing power than they would have had in 1949. Figuring 1949 as a basis of 100, the purchasing power of net farm income in 1953 works out at 90.
On this occasion the Canadian Federation of Agriculture pointed out to the public and to the government that there must be a basis of relationship between what the farmer gets and what he has to pay for the costs of production in order to establish his real income.
As I said before, under the present system of marketing it is impossible in practice for the farmers to get a just and fair price for their livestock. From the time that the price spreads commission in 1934 indicated that a national livestock marketing board was necessary to market livestock for the protection of both the consumer and the producer until

the present time we find that the situation has grown immeasurably worse from the producers' point of view.
We have four major packing plants controlling the purchasing of livestock in Canada. With this monopoly control it is virtually impossible for farmers to have anything to say about what they get for their livestock. I am sure no hon. member would say that there can be any justification for this state of affairs, or any justice to the producer in it. A farmer can take a carload of cattle and send them to the Winnipeg stockyards and get perhaps 18 cents a pound at the week end. Then on Monday morning another car from another neighbour can come in and there will be a variation of three cents or four cents a pound. Yet there has been no visible change in the situation in regard to the demand and no change in regard to the supply. Hon. members can readily see the injustice of that situation.
The problem that faces agriculture can be laid at the doorstep of the Liberal party, owing to the fact that they did not keep on price controls as they should have until things had levelled off and thereby maintain a decent price relationship between producer and consumer in Canada. Then there is also the fact that we have lost most of our export markets to Britain, which was our historical market, and that has come about because of the policies of this government.
I do not want to go into that in detail other than to illustrate to the house what has taken place by some figures that I received in a return on March 18 to a question I asked of the department. In 1944, the year before the end of the war, we were shipping 980,800 hundredweight of beef and veal to Britain; 11,356 hundredweight of mutton and lamb; 103,751 hundredweight of fresh pork; 21,650 hundredweight of poultry and 6,923,103 hundredweight of bacon and hams; 338,378 hundredweight of canned meats; 142,300 hundredweight of edible offal and 408 hundredweight of other meats. That was in the peak year. In the second peak year, which was 1945, Canada shipped to Britain 1,843,777 hundredweight of beef and veal; 73,579 hundredweight of mutton and lamb; 4,460,693 hundredweight of bacon and hams; 160,441 hundredweight of canned meats; 103,186 hundredweight of edible offal and 6,082 hundredweight of other meats.
Then we have the picture of the post-war period in relation to the livestock products from Canada going to Britain. This is a record of our trade with that country. In the year 1953 we shipped 64,501 hundredweight of beef and veal; no mutton and lamb; no fresh pork; no poultry; no bacon and hams

and only 27 hundredweight of canned meats; no edible offal and only 10 hundredweight of other meats.
Is it any wonder that this government, through its fiscal policies and trade policies, has failed to keep that historical market for our agricultural products? I recall very well the hog prices in the period between July 21 and September 22 of 1951, when they dropped 25 per cent. Surely, no one can say that such a condition, when the price of our livestock drops 25 per cent in that period, can be justified.
Then we come into the supply situation. I hold in my hand a submission to the government of Canada by the Interprovincial Farm Union Council, submitted on February 15, 1954. It indicates that there is no justification for the present drop in beef prices to the producers in Canada. In this submission to the government we find the following:
We note in the September issue of "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada" issued by the federal Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, that we in Canada consume 95 per cent of our total marketings of cattle, and that only approximately 5 per cent was exported during the first seven months of 1953. Latest statistics even show that stocks of meat held by packers, abattoirs, and cold storage warehouses on December 1, 1953, were 13 million pounds less than on the same day the year before.
I want to draw the attention of the house to the figures which correspond to this period I am reviewing. In Montreal in 1951 the price, taking the over-all average, of beef was $24.82 a hundredweight; in 1953 it dropped to $14.31. The Toronto market in 1951 was $29.76. It had dropped in 1953 to $17.34. The Winnipeg market in 1951 was $27.40, and it had dropped to $14.17. Who makes all the money in the process?
The farmer.

Somebody said "the farmer". That shows how little he knows about what he is talking. I do not know whether he wants to get a rise out of me. I will not mention his name because I do not think it would be fair to him, but surely he must have a better understanding of the situation than that. When we come back this fall I am sure that the hon. member who is now interfering with my attempt to present the farmers' plight will be one of those who will be rising in his place when we have delegations here wondering what is wrong with the employment situation in Canada.
This whole problem, Mr. Speaker, of a fair and just income to the farmer, is tied up with the welfare of everybody in Canada.
Livestock-Floor Prices The fact that we have already had delegations representing the agricultural implement industry in Canada coming to Ottawa to see this government is an indication that the income of the agricultural producer has been drastically cut in the last two years; and more people will be coming here unless this government takes action and does something along the lines that we are suggesting. What we need today is a national livestock marketing board with producer representation.
This government should take the Agricultural Prices Support Act off the shelf and use it, and not leave it hidden away some place. This act should be used to protect the agricultural industry of this country. It is all right for this government to subsidize the gold mining industry which in five years has been subsidized to the extent of some $60 million. It is all right to dig gold in Canada and then send it down to be buried in Kentucky. But when we come here and ask this government to get busy and set up a marketing plan and use the Agricultural Prices Support Act to protect the agricultural industry of this country then our case is ridiculed by hon. members opposite.
I have posed the question as to who makes the profit when we have a decline in return to our agricultural producers.
The Liberals.

Well,
according to statistics issued by the Department of National Revenue for 1951 the entire packing industry in Canada made a net income of $7,552,000 or 30 per cent on the capital shares of the gross amount earned by the industry. I have already indicated that the market is very unstable under the present conditions and there is nothing to protect livestock producers. Part of their difficulty is due to the fact that these agricultural producers cannot sell their wheat. However, I do not think it is within the orbit of this discussion to go into that aspect of the problem in any detail, but I would like to point out to the house that during the eight-month period of August to March,
1952-	53 compared with the same period for
1953-	54 there was a 53,167,433 bushel drop in the amount of wheat marketed, and that has resulted in a drastic lowering in the income earned by the agricultural industry.
It is all very well for members of the government or anyone else to go around and say to the farmers, "That wheat in your bins is as good as money in the bank". During the Easter recess when I visited my own constituency I saw piles of grain amounting to as much as 4,000 bushels lying out exposed
