Livestock-Floor Prices to the weather. That should not be, and our farmers should have an income sufficient to allow them to bin that grain properly so that it is protected from the weather conditions in western Canada.
I would again point out to the government that due to the fact that our agricultural prices have dropped, and the fact that they cannot sell their grain, farmers today are not in a position to buy the building materials necessary to enable them to store their grain properly. I would therefore appeal to this government to consider this amendment so that our agricultural producers will have some protection. It will not be sufficient to undertake a scheme such as is now applied to the production of eggs where it is not the producer who is subsidized but the packer. A few years ago I consulted one of our local merchants and at that time I understood this government had a floor price for eggs. During that period there was no packing station. The local merchant collected his eggs and shipped them to the packers and he paid the farmer about 22 cents a dozen. I said to this merchant, "Well, I understood the government had a floor price for eggs". He replied: "We see nothing of that. These eggs are packed and shipped to the packer and this is all we get. There is no further payment and the price for which we sell these eggs is the only payment we receive". That sort of scheme will not be sufficient in this case and certainly was not sufficient in the case I have illustrated.
What we want is to see both consumer and producer protected. We do not want the packers to be able to hog all the profits.
They can take the squeal.

We
feel there could be set up in Canada the kind of organization suggested to this government by the various farm unions and organizations in Canada. I recall back in the period between 1945 and 1949 when I was in this house, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture appealed to the government to set up a national livestock marketing board. Since that time we have seen the growth of the farm union movement in Canada, and this movement now represents farmers in practically every province of Canada. Through their organizations the farmers have requested the federal government to set up a producer livestock board with producer representation under which the farmers would have some say in the marketing and control of their products.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say that many hon. members, at least on the other side of the house, do not seem to be particularly interested in this problem.


It is my belief that by next fall, unless some action is taken by the government, we will find the hog industry in a much more serious position than it is today. Today the farmer obtains a reasonable price but by next fall, unless the government is prepared to put a proper floor under hogs and beef cattle and relate that to the cost of production, we are going to have a very serious marketing situation throughout the entire hog industry.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to appeal to the government. During this session we have asked them to take cognizance of the fact that the farmer has not been able to sell his wheat. I recall during the last election campaign there appeared statements in a western newspaper attributed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Interviewed in one of the maritime provinces and questioned on the sale of Canadian wheat the minister said in effect that he did not think there would be any serious difficulty in marketing that wheat. He advised "if they got a hurry on" the wheat could be marketed. I am now asking the government to pick up its feet and take some action. I would urge them to get cracking on this very serious problem of formulating a program under which we can market our livestock profitably so that the producers of our farm livestock products and the consumer will be protected.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks let me say that we in this group do not like the way in which this amendment has been worded. On the other hand, we dislike even more the situation which is developing in this country in regard to agriculture. However, as we believe in the general principle of supporting agricultural prices at parity we will support this amendment for it at least guarantees a price equal to and not less than the parity price for livestock products.
I am not suggesting for one moment that in western Canada there is what one might call a real agricultural crisis. On the other hand, there are plenty of danger signals for those who are not too blind to see. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech pointed out that the price of agricultural products had fallen and that the net income for farmers during the past year had fallen by 14 per cent, while the net income of industries other than agriculture had risen by 8 per cent, leaving quite a disparity between agriculture and other industries.
If you take the fall in farmers' net income for the past two years you find there has been a drop of around 23 per cent. The question of the falling off in farmers' net income combined with the piling up of surpluses is causing a great deal of concern

to farmers and farm organizations. I am afraid that the Minister of Finance in his budget speech did not in any way remove that concern because he stated that government intervention would not be a cure for that situation. In order to meet the present situation he said it would be necessary for industry to increase their efficiency, to cut down their costs and to try to find new markets. On the other hand, he said that government intervention, in his opinion, was no cure for the situation.
Let us just examine those points he mentioned so far as agriculture is concerned. Let us first of all take the question of efficiency. Would anybody argue that agriculture today is not as efficient as, if not more efficient than other industries in this country? Let me quote what the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had to say in his address before the annual convention:
In our office Dr. Hope attempted to compare the efficiency of farmers with the efficiency of Canadian workmen as a whole. He took the years 1930 and 1950 and compared the value of production per worker in agriculture with the value of production over all workers and made appropriate adjustments to get the results in terms of constant dollars. His calculations turned out favourable to the farmer. He found that production per worker in the whole economy increased from $906 in 1930 to $1,688 in 1950

an increase of 86 per cent, while production per worker in agriculture increased from $357 in 1930 to $685 in 1950-an increase of 92 per cent.
Using that statement as a basis, I think one may well argue that agriculture is just as efficient as are other industries, if not more efficient.
As to the question of costs, there are many people perhaps who will think that the farmers are receiving prices well above their cost of production. If anybody is under that delusion, all he has to do is to read the speech that was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) before the food and agriculture organization dealing with this matter. I want to quote from that speech. It is reported in the Ottawa Journal of December 8. Speaking before the food and agriculture organization at Rome the Minister of Agriculture stated:
Our costs of production are very high. I do not think there is any country in the world today which can afford to buy some of our products at the prices our farmers must charge if they are to make a living.
After that statement nobody could argue that the farmers are receiving prices greater than the cost of production. The minister is there pointing out that our costs are so high that he is extremely doubtful whether people in other countries can afford to pay them.
Livestock-Floor Prices
What can we do in order to try to bring down the cost of production? I would say that government policies play an important part in relation to the cost of production. For instance, if the government were prepared to eliminate the 10 per cent sales tax they would be bringing about a considerable reduction in the cost of producing farm products in this country. Then if the government were prepared to restore the value of the Canadian dollar to the level at which it was a few years ago the farmers in this country would be in a much better position to meet the competition of other countries.
Today the Canadian dollar is above the value of the United States dollar. A few years ago it was held at 90 per cent of that of the United States dollar. As a result of that change the farmers are losing 18 cents a bushel on wheat alone. The same thing applies to all agricultural products. As a result of the government's policy in appreciating the Canadian dollar, the farmers of this country are severely penalized. Some may say: That is true of all exporting industries. That may be so; but there was at least one case where the government took steps to relieve an industry of the burden caused by the appreciation of the Canadian dollar. I have in mind the gold industry. We subsidize the gold industry to t*ie extent of about $10 million a year. This year I think it was $17 million. In the past five years we have subsidized it to the extent of over $50 million. When the subsidy was first paid, it was paid largely on account of the fact that we had appreciated the value of the Canadian dollar.
Can anyone argue that there is any justification today for maintaining the Canadian dollar above par with the United States dollar? What is supposed to determine the value of a nation's currency? The determining factor is supposed to be its purchasing power. How does the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar compare with that of the United States dollar? Obviously anyone who has travelled in the United States will know that the United States dollar has a higher purchasing power than has the Canadian dollar; that is to say, the United States dollar will buy more goods in the United States than the Canadian dollar will buy in Canada. On that basis, therefore, the Canadian dollar should be valued below the United States dollar.
Another matter that is supposed to decide whether a nation's currency should be appreciated or depreciated is the question of the balance of trade. For a number of years

Livestock-Floor Prices we have had an adverse balance of trade with the United States. Hence on that score you would expect the Canadian dollar to be valued below the United States dollar. The main reason the Canadian dollar is above par is that the United States is making heavy investments in this country. In other words you might say that the reason the Canadian dollar is above par is owing to speculation. The Canadian government, if they so desired, could easily control the Canadian dollar at 90 per cent of the United States dollar. In that way we would greatly help the exporters of this country-not only the farmers but all other exporters-to compete in the markets of the world. But so long as our currency is appreciated in value in the way it is we are having to face extremely unfair competition with those nations whose currency is depreciated below the United States dollar.
The next question that comes to mind is this: Are farmers justified in expecting the government to underwrite the price of agricultural products? I get sick and tired of reading newspapers in which the charge is made that the farmers are asking for a handout from the government. All the farmers are asking the government to do is to honour their obligations or the promises they have made in the past. The farmers have already paid in full for any help they might get in having agricultural prices stabilized.
Let me go back a few years; let me go back to the 1930's. We all remember how the prices of agricultural products then fell to extremely low levels. When the farm organizations asked the government to guarantee the prices of agricultural products in those years, we probably remember how they were told by the government that the government could do nothing because those prices were set by an international market; in other words, the farmers must sell at world prices. Hence during those years of the depression the farmers had to take extremely low prices for their products and, as a consequence, they went heavily in debt.
Then the war came along. Shortly after the beginning of the war the prices of agricultural products rose. Then shortly after, the government placed a ceiling on the prices of agricultural products. They told the farmers that they could not have world prices because those prices were too high. May I say that you cannot have it both ways. If the farmers had to take world prices during the depression, they were justified in asking for world prices when prices rose. However, when the government placed a ceiling on agricultural prices they told the farmers that this was part of a stabilization


program' under which they would guarantee to stabilize agricultural prices after the war. I remember that, some days ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce seemed to be extremely doubtful whether that guarantee had ever been made. I should therefore like to quote from a speech that was made by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King in a radio broadcast delivered on December 4, 1943:
I wish to thank the farmers of Canada for their magnificent contribution to the battle of production. I wish again to appeal to them to continue to help hold the front line against inflation by continuing to support the price ceiling. If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to ensure them against an agricultural depression after the war. As an essential part of its post-war policy, the government intends to ask parliament at the next session to place a floor under the prices of main farm commodities.
We all know that after the war the prices of farm products remained fairly high for a number of years. It is true that the government appeared to implement their promise by introducing the Agricultural Prices Support Act under which the government could guarantee farmers what you might call parity prices. In other words, they would step into the market and buy agricultural products when the prices fell below a level that would bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities. They were not required to take any action until 1949. In 1949 the first severe drop in agricultural prices took place involving hogs and one or two other commodities. The government did place a support price under hogs and some other commodities but the farm organizations were not satisfied with the support prices that were established.
I was at the convention in Niagara Falls in 1950 and the farm organizations asked the Minister of Agriculture what was the formula for establishing support prices. The Minister of Agriculture stated that they had a formula under which these support prices were established. He said that the formula was that they would support the price of agricultural products so their price would bear the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as had existed in the three years, 1943, 1944 and 1945. Since that time most of the support prices, with the exception of those applying to livestock, have been below that formula.
Of course wheat does not come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, but it is rather interesting to note that on the basis of that formula the price of wheat in 1951 should have been $2.53 a bushel. The price of wheat has of course been well below the price that would have been paid if the formula had applied to wheat. But, as I say,

with the exception of livestock prices, the support prices established by the government have been below the formula. I think the question that is worrying farmers today probably more than any other is to find out exactly what the government's policy is regarding support prices. The Minister of Agriculture has given farmers reason to believe that no support price is going to be established under livestock products. I have here a copy of the Western Producer of April 29, 1954 which contains an article referring to a press conference with the Minister of Agriculture. It is pointed out that the minister stated to the press that the federal government is not considering establishment of a support price of all livestock.
As a result of the fall in the prices of many farm products that has taken place, a great deal of interest is being shown in the establishment of marketing boards. I believe that enabling legislation has been set up in most provinces but up to the present such legislation has not been passed in the province of Alberta. In Alberta there is a very wide difference of opinion among farmers on this subject. Right at the present time quite a war is going on between one group of farmers and another as to whether or not marketing boards should be set up. The policy being followed by the province is that if the majority of the farmers appears to be in favour of marketing boards a plebiscite will be taken, and if two-thirds of the farmers are in favour of such boards no doubt enabling legislation will be passed.
I think there is a very good reason why the farmers of that province are somewhat leery about whether or not they would benefit under a marketing board for livestock or any other commodity. That reason is that the Minister of Agriculture has made it quite clear that if marketing boards are set up prices will be guaranteed not so much under the Agricultural Prices Support Act as under the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act, and that act does not guarantee any security at all for the farmers. It is true that the act provides that the government may guarantee an initial payment up to 80 per cent of the average price of the past three years, but the whole value of that is nullified by subsection 3 of section 3 which reads as follows:
An agreement made under subsection 1 may include a provision that the minister may on such notice as he deems fair and reasonable require that the delivery of an agricultural product to a cooperative association, processor or selling agency shall be discontinued with the result that the min-inister shall not be liable in respect of any agricultural product delivered to the co-operative association, processor or selling agency after such requirement.

That just means that if a serious fall in the price of any agricultural product takes place the government can relieve itself of any responsibility by instructing the board to refuse to accept any more of the commodity, and in that case the guarantee would disappear entirely. If we are going to have agricultural products marketing boards set up by the provinces, then we should have a guarantee from the government that they will provide support prices for those products under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. That is what the Agricultural Prices Support Act was set up for, in order to underwrite the prices of farm products. That guarantee was given by the former prime minister during the war. Is the government of today not prepared to live up to the guarantee given by the prime minister of this country during the war? If they are prepared to live up to it, it is time they made that quite clear to the farmers. If that were made clear to the farmers I think we would then find it a whole lot easier to establish these marketing boards because the farmers would know that if a marketing board was set up the initial payment could be made with safety without any danger of the marketing board finding itself in the very difficult position in which the wheat pool found itself in 1929, I believe.
We in this group believe in a two-price system for agriculture, and in view of the fact that about 95 per cent of all agricultural products with the exception of wheat are consumed in Canada we cannot see why the 5 per cent that is exported abroad should be allowed to determine the price of the other 95 per cent consumed in Canada. We feel that the government should guarantee parity prices for agricultural products consumed in Canada. The surplus could be exported abroad and sold for the very best price that could be obtained. We can no doubt help to find markets for our surplus goods by advancing credits to nations unable to pay for the goods they desire, or by being willing to accept their currency in payment.
But the point we want to emphasize is that the all-important market for agricultural products is the home market. In the final analysis the only market we have is the home market because imports brought into Canada in exchange for the exports we ship out have to be consumed in this country. The result is we have to be able to consume the total production of the country or the imports brought in in exchange for our exports. I do not think anybody would argue for one minute that we have anything like developed our own home market.
We have a tremendous potential market in this country. This potential market is

Livestock-Floor Prices represented by the thousands upon thousands of people in low income groups; the people in the old age pension brackets; the war veterans; the people with disabilities, all of whom are having to accept low incomes today. Then there are the unemployed. I know it has been argued, I believe by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), that a program of increased pensions for these people would be very costly. I wonder whether the government has ever stopped to calculate what it is costing the country to have half a million unemployed people?
Supposing the half a million unemployed people were earning a moderate income, say $2,400 a year or $200 a month. This would mean that we could be having in this country another $100 million a month in goods and services, another $1,200 million a year. Would that not more than offset the cost of paying a decent pension to the old age pensioners, the war veterans and the physically disabled? By paying a decent income to these people we would also stimulate the market for agricultural products. I do not think anyone will deny that the world needs expansion in the production of food, and that any surplus produce should be stored to take care of crop failures. Then in years when there were crop failures we would be able to draw upon our stored surplus to make food available to the nations needing it.
I believe that expanding the production of food would bring prosperity to the farmers, provided they were guaranteed fair prices. Let no one forget that as long as agriculture prospers, Canada will prosper because the people engaged in agriculture provide one of the very best markets for the products of other industries in this country.

I am
sorry, Mr. Speaker, but because I was in the agriculture committee this afternoon I did not hear the hon. members who took part in this particular debate. However, the two speakers whom I have heard tonight have laid a great deal of stress on the dangers facing agriculture in Canada today. I am fully cognizant of the dangers facing agriculture. As a matter of fact about two weeks ago last Friday, during the debate on the agriculture estimates, I believe I made that abundantly clear. I shall not, therefore, repeat anything that previous speakers have said concerning this difficulty or anything that I said at that time.
Although I am thoroughly cognizant of the dangers facing agriculture, I do not believe the solution proposed by this resolution is the answer. As a matter of fact.
[Mr. Quelch.l
the answer to most of our agricultural problems lies in expanded markets for our products. Our difficulties so far as the wheat surplus or what many prefer to call the "so-called surplus" is concerned lie in selling that wheat to people in other countries who could use it, as well as expanding the market for it within Canada. The same remarks would apply to livestock products. When we have sufficient market for our products we do not need to worry unduly about the price, and perhaps we do not need to worry unduly over putting in floor prices, as has been suggested here.
I feel that this resolution was prompted by very grave fears that exist in Canada today concerning what the future may hold for the livestock industry, and as to what may happen to the price of cattle and hogs particularly, the two main products of that industry. There has been a widespread demand, of course, amongst farmers for a long time for some system of floor prices in this country. This demand has been met to a limited extent. A floor price was established for hogs some time ago, and a floor has been established for butter. As I say, the demand has been met to some extent by floor prices under one product here and one product there, but there has been no general system of floor prices for agricultural products. There is undoubtedly a very strong demand amongst farmers in this country for some system of that sort.
In my opinion, if this resolution were put into effect it would be, more or less, complete socialization of the livestock industry. Most livestock producers of whom I am aware do not want their industry socialized. They want to have that industry remain on the basis of free enterprise. As a livestock producer myself for many years the last thing I want is to have control of the sale of my livestock taken completely out of my hands and put into the hands of a government or a board appointed by the government. As I say, most livestock producers want the same thing. The demand for a solution such as is proposed here, a socialized livestock industry, does not come from the majority of the farmers producing the majority of the livestock. There are no producers with reasonably sized livestock farms of whom I am aware who want a solution of this sort. The only people I have met who want a solution of this kind are the people who produce a very small amount of livestock, and I, personally, have met very few of them.
I am not going to go into the extremely complex subject of floor prices for agricultural products; what those floor prices should be, or the formula that should be used to arrive

Livestock-Floor Prices
at them. That is a matter upon which one might make a dozen speeches of the length to which we are limited in this house, and still not nearly exhaust the subject. In my opinion this particular proposal comes very close to being complete nonsense, and I think bears no relationship to any realistic conception of what the livestock industry is, what conditions are or anything of that sort. It merely says there should be a floor price put under cattle and hogs of not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31, 1953, a period of three years.
There are many people who would argue that during the early part of that period the price of hogs was too low, and now it is too high. There are other people who would argue that during the earlier part of that period the price of cattle was too high, and now it is too low. The idea of taking any particular three-year period and saying the average price of those three years should be the price for the next one or two years, does not take into account at all the present price of livestock feed stuffs or other important factors. Certainly, it is not the kind of formula that anyone who has made a real study of this matter would recommend. For those reasons, perhaps, the formula is not a reasonable or realistic yardstick to use. The whole purpose of this resolution, if carried into effect, would be to socialize the livestock industry. Personally, I oppose it, and oppose it very strongly.

When I looked across the way this evening and saw the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was not in his place, I wondered who would tell us the government's position concerning the resolution before the house. I think the speech delivered by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) has filled the bill very well, for the Minister of Agriculture; and it may not be necessary for the minister to make a rebuttal since, I imagine, he would be making about the same type of rebuttal as that made by the hon. member for Calgary North.
You had better let him speak for himself.

I think the speech delivered by the hon. member for Calgary North was ridiculous, foolish and downright silly. I have never heard anything quite so ridiculous in this House of Commons for a long time- and I am referring to his statement that the establishment of floor prices would result in the socialization of the livestock industry. Because I say to him that floor prices couldn't possibly result in the socialization of the livestock industry.

On a point of order; I must object to the hon. member's putting words in my mouth which were never there. I did not say that floor prices would result in the socialization of the industry; I said the effect of this whole resolution would result in that, if it were put into effect-but not floor prices. I went on to say that floor prices were themselves a big subject which I would not take the time of the house to discuss tonight.

A far bigger subject, I suggest, than the hon. member would be capable of dealing with. But I come back now to my statement, as to the remark he made in referring to this resolution, when he said that it would mean the socialization of the livestock industry; and I say that that remark was completely foolish.

And that is another silly question-it is perfectly silly.

I will answer it then. I will say that so far as I am concerned, the livestock industry as it is now operated and managed by the producers of livestock is the best possible system for the livestock industry. To my mind it is a system that should be preserved, and this government should not allow farmers to go into bankruptcy because it has failed to act under the powers of any one of three statutes now on the statute books, and which could be used to provide floor prices to deal with this situation.
I come back now to the terms of the amendment, and the suggestion that if it were implemented it would result in the socialization of the livestock industry. We have in the United States right now, operated by a Republican government, a government that is not too often criticized by members of the Conservative party in Canada, a system of parity floor prices established under the main agricultural commodities in the United States.
And what a headache that is!
Someone interjects by stating, "What a headache that is!" Well, I would far rather be a farmer in the United States-
Go ahead, then.

-with the headache of receiving more than $2 a bushel for wheat, and floor prices under all the main agricultural

Livestock-Floor Prices commodities than a farmer in Canada producing under a total lack of adequate legislation and adequate floor prices for the livestock industry, as we see it under this government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It gives a headache even a doctor could not cure.

If this amendment we have suggested would result in the socialization of the livestock industry then all I can say is that the Americans socialized their livestock industry years ago, because they have adequate floor prices and adequate parity prices.
The Minister of Agriculture believes in floor prices. During the transitional period from war to peace he has had legislation placed on the statute books for the support of agricultural prices. Under that legislation prices can be supported. Then we know that there is an act to provide for the establishment of an agricultural products board. He could establish floor prices under that act. Then if he did not like the way those two acts read, he could turn to chapter 5 of the statutes to assist and encourage in the cooperative marketing of agricultural products.
The Minister of Agriculture has three separate statutes under which he could do the very thing advocated in this amendment. Of course he likes to have all kinds of legislation to confuse people, and then do nothing about it. For many years western agricultural producers fought to get orderly marketing of their farm commodities. In spite of the many speeches delivered against the principle of orderly marketing, speeches such as the one delivered tonight by the hon. member for Calgary North, they have been successful in obtaining the Canadian wheat board. I submit the wheat board is an outstanding body providing for the marketing of wheat and other grains in an orderly fashion.
The Canadian wheat board establishes an initial price, which acts as a floor price. Yet it has no more socialized the wheat producers of western Canada than in my judgment this amendment would result in the socialization of the livestock producers.
If I were considering the kind of policy we should adopt in relation to the livestock industry one of the first things I would do would be to read the resolutions passed by the various farm organizations. The Saskatchewan wheat pool in its outlined future policy states in its annual report on page 49, and this is the seventh plank in that policy:
Increased use of the Agricultural Prices Support Act as a means of providing adequate support prices for those farm commodities to which the act applies.


8. The establishment of support prices on all livestock marketed through licensed stockyards.
That is exactly what we are attempting to have done by pressing this motion. We are attempting to have a floor price set on livestock and to have greater use made of the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
At this time the farm unions of western Canada have taken great interest in the idea of marketing boards, and have established in Manitoba, and I believe also in Saskatchewan, an interim marketing board. It is their hope that they will be able to handle livestock and receive from the federal government support in the way of adequate support prices underwriting the operations of those livestock boards. I hold in my hand the Western Producer for Thursday, April 29. In it is outlined the result of a very successful conference held in Saskatoon regarding the establishment of a livestock board. An interim livestock board was established, and here are the members of that board: Mr. E. A. Boden, Cutknife, prominent hog breeder and wheat pool director for district 12, who will serve in an individual capacity; Mrs. Eric Lund, Borden, S.F.U., woman director; Don Griffin, farmer, Alameda; Jim Gray, S.F.U. official, Saskatoon; Percy Wright, Tisdale, former C.C.F. member of parliament for Melfort, and Fred Messenger, Kelvington, vice-president of the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities.
The board is headed by a chairman, Mr. Speaker, who is well known to members on both sides of the house, a former colleague in this house, Mr. Percy Wright of Tisdale. I suggest that the honour that was bestowed on Mr. Wright by selecting him as chairman of the board demonstrates something that all of us who have been associated with Mr. Wright over the years have come to know, namely, that he is an extremely able person and was the very best choice in my opinion that this conference could make to head the interim livestock board. I do not have the press report here, but I understand that an interim board has been established in Manitoba and that Mr. Scottie Bryce, an able former colleague, is a member of that board. Scottie, by being back closely associated with the livestock industry, is once again engaged in the work that has been so dear to him throughout his lifetime.
The establishment of those interim boards by the farmers' unions in western Canada, supported as they are by farm unions in Ontario to British Columbia, demonstrates that the livestock producers of Canada want orderly marketing through livestock boards, and further desire that adequate support prices be placed under livestock. I might say

in this regard that the report of the conference in the Western Producer states of Mr. Phelps:
He reported that S.F.U. officials had held a successful conference with federal agriculture minister J. G. Gardiner the previous day. The minister, said Mr. Phelps, had promised that if a producers' board were established, the federal government will provide-
And this is very interesting:
-financial guarantees under the Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939 to enable payment of an initial price. Mr. Gardiner had also promised consideration of a national board of livestock commissioners.
However, it is perfectly correct, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) pointed out, that in the same issue of the Western Producer the Minister of Agriculture is reported as having said that there will be no financial assistance from the federal government. All I can say is that that proves to me at any rate that the Minister of Agriculture was in Saskatoon and discussed with two different sets of people the question of some financial support for the livestock industry. He is now able to get up in the house, or in any other place, depending which side of the argument he takes at the moment-he may take his pick as to which part of the Western Producer of April 29 he decides to quote- and prove that the government is either going to support financially the livestock marketing boards or he can demonstrate that the government has no intention of providing such financial support. I am hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that since the president of the Saskatchewan farmers' union says that the Minister of Agriculture did say to him that the federal government would provide financial support for livestock marketing boards that commitment of the Minister of Agriculture will be fulfilled.
We want marketing boards; we want financial support for the livestock products that are marketed by those boards. If such floors were provided, then the statistics I have before me show that such a proposal would provide a floor price for good steers, basis Toronto, $26.50 a hundred. I would say that for an average grade steer in the various parts of Canada it would result in something under 20 cents a pound live weight. I suggest that such a floor price is fair and moderate and will give the producer a reasonable return but nothing more. The floor price under hogs would be $29.65 a hundred for grade B1 hogs at Toronto. I suggest that such a floor price under hogs is reasonable and would keep the price of hogs in fair relationship with the stated support price for cattle. I am hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that all members representing rural constituencies and agricultural ridings will give this
Livestock-Floor Prices motion very serious consideration so that the agricultural producers of Canada may make further progress in their battle for orderly marketing and stability, and may make one further step toward obtaining the same kind of stability that the United States farmer has now enjoyed for a great many years.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

I have a word or two on this matter, Mr. Speaker, which is of particular importance to Canadian agriculture. Most of the arguments have already been made in support of the establishment of a livestock marketing board for Canada and something being done in these days to see that the Canadian people, both producers and consumers, get the same kind of a fair deal.
There are very few people in Canada, and certainly one would not realize it if he listened to the debates in this house, who are familiar with the extent of the livestock marketing industry in Canada. Figures show that it is in volume of gross value of business done the second largest business in the whole of Canada, surpassed only by the pulp and paper industry. However in this industry hundreds of thousands of farmers, and millions of Canadian people indirectly, are involved in the producers' side of this business, and practically every Canadian family is very directly affected from the consumers' side of the question. Therefore I consider that from the standpoint of importance to the Canadian people there is no industry which requires more of the attention of the people than does the livestock industry at the present time. More and more people depend for their livelihood upon the livestock industry, and the cost of living for everyone generally is seriously affected by the amount charged for meat and meat products. There are all kinds of by-products, margarine, animal fat, oil, bone meal, fertilizer, hides-
Bologna.

If that is a by-product then we are seriously affected by it in this house. The sales of Canadian produce in Canada in 1950 amounted to $757 million. In 1951 they went up to $892 million and-an interesting fact which reveals the trend in Canada and which every Canadian interested in agriculture and livestock production should realize -our exports of livestock are dwindling very rapidly. The Canadian producer is becoming more and more dependent upon the returns he receives from livestock as years go by. In 1947 about 23 per cent of Canada's production of livestock was exported; in 1948

Livestock-Floor Prices only 22 per cent was exported, and in 1949-50 13 per cent. The following year it fell to 10 per cent, and gradually but eventually we are losing our livestock markets abroad. If that trend continues Canadians are going to be in a very difficult position with regard to our export position.
The one danger, and the one evident factor in the situation today which causes the Canadian people, particularly organized agriculture, to ask for a livestock marketing board, is the fact that competitive markets are disappearing. There are 155 slaughtering plants in Canada, 61 concentrated in Ontario and about 37 in Quebec with the remainder in other provinces, and three large firms control 60 per cent of the entire business. Even the royal commission which investigated prices underlined this in the report they issued for consideration by Canadians and by the Canadian parliament. They said, and I quote:
. . . the processing-
That is meat packing.
-industry shows a high degree of concentration. The three largest firms account for about 60 per cent of the total inspected slaughterings in Canada, which would indicate that competition operates within a fairly restricted framework, though there may be considerable rivalry among these firms. These large firms are efficient in their operations and, though realizing small profits per unit of output, earn substantial returns on their investment, The very heavy capital investment required, together with decreasing cost ratio as the scale of the business expands, tends to keep additional competitors from entering the field.
What the Canadian producers are asking for in almost every one of the briefs and through every one of their farm organizations is that there should be a livestock board established in Canada to see that adequate and proper prices are maintained for the producer, and to see that there is not a wide disparity between what the farmer receives and what the producer has to pay.
Prior to 1950-51 western farmers received for a good steer around $250. Today the average price for a good steer is down to between $100 and $120, but there has been no corresponding decline in the price paid by the Canadian consumer. These large firms which control to a large extent both the price the farmer receives and the price the consumer pays rush out stories to demonstrate the very small margin they receive per pound of beef on each of the groups going through their plants, but they have not yet explained to the satisfaction of the Canadian people why there should be this wide disparity between the price they had to pay for meat products three years ago and the price they have to meet today.
The producer is receiving less and less in actual return and that is why he wants an
[Mr. Castleden.l
adequate marketing board. They have no bargaining power whatsoever with the few large firms which buy their commodity. The farmer is in their power and all these firms have to do is to refrain from coming to any formal agreement as to the price. By adopting that method they avoid any violation of the anti-combines act.
Today the pressure on agriculture is becoming more and more severe. When the farmer received a good price for his wheat he could afford to leave the livestock industry to those who were interested, particularly when the amount of return he was likely to receive did not appear attractive to him. But today, when he cannot deliver his grain, when he is cut off from deliveries to the extent in 1954 of about 130 to 140 million bushels, he has to depend to a larger and larger extent on the sale of his livestock.
But cattle prices have tumbled to a terrific extent and the only thing left to him, as has already been pointed out here this evening, is the hog industry. The farmer is now turning more and more to the good prices he can receive today for his hogs. The result has been that at the present time, and government statistics will bear this out, the farmer is turning more and more to raising hogs in the hope that the present prices will be maintained.
However, the fact is that these prices cannot possibly be maintained without a much larger consumption, particularly in view of the fact that Canada's export market for hogs has virtually disappeared and the Canadian people practically constitute the only consumers. Under these circumstances the important thing is to guarantee Canadian producers some decent return for their produce, grant them some form of stability and security in prices. Nothing could do more to guarantee a greater security to the producers of this country than the establishment of a livestock marketing board. Under such an arrangement the farmer would feel satisfied that in accepting a price for his meat he is not contributing to a monopoly in the industry which is allowed to go on at the present time, as it has been for a number of years, without giving an account of its stewardship to the producers and consumers of Canada.
In this connection I would point out that the one thing which has satisfied the western farmers in Canada and given them some hope for the future has been the establishment of the wheat board under which orderly marketing of his produce is guaranteed, and under which he is today protected from the

kind of competition he had to face in the Winnipeg grain exchange. The Winnipeg grain exchange enjoyed that competition, but the farmer in effect was being fleeced year after year. The wheat board now undertakes this marketing of the farmers' produce. It is taken in, graded properly, and the board handles the selling of that commodity either on the home or export market. But whatever the price the farmer receives for his produce, whether it be for grain or anything else, it is the actual price less the cost of handling. He sees today an extremely wide spread between that practice and the one which is operating with him with his livestock produce, and this request is uniform throughout the producers.	,
You will find the same thing coming from producers everywhere that they can possibly get organized to discuss their problem. The basic principle of the livestock marketing board is accepted by the producers of the west and the producers of the east. A livestock marketing board is one thing which will restore some confidence in the hearts of the producers and give to Canadians some assurance that they are not being exploited by those who are able to take control of a commodity, buy whatever they wish at whatever the market can stand for the stuff they get, process it into a commodity for all the Canadian people and then sell it to the Canadian people for whatever price the market will bear. That kind of thing must be eliminated in Canada. We call upon every member of this house, by his vote on this resolution, to show what he thinks of it.

Mr. Speaker, to hear our friends to my left in the C.C.F. group talking about their theory of how you are going to market beef in this country is certainly not an eye-opener to those of us who have been sitting here for a few years. We have shipyard workers in my part of the country who are out of work. Maybe our friends can suggest some method they know, tried and true, that will put those men to work. They like to pick at and pull apart good industries in the Dominion of Canada who are doing a great service to this country. I am sick and tired of that sort of thing. Have they offered one suggestion by means of which to market the farm beef after it leaves the farm? They like to forget all about the trials and tribulations connected with the handling of the beef until the time it reaches the consumer. Is it the great packers who rob the public, as they have been accused of doing? Is it the retail butcher?
Livestock-Floor Prices
Some farmers are not satisfied with beef prices today. Nobody is ever satisfied with the price at which he sells his commodities. But let us have some honest reasoning from these people here rather than the pulling of people down and the tearing apart of great industries. I have not a share of stock nor have I ever had one in any great marketing organization for meat products; but I hate to sit here and listen to these people being torn apart when they do not deserve it. The farmers in my part of the country would not stand for it. They would not jump into a marketing board as quickly as some of these people suggest until these people here to my left-these great theorists-can tell us how to market the beef after it leaves the farm, how to keep the prices up and how to make me or anyone else eat more beef. Who makes the profit? Is it our butchers? The local butchers slaughter in my own home town. They are not growling. They are fairly friendly with the farmers. I hear many farmers say they would like 34 cents a pound but they also say that they are not doing too badly at 24 cents. What I believe they need-and what I should like to see them have-are parity prices for farmers. But I certainly do not think the time has come when we can tell these fellows who talk like the great Socrates to take over from coast to coast, because none of them, I think, has much business experience.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?
What about the wheat board?

I should like to remind my friend that the wheat board cannot compel export buyers to buy wheat in Canada. The surplus is just one of those things we are troubled with. We would all like to sell this wheat at $2.25 a bushel. Maybe they could tell us where the market is. There is no market at the present time. They cannot tell us where they are going to get a market.
It is better than the grain exchange.
Tell us your system. You tell us.
I am not talking much about something I do not know anything about.

The
amendment that we have before the house at the present time I consider to be an extremely important one. I have listened to the discussion thus far this evening with a great deal of interest. Unfortunately I am in the same position as that of the hon. member
4812	HOUSE OF
Livestock-Floor Prices for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness). I was absent from the chamber this afternoon because of my duties on the agriculture committee and therefore did not hear the discussion that took place in a preliminary way on this amendment. I understand that as yet there has been no statement from the government side of the house on this subject. I think that is an unfortunate situation because it is a matter which is important to the farmers generally and particularly to the livestock producers. The fact that so much enthusiasm and almost emotion has been generated in our discussion this evening would suggest that it is a highly important subject and, at the same time, an extremely controversial one.
I rise to say a few words on the subject because some reference has been made to certain discussions going on in my own province of Manitoba at the present time concerning the matter of setting up a producers livestock marketing board. As I have listened to the references in this chamber to the discussions on this matter that have taken place in Manitoba, the impression I have received is that the farmers generally are in support of the marketing board proposal that is before them at the present time. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is far from being the case. Although I have not been home in the province during these discussions, as I read the press reports from various parts of my own constituency as well as from neighbouring constituencies it would appear that discussion of the proposed producers livestock marketing board that is at present before the livestock producers of my province is producing just as much heated controversy, I might say, as we have seen generated in this chamber this evening.
As a matter of fact, the present plan has been repudiated by the majority of livestock producer groups in the province because it is too compulsory and, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Calgary North, it approximates socialized marketing. Among the groups who have not given their support to the plan are the Manitoba pools, which in a largely attended meeting in the city of Brandon just a few weeks ago, while supporting the broad principle of producer marketing boards, opposed to the extent of 90 per cent the proposal that has been put forward by the Manitoba farmers union. Also the Manitoba cattle producers association is opposed to the present plan.
As a result of the controversy that has arisen, the livestock farmers have organized themselves into a voluntary association which they have named the independent livestock producers association. They are moving


throughout the province at the present time, holding very enthusiastic meetings, in order to arouse the farmers of the province to the dangers that are inherent in the compulsory plan that has been put forward and to which I think the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) referred to as being a plan generally acceptable to the livestock producers of Manitoba. I have before me certain of the proposals contained in the plan that has been presented, and to demonstrate their compulsory nature I shall read one or two excerpts. First of all there is this provision:
The hoard shall have all the powers of a body corporate and, within the province, shall have power to regulate and control in any or all respects the marketing of the regulated product, including the prohibition of such marketing in whole or in part and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, shall have the following powers . . .
Then a long series of powers is set out. I should like to refer to paragraph (c) of the official document, which reads as follows:
To prohibit in whole or in part the marketing of any grade or class of the regulated product of any kind or variety thereof.
Paragraph (h) reads as follows:
To seize, remove and dispose of any of the regulated products marketed in violation of any order of the board and retain or otherwise dispose of the proceeds thereof.
I think that will serve to give some idea of why the majority of livestock producers of my province are so vehemently opposing the plan for a producers' marketing board that has been put before them at this time. While saying that, I must reiterate that from time to time during recent years strong support has been voiced for the principle of a producers' marketing board in the field of livestock. With such widespread general support, it is unfortunate that a proposal has cropped up which has tended to disturb the livestock producers and caused them to repudiate the scheme to the overwhelming extent that I have already indicated. Returning to the amendment before us it reads as follows:
In the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951, to December 31, 1953.
The language is very vague. First of all it makes reference to the broad principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards. Then, having thus sponsored the idea of marketing boards, it moves on to emphasize floor prices based on a certain production period. No one can say whether prices during that period were average, above average or below average. Because of this I would be interested in hearing some

spokesman from the government side outline their attitude toward the amendment now before the house. It deals with an important topic of a highly controversial nature. The farmers in my own province are aroused, and before we jump off the deep end and give our support to a measure as important as this I think there should be some clarification from official government sources.

Mr. Speaker, because of the illness of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, I did not vote.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
