speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the committee is aware, since the budget I have received a large number of representations from members of the house and others regarding paragraph 6 of the income tax resolution which deals with the tax status of mutual insurance companies in the fire and casualty field. I might explain that this paragraph does not introduce new policy with regard to the tax treatment of mutuals but is intended merely to enable past policy, adopted in 1946, to be continued.
In the representations made to me by members of parliament and others it has been emphasized that by far the great majority of the companies affected by this policy are small local companies insuring farm property where there is no organized fire protection. They are not in competition with the ordinary profit-making insurance companies. In fact it is claimed that they are compelled to provide this service in their communities for themselves owing to the reluctance of ordinary companies to enter this field.
In the light of these representations I have reviewed the results of the study of this situation by the McDougall commission. After careful consideration of all the facts placed before them the members of the royal commission recommended:
That the income of any insurer, mutual or otherwise, shall not be liable to taxation when in any year the net premium income in Canada is derived, to the extent of not less than 50 per cent thereof, from the insurance of farm property and other property not protected by municipal or other firefighting organizations, or is derived wholly from the insurance of churches, schools, or other religious, educational and charitable institutions.
I am prepared to accept the general principle of this recommendation and I am now suggesting an amendment to the income tax resolution recognizing this general recommendation. The McDougall recommendation dealt mainly with farm insurance. The amendment I am proposing deals likewise with fishermen and applies the same general rule to insurers giving protection to their property.
I would therefore ask one of my colleagues to move:
That the resolution to amend the Income Tax Act be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
7. For the exemption from taxation for the 1954 and subsequent taxation years of insurers, not less than 50 per cent of whose gross premium income was in respect of the insurance of farm property, property used in fishing or residences of farmers or fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I so move.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest if the amendment is adopted that it be discussed with the resolution when it is called later, if that meets with the approval of the committee.

I would merely like to say that, while one always wants to study carefully the full effect of what is proposed by way of relief, I think that prima facie, at any rate, those who have been appealing to the minister will view with satisfaction what has been done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The resolution with regard to the Excise Tax Act. Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, there is
another matter in relation to the resolution respecting amendment of the Excise Tax Act to which I should like to refer. It is not a new matter. It was discussed extensively a year ago when the budget resolutions were before the committee of ways and means on March 31, 1953. The matter was also referred to briefly on that previous occasion, May 4 this year, when the house began its review of the budget resolutions.
The matter I should like to mention, sir, is not to be found in the resolution as such. My purpose is to express regret that no action has been taken by the Minister of Finance in regard to the matter. I refer specifically to the need for extending the exemption from sales and excise taxes to those charitable and welfare organizations that are not now exempt from such impositions.
I believe that it would come as a profound shock to many people in this country to realize that the federal government is levying substantial taxes upon welfare and charitable organizations, engaged in work that commands the respect of all citizens and commands, I hope, the active support of all of us in this house. The fact of the matter is that, with some exceptions, charitable organizations in general are not exempted from the full effect of the sales and excise taxes levied by the federal government.
These organizations exist in large measure, and are enabled to carry on their beneficent work, only because generous citizens contribute to their support. They do not receive assistance from the federal government. Whatever assistance they receive from governmental sources comes at the municipal level. Most of them function entirely upon assistance received from charitably disposed citizens. Yet the federal government is applying to organizations of this kind, engaged in work of the highest value to this nation, the full weight of these heavy sales and excise taxes.
In the year 1950 the house did give some relief in this field by amending the Excise Tax Act to exempt from those taxes otherwise levied under that act certain definite charitable organizations. The group so defined 83276-305
Excise Tax Act
is altogether too narrow in its scope. There was not, as I recall it, any opposition in this house to the amendment then to the Excise Tax Act. The criticism that was made at that time was that the exemption was being extended to an altogether too narrow group of charitable organizations. The group defined by the 1950 amendment is as follows:
(a)	a bona fide public institution whose principal purpose is to provide permanent or semi-permanent shelter and care for children or aged, infirm or incapacitated persons who reside in the institution; and
(b)	in receipt annually of aid from the government of Canada or a province for the maintenance of persons specified in paragraph (a).
The exemption, of course, applies only in the event of purchases by such organizations of goods for their own use, and not for resale. In anything I have to say today on this subject I am confining my request to circumstances under which charitable organizations purchase goods for their own use and not for resale.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, how very narrow is the relief extended by that 1950 amendment. It does not include the vast majority of organizations in this country engaged in charitable and philanthropic work. It does not, for instance, include welfare agencies that, in the bulk, constitute the membership of the various community chests of the larger cities of this country. It does not include, for instance, children's aid assistance, family welfare agencies, the various visiting nurses associations, community chests and welfare councils. My submission to this committee is that this principle ought to be extended to the full scope of all charitable organizations that have a well organized existence.
There may be some charitable organizations that are not sufficiently organized to have established their identity, with the prospect of continued existence, to satisfy any reasonable government demand. But I am dealing in the main here with organizations with well established positions, permanent in their nature, and undertaking to do that work which, unhappily in many cases, is bound to be virtually permanent in its nature.
In 1950 the house recognized the principle of exempting certain charitable organizations. By what authority, by what logic, upon what principle, does the government or this house stop at that point and deny other charitable and philanthropic organizations the same kind of exemption? I make bold to say that if the people of this country fully realized the present situation, the public conscience would be shocked to think that the federal government

Excise Tax Act
is dipping into the treasury of organizations functioning with funds contributed by charitably disposed citizens, dipping its big hand into the coffers of those organizations whose only source of revenue is charitable donations.
Let us remember always that these excise and sales taxes are hidden taxes. In the main, those who pay them are not aware that they are paying them. They are levied at the manufacturers' or producers' level. The consumer has no knowledge of the proportion of the price that he pays that goes to pay these federal taxes. Let us remember as well, sir, that because these taxes are levied at the manufacturers' level they attract mark-ups as they pass from hand to hand through the wholesaler, the jobber and the retailer. A tax that starts out at the manufacturers' level at 10 per cent in most cases has doubled itself in the course of these mark-ups applied by those who are handling the goods before they ultimately reach the consumer. In the case of most of these goods it is no exaggeration to say that what the consumer is paying is ordinarily closer to 20 per cent than 10 per cent.
The public, I am sure, has only been lulled into the position in which it is today on this matter by reason of the fact that these taxes are hidden. How much is the government taking out of the pockets of charitable organizations in this country through these sales and excise taxes? Well, nobody knows. There has been no nation-wide estimate prepared. The government does not segregate that portion of its sales and excise revenues that are collected from charitable and welfare organizations. I may say that a study was made a year ago by the Canadian Welfare Council in an endeavour to ascertain, as far as might be possible with the sources of information available, what might be estimated to be the amount collected in a year through the sales tax from charitable organizations. I think it will astound members of this House of Commons who have not seen the figure before when they are told that the result of that inquiry by the Canadian Welfare Council was an estimate that the amount of sales tax collected by the federal government in one year from charitable organizations in this country was in excess of $500,000.
The work these organizations are doing commands the respect and admiration of us all. I am sure each member of the house in his own way and according to his own means is trying to contribute to the assistance of these charitable and welfare organizations. How then do we as members of the house justify the imposition by the federal government of taxation upon these organizations?
I hope we are not going to be told by the

government that there are administrative difficulties in the way. That old excuse has been worn threadbare by this government.
I submit there could not be any administrative difficulty involved in the proposal I am submitting to the house today that was not already involved in the amendment the house approved in 1950. The same problems exist; the difficulties are in no way different in kind.
I, for one, am convinced that if in the face of any administrative difficulty that might be suggested the government would apply to that difficulty the same kind of ingenuity they apply to many other fields, particularly in the levying of taxation, any administrative difficulty could be overcome quickly and effectively.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, while it is evident that the government is not going to do anything about the problem this year- because there is no provision in the budget resolutions to deal with it-I wish to say that I deplore the fact that the government is taking no action in the budget this year. And I say to them that before another year rolls round I would hope that the government's conscience will be roused in this matter, and that it will set itself resolutely to removing what is a crying and cruel injustice.
Sir, this is not a small matter. It is not a small matter in its scope; much less can it be said to be a small matter in the principle involved. Therefore I am appealing to the conscience of the government in the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter the hon. member for Eglinton has now spoken about is one I indicated on May 5 I would like to raise when we reached a later stage, possibly that of second reading of the bill. However, as the parliamentary assistant realizes, my reason for making that suggestion on May 5 was to facilitate the passing of the resolution on that day, if possible. Since that was not done I see no reason why we should not have a full discussion now, and I am glad the point has been raised again by the hon. member for Eglinton.
As I said, when I made reference to the question on May 5, as reported at pages 4447 and 4448 of Hansard, the subject was pretty well covered on March 31 last year in speeches made by the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Spadina and myself. One of my reasons for indicating last year's Hansard reference when I spoke on May 5 was so that the parliamentary assistant might be prepared to deal with the question on a later occasion. I hope he is now ready to deal with it; and I also hope that that does

not mean that he is only ready to say no. I would hope that at this time more favourable consideration would be given to the requests from the charitable organizations which have been made to the government on several occasions through the Canadian Welfare Council.
As the hon. member for Eglinton has just pointed out, there is no way of estimating accurately the total amount of sales tax collected from these charitable organizations and institutions; but it has been estimated that something more than half a million dollars is being collected annually from those agencies which come under what are known as community chests.
Those who have been interested in the matter have tried to address themselves to the difficulties raised by the department. I believe it is correct to say they have gained the impression that the main problem raised by the government is the administrative one. Addressing themselves to that objection, the Canadian Welfare Council has made certain specific suggestions to the government as to how the administrative problem might be handled. It seems to me the suggestions they have made could form a basis upon which the question could be handled.
They suggest that in order to qualify for the exemption from sales tax any charitable organization should be one certified by the Department of National Health and Welfare as a bona fide social welfare agency. They suggest also that it might be required that any such charitable organization should be one to which donations are permitted as income tax deductions. Then there are one or two other qualifications to which these people are prepared to agree in order to assist the government in working out the administrative details.
I share the views expressed by the hon. member for Eglinton as to the vicious nature of this tax. The hon. member has expressed himself in his usual strong language concerning this procedure of imposing a sales tax on purchases made by these various charitable organizations, and it is not necessary for other hon. members to repeat what he has said. However, I do press upon the parliamentary assistant and, through him, upon the government the reasonableness and the responsibility with which the Canadian Welfare Council and others who are interested have made their requests to the government. I would impress upon the parliamentary assistant the fact that these people have set out specific proposals and have suggested specific qualifications that might be laid down. I support 83276-305i
Excise Tax Act
wholeheartedly their appeal for the extension of sales tax refunds to these bona fide charitable organizations.
I fully realize the hon. member for Spadina is not in his seat at the moment because he is actively involved in the deliberations of one of the five or six committees meeting today. I mention his name, however, because I am sure if he were in the house this afternoon when this matter is being discussed he would support this year, as he did last, the representations being made.
Earlier this afternoon we had an example of the Minister of Finance paying some attention to representations made to him after the bringing down of his budget. I hope that will not be the only example in this session. I would hope that consideration might be given to these representations and that even yet the necessary amendment might be made to the budget resolutions to provide sales tax exemptions for the benefit of these charitable organizations.

I do not know whether the parliamentary assistant wishes to answer the particular question asked at the moment. If he does not, I should like to say a few words on this legislation. With the minor tax reductions which have been made under the act, I am in accord, but I am sure the parliamentary assistant will forgive me if I say they are completely inadequate. There is no tax that is pleasant; but, as I see it, these hidden taxes that hit the taxpayer when he is not looking are particularly insidious. Last year, although most Canadians failed to realize it, the government collected about $115 from each citizen in indirect taxes. That amounts to about $575 for a family of five. There is an excuse for hidden taxes of that size in wartime, but I cannot see where there is any justification for them in peacetime. The collection of such a large proportion of our taxes by the indirect method is unhealthy to our economy for a number of reasons. In the first place, these excise taxes bear most heavily on the people in the lower income tax groups. In other words, this taxation is not based on ability to pay. For example in purchasing a car, a poor man, or a man in the lower income tax group, must pay the same amount of tax as a wealthier citizen. Such a principle in taxation is not sound.
In the second place, I feel that these excise taxes are discriminatory because they tend to penalize some industries selling in the consumer market, as compared with others. For instance, our automobiles today have a 15 per cent higher tax imposed on them than

Excise Tax Act
furs. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, the automobile industry is one industry that should have been given some kind of tax relief under this bill we are discussing today. The automobile is certainly not a luxury. A modern car is part of our Canadian way of life. Yet during the past fiscal year, the government collected from the automobile industry in sales tax and excise tax $162 million. That amount of money was actually more than the automobile industry paid out in wages. Surely, there is something wrong when a situation of this nature can occur. I say that this level of taxation on the automobile industry is discrimination of the worst kind, which simply cannot be justified. There are about 200,000 persons in Canada engaged in producing automobiles and supplying the automotive industry. In keeping this excise tax of 15 per cent on automobiles today, the government is gambling with the future of thousands of working people in that industry.
In the third place, I think it is fairly obvious that these excise tax levies are keeping up prices in many fields unnecessarily. In the fourth place, I think this deceptive form of taxation is poisonous to our democratic way of life. Today there is not one taxpayer in Canada out of a hundred who has even the faintest idea of the amount of tax he is paying each year to this federal government. The average citizen seems to feel that he, at least, is not the one who is paying very much of the nation's tax burden. Many citizens seem to be confident that it is the corporations or the wealthier citizens of this country who are paying most of the federal taxes. Because of that attitude, they often have no hesitation in asking the government for bigger and better federal spending projects. As I see it, those citizens are mistaken. Today it is the Canadian consumer, directly or indirectly, who is shouldering the bulk of the tax load. Today the average citizen is paying 33 cents out of every dollar he earns to one government or the other, whether it is federal, provincial or municipal. But unfortunately, because many of our people cannot see their federal tax which is absorbed in retail prices, they remain blissfully ignorant of the astronomical figures involved in this federal budget that we are now discussing.
I for one do not believe that any tax should be relatively painless. Every citizen should realize the amount of money he is paying in federal taxes. He should realize that every time he makes a our chase today the government is dipping into his pocket. He should realize that no matter how low his income may be, he is still contributing to the cost of governing this country.
fMr. Thatcher.]
I know that today it would not be feasible for the government to wipe out all excise taxes; but failing that, I suggest it would be a great forward step if manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers were required to label their goods in such a manner that the federal tax would be shown separately and distinctly. Then, when a citizen went to purchase a new car, a refrigerator or clothing he would see how much he was actually paying in federal taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member do that in his business?
No, but I think it would be a very good idea if all retailers did so on a nation-wide basis.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member not know that he has the privilege of doing that? I do not want to interfere with his business. Perhaps it is none of my business, but I should be quite surprised if the hon. member did not mark up his goods with the tax included, and take his profit on both.

The minister need not be so touchy. I made a suggestion which I thought might be a good one. If he does not wish to carry it out, of course that is his privilege. But I suggest it would be a good thing not only for citizens generally, but also for the minister, if it were required that taxes be shown on sales tickets. If such a procedure were followed the citizen would comprehend much more clearly that before any government can spend a dollar or give away a dollar, it must first of all collect that dollar in taxes. If the citizen realized that the dollar which was being spent might be his own, he would exercise greater care in the future in making demands on the government. Most citizens under those circumstances would regulate their demands for government spending, in accordance with their willingness to pay taxes. In other words, I think that such a policy would make citizens more tax conscious and more government conscious. I repeat, Mr. Chairman. in my opinion the government today, in collecting 34 per cent of its revenue by the backdoor method, is making a serious error. If they continue to do so, there may be repercussions in the future.

Since the Minister of Finance brought down his budget on April 6 I have had some correspondence from members of the soft drink industry, and I hope the committee will not mind my mentioning the soft drink industry because it is of that industry that I have some knowledge.

The soft drink industry is concerned over paragraph 6, which reads as follows:
That provision be made to require the payment of sales and excise taxes on the packaging used to contain goods subject to these taxes and on any other articles packaged with them whether the goods are imported, or are manufactured or produced in Canada.
I rise merely to have that point clarified. We in the soft drink industry are in this position with regard to packaging. The title does not pass. The bottles in which the goods are contained are put into the store on a deposit basis, and therefore it seems to me that we would not be taxable. But with respect to this section on packaging, the industry has expressed some concern. I merely want the assurance of the parliamentary assistant at this time that it is not the intention to impose any further taxation in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, it is my intention at this time to discuss at some length paragraph 4, subparagraph (c), of the Excise Tax Act. I have made some extensive inquiries among practical experts in municipal affairs, Mr. Chairman, about this paragraph, but I have not been able to find anyone who had a word to say for the government's reply to the many pleas and representations that have been made by the 4,000 municipalities in our country. Nor have I found anyone who could explain the purpose of this, with the possible exception of a few realists who seem to think that this is another one of the government's tokens, tokens to which we have become accustomed in the past. Our hard-pressed municipal administrators are too close to the realities of ever-mounting expenses and the ever-widening gap between revenue and financial responsibilities to be taken in for a moment by the niggardly action described under paragraph 4 (c), which reads as follows:
(c)	equipment sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale, at a price in excess of one thousand dollars per unit, specially designed for use directly for road making, road cleaning or fire fighting, but not to include automobiles nor ordinary motor trucks;
In the first place it is limited to two classes of municipal expenses, those on roads and those on fire-fighting equipment. In the second place it limits exemption to purchases within these categories where the per unit cost exceeds $1,000. In the third place the road equipment is limited to road making and road cleaning. In the fourth place it attempts to set up a new category of equipment unknown in the business world, and that is the phrase "ordinary motor trucks".
Excise Tax Act
I shall discuss these absurdities in detail in a moment. First of all, however, I think it should be said that the offhand and careless manner in which this important subject has been dealt with in the budget appears to me, and to many others with a special knowledge and experience in municipal finance, to prove as conclusively as nothing else could the complete unconcern of the government at the plight of the municipalities in this matter of excessive federal taxation.
Here in this expression of government policy, Mr. Chairman, we have the evidence that the representations of worried and harassed municipal officials and their associations are regarded by this government as unworthy of serious attention or honest thought, and even of reasonably precise draftsmanship.
The shock with which the budget announcement was received by municipal officials throughout Canada was twofold. First of all, there was the keenest disappointment that the request for fair treatment for the municipal level of government had been so arbitrarily-I might say almost jocularly- brushed aside. The fair treatment which they demanded, and which they still demand, is the same treatment in the matter of tax exemption for the poorest level of government, that is municipal, as that enjoyed by the richer provincial and federal levels of government. Instead they received this thoughtless brush-off, and I for one can only hope that we can impute to it no more sinister motive than political expediency, or a misguided ministerial or departmental sense of humour.
Secondly, there was something close to despair when it was realized that the detailed representations made by the municipalities have resulted only in this impractical declaration of policy with which a first-year school trustee would have been ashamed to be associated.
The first absurdity is the limitation of exemptions to road and fire-fighting equipment. What possible sense can this make? Does this government really think that roads and fires are some special kind of municipal responsibility? Apparently so, and it would seem, therefore, to be time for somebody to make it clear that these are only two categories, of hundreds of categories of municipal services, which are today of the utmost importance to millions of Canadian home owners. I cannot believe that anyone with any knowledge of municipal government would have omitted, for example, school expenditures, hospital and social welfare expenditures, when these exemptions were being considered.

There are, of course, some general exemptions applicable here, but the fact remains that millions of dollars are still being exacted in tribute by the federal government from the efforts of our municipalities to provide adequate education for our youth, hospitalization for the sick, and comfort for our senior citizens in their old age.
We all know, Mr. Chairman, that in other fields we regard some kinds of money as tainted. I respectfully suggest to the government that any money it obtains from these sources falls into that category. We know that, according to current fiscal policies, some fields of taxation are regarded as especially fair game to the taxing authorities. I suggest that the field of school, hospital and social welfare expenditures by municipal governments is one on which our people would, if they could, post "no hunting" signs, and expect them to be honoured, even by the federal government.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is not too much for the municipalities to ask, even at this late date, that an immediate survey be made by the government of this whole field of municipal expenditures so that whatever action may be taken in the future it will at least be realistic, practical and in keeping with the facts of the situation, not just with the fancies of some dreaming draftsman.
To give only a single example from a jurisdiction with which I am familiar, a general exemption from sales tax of school board purchases in the city of Oshawa alone would mean a saving of some $35,000 to $40,000 to the citizens of that community. To carry the matter further, the decision of the government to grant equal and fair treatment to municipalities in this whole matter of sales and excise taxes would mean a saving to that one community alone of almost $200,000, or more than three mills in the municipal assessment. The second absurdity-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When my hon. friend refers to $35,000 as a tax saving for the school board in Oshawa, is he including in that amount the expense of construction?

No, just ordinary purchases of school supplies. The second absurdity in the token treatment the municipalities received

last April is the limitation of the exemption to unit purchases exceeding $1,000. What possible sense can this have? Does it mean that this government believes that there is some virtue, worthy of special reward, in big and better spending? Perhaps so, for we have some evidence that some of our federal departments seem to think so. But, Mr. Chairman, municipalities have not yet, the Lord be praised, caught this glamorous federal government disease. They are not big-time spenders; at least they do not have a big-time spending mentality. Yet, under the present policy of the government, they would be foolish to pay a mere $900 for a road machine, when they could actually win friends in this government, and even save money, by paying $1,001.
But apart from that aspect, I am wondering if the government in its mania for large spending, has completely forgotten that $1,000 in many little items is just as important to the municipal taxpayer as $1,000 spent on a single item. The very nature of municipal financing means an excess of small over large items. It is part and parcel of the thrift and good housekeeping which characterizes municipal spending. Yet it is currently penalized, and penalized heavily, by the federal government.
The third absurdity-I might almost call it a prize boner-is the limitation of road equipment exemptions to road making and road cleaning. Has anyone in this government ever stopped to think that the making and cleaning of roads constitutes actually less than 50 per cent of average road expenditures by municipalities? In other jurisdictions, of course, these may well represent a larger proportion of the whole, but on the municipal level road maintenance is the big item. Then why was it not mentioned? Perhaps some will say that this is a mere technicality, but I cannot agree. The words as they stand are specific and they do not include maintenance; nor do they include bridges which are also an important item in municipal expenditures. If the omission was merely carelessness-as I suspect it was-then our municipalities at least know to what extent they may in the future expect serious, thoughtful and painstaking consideration of their problems by the present government.
The fourth absurdity-and it has already caused endless difficulty-is the careless phrase "ordinary motor trucks". Can anyone on the government side of the house-or anywhere else, for that matter-tell me what an "ordinary motor truck" is? Is it a motor truck to which no snowplow is attached? If so-and I believe that is the current ruling- does it cease to be ordinary when the snowplow is attached? Should the municipality,

therefore, pay its toll to the federal government in summer but not in winter, in good weather but not in bad? And what, Mr. Chairman, may I ask, is so terrible or wrong about ordinary motor trucks? Again, are municipalities to be encouraged to purchase extraordinary equipment just because the federal government has some strange animus against municipalities buying the simplest and cheapest equipment that will serve their purposes? I confess that I do not know the answer to these questions, nor indeed do any of the many municipal officials I have asked.
These are absurdities, Mr. Chairman, but I do plead with the government when next it addresses itself to this urgent problem-if it ever does-not to be content with merely removing absurdities. Surely, sir, in all humanity and fairness, it must go much farther. It must give the most serious consideration to the complete removal of the present discrimination by one government against 4,000 others. That, in the last analysis, is exactly what the present situation is. It is more than that. It is a sort of discrimination which is beating the weaker brethren of the family into the ground. That is no exaggeration. Has anyone in this house ever heard of citizens going around from door to door, begging money on behalf of the federal government? Of course not. Even to suggest it seems ridiculous.
The federal government is the well-heeled big-time spender among the Canadian governments. It is one in 4,011 governments in Canada which has no money problems. It has unlimited powers to raise money and it uses them often and flamboyantly whenever a need, or fancied need, arises. We are all admittedly envious; this is especially so of the municipalities. They are so far from well-heeled that, today, every one of the
4,000	has to depend on the charity of its citizens for its most essential services. I wonder if there is, at this moment, a single municipality in all Canada where citizens are not voluntarily going from door to door, from farmhouse to farmhouse, begging for funds for a hospital, a school, a library or a school bus-probably just an ordinary bus, which the federal government would not even give garage room to.
Our people are giving-and giving generously-to these appeals. And yet, Mr. Chairman, those very donations will sooner or later be reduced by 10 or 15 or even as much as 25 per cent, if they are applied against purchases upon which the federal government insists on its preposterous rake-off. Of course, we can warn them not to buy "ordinary motor trucks" and to insist instead on their money being used to buy
Excise Tax Act
extraordinary ones; but it is more likely than not, sir, that these charity donations will be applied against a variety of small and simple needs, the very category of municipal expenditure on which the federal excise tax of 15 per cent and sales tax of 10 per cent are levied. It should be added here, perhaps, that every municipal official knows that the alleged 10 per cent sales tax is nothing but a statistician's fiction. Actually, when markups are added all along the line to the manufacturer's price plus sales tax, the federal government is found to add 15 or 16 per cent to the consumer's cost.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has presented many briefs to the government on the subject, because they know that their members regard it as the most urgent matter of relief which they need to face the emergencies of supply before them. Many of them have seen their populations double and even treble in the post-war years, and yet they are allowed a much smaller share of the Canadian tax dollar than at any time in Canadian history.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is an acknowledged principle of our way of life that the strong must help the weak, that the rich must assist the poor, and that great power involves great responsibilities. If those principles, upon which I am sure we are agreed in this place, are applied to this request, I am sure that there still will be no doubt about its disposition. I hope that the government will give this matter more careful consideration and eventually accede to the pleas and demands of the municipalities and the Canadian home owners at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few remarks to make on these budget resolutions. First of all I should like to say that I thoroughly support the remarks that have already been made by the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and that I do not propose to reiterate what they have already said. However, I should like to say that I think the 10 per cent sales tax and the excise taxes that are levied against bona fide charitable organizations and national organizations of a health and welfare service nature such as the Canadian Cancer Society should not be levied and that consideration should be given by the Minister of Finance to the removal of those taxes. In view of the change of mind that we had in the minister with respect to mutual insurance companies already, I hope that before the session ends we might have another change of mind with respect to such organizations as I have just mentioned.
I mention the Canadian Cancer Society because it is an organization that I have had

Excise Tax Act
the honour and the pleasure of working with in the past. The matter of this 10 per cent sales tax on material that is purchased by the Canadian Cancer Society is a very real item. I think we all know that the Canadian Cancer Society is doing an extremely fine job in this country in combating one of the most dread of all diseases that we have not yet found a method of coping with adequately. The Canadian Cancer Society spends a great deal of its funds on research and on public education and information so that people can get medical treatment in time for, if not a cure, at least an extension of life. The Canadian Cancer Society also provides free dressings and comforts for those who are unable to provide them themselves. At the present time this particular association is attempting to raise funds. I think it is rather appropriate for me to make these remarks at this time, having regard to the great expenses involved in printing and stationery, advertising and in canvassing material for all the thousands of voluntary canvassers all over the country. If the 10 per cent sales tax were to be removed from all this printing and stationery that is necessary for this purpose it would make a real contribution to helping the society carry out its work which is of a type that could affect every hon. member in this house in a very personal way at some time as well as every person in the dominion.
In closing these remarks, may I say that it has always seemed strange to me that, whereas a person is allowed to make certain deductions from taxable income for donations to organizations such as the Canadian Cancer Society and so on, the government, giving with one hand, should with the other hand proceed to levy a sales tax on those contributions to welfare and charitable organizations. It does not seem consistent. It does not seem to make good sense, and I hope that some consideration will be given to removing this very offensive tax.

I should like to say a word or two. Before the parliamentary assistant closes this discussion, I hope he will clarify in the minds of some of us the question of taxes paid by charitable organizations on purchases that they make. I listened to the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The last speaker said that the Canadian Cancer Society should not have to pay the tax on the dressings that they purchase. They should be entitled to relief, but I am not so sure about the question of advertising. Newspapers are going to charge full rates for advertising and if the tax is going to be charged then let it be charged. Nobody

should make any money out of it. I want this matter cleared up in my own mind. Some organizations are entitled to exemption and some are not. Let us know which are and which are not and the reason why. For many reasons I think it is necessary that that should be known.
There is one type of charitable organization that I think should receive some consideration. I have had correspondence with the department in the past about this matter. All across the country you will find church groups organizing boys' camps. It costs a lot of money, and the money has to be collected from the community. When such a camp is established it is necessary to purchase baseball and other equipment in order to promote sports and carry out the purpose for which the camp is organized. Such equipment is taxed. On several occasions I have appealed to the department and have cited specific cases but up to this time the situation remains the same. The tax was not changed.
There is another problem which, although it may be isolated, does arise from time to time in many communities. Many communities throughout Canada maintain local bands. A year ago I wrote the minister about a certain band in a rural community. This band has been in operation since 1914. They do not have very much money. When there are military or other demonstrations in the community the band plays and serves the purpose. Under the regulations a band of this description cannot get an exemption on the purchase of equipment. The band to which I have referred gathered together enough money to buy some instruments and found that by purchasing them in the old country they could save over $1,000. When you have to knock on doors and collect ten cent pieces to buy equipment a saving of $1,000 means a great deal. But when the equipment arrives in Canada the tax on it pretty well cuts the saving in two. This is not a commercial band. The people do not get paid for appearances at Legion gatherings and so on.
In any event, the tax has to be paid. The minister was sorry but the regulations did not permit him to make any changes. Apparently no change is being made by these amendments, but the matter might be taken under advisement for next year. The extenuating circumstances might be looked at and something might be done to relieve that type of organization. There are community bands in many places throughout the country, but I have pinpointed this one because I happen to live nearby. The application of the sales tax to another category is, in my opinion, discriminatory.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he suggest that the tax be taken off bagpipes?

I do not suggest that. If the
hon. member is asking me that question, I suggest that he get in touch with Senator Reid and ascertain first of all whether the bagpipes are a weapon or an instrument. If it is his interpretation that they are a musical instrument then I will go along with removing the tax. I was about to direct the attention of the parliamentary assistant to another matter involving manufacturers of cabinets and equipment of that kind who employ quite a large staff. The sales tax does not apply in that case because as far as such a manufacturer is concerned he does not sell directly but farms out his product to retailers. He is not taxed on the cabinets, window frames and so on that he manufactures. There is no sales tax.
I have had a decision from the department within the last year involving a small shop. A small shop in the same city may employ two or three people and the owner also works. He turns out the same type of equipment but on a much smaller scale and sells directly.

is put in a very bad competitive position when there is a large plant nearby doing the same type of work that does not have the additional handicap of the sales tax.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and others have referred to the application of the sales tax. Every time I hear that matter discussed I always think about dominion-provincial relations. I cannot understand how some people can reconcile the attitude of asking the federal government to pay everything while at the same time authority remains in the hands of other bodies. I agree with the member for Ontario in his plea for the municipalities, but to help the municipalities you have got to go through the provincial governments. The federal government cannot make any grants or concessions directly to municipalities.
They are already making them.

Well, I do not think it is going to help them very much. There is a lot of thinking to be done on this problem. We have to look at the British North America Act, and at the interpretation the Supreme Court of Canada has put upon it. In my opinion you will find the Supreme Court of Canada has completely nullified the intentions of the fathers of confederation. These things are all tied in with this whole question.
I feel that a municipality that buys firefighting equipment, largely on orders from the civil defence organization today which is demanding uniformity of hose couplings and that sort of thing, should at least be exempt from paying taxes on that equipment. This is part of our defence set-up. In the first place, I believe it should be the responsibility of the federal government to supply this equipment, because there are many small communities that would be very important in the chain of civil defence, and who could very well get along with a less expensive type of equipment, that are forced to have this interchangeable equipment because of a large community close by. This expensive interchangeable equipment is a part of our national program today. I am not going to repeat the argument made by the hon. member for Ontario, because I agree with him.
There are many municipalities across Canada that are nearly bankrupt, and that have no means of taxation except the property tax. This tax is about as high as it can go. I feel the problem has to be argued through the provincial government, and some uniform system arrived at. We could make a start by helping the municipalities, as the hon. member for Ontario has suggested.

Excise Tax Act
Now, this sales tax generally, as it is today, does not amount to 10 per cent at all. Take as an example an article you are importing from the United States, such as a part for an automobile. When it comes into the country it costs perhaps $2. The person who imports it passes on the cost of the article plus whatever duty he paid on it, and then on top of that he adds the 10 per cent sales tax. The article goes to someone else in the city of Toronto, and he adds the 10 per cent sales tax on top of the other fellow's mark-up, the sales tax he paid and the duty he paid at the border. By the time the article passes through three or four hands, as it will in many instances, and the consumer gets it in the maritimes or out in British Columbia, that sales tax amounts to over 100 per cent. It is the method of applying the tax that is wrong.
If we are going to have a sales tax, it should be imposed at the manufacturers' level and the article stamped to show the sales tax has been paid. Then, when it is resold, no one in Canada should be permitted to charge any more sales tax on it. The tax was paid at the manufacturers' level and it was worked into the cost; that is where it should end. It is the pyramiding of this tax right along the line, and the tax being added to a profit of perhaps 20 per cent or 30 per cent by someone along the line, that is the thing that really hurts in the application of the sales tax. If the tax is going to be applied by the retailer, then no one but the retailer should charge that sales tax. If the hon. member for Moose Jaw, for example, were to sell me a refrigerator and the sales tax were going to be paid by him, then no one else should impose it. He should mark the 10 per cent tax on the bill he issues to me, then show the cost of the refrigerator so that I would know what I was paying. That would be a direct tax.
The way this tax is imposed now, it is an indirect tax. It has become a tax on a tax, and a tax on a profit, and instead of being 10 per cent in many cases it runs over 100 per cent. I know the department is aware of this because the subject has been mentioned year after year. I have read speeches made in this house years ago that mentioned this very thing. I believe it is time someone in the department began to sort it out. I know the popular thing to do is to say you are against taxes altogether, but if we are going to function we have to have them. I feel they are misused and abused. I believe the government is getting a lot of blame it does not deserve. The only people who set out the tax as a separate item are the printers. If you go into a printer's shop

and get a bill you will see that the printing is shown as so much and then the sales tax is added to that. You know what you are paying. This idea of telling the small manufacturer that he is to apply that sales tax but not to show it, to work it into the cost, is bad. The minister has a file on this kind of thing that I sent him dealing with printing in one instance, and dealing with the small-

I am not going to argue with the minister, because I intended to do so by correspondence last year. I had the whole case outlined; the instructions from the inspector, the fact they were reviewed at Moncton, and I had the whole thing outlined. I was told that was the way it had to be done. The only reason for making these rambling remarks was the question of purchases made by different charitable organizations in this country. I should like to have that question clarified for my own benefit. I should like to know who are entitled to the exemption, and why they are entitled to it. I should like to know why one charitable organization gets an exemption and another does not. As members of parliament, we are questioned along these lines from time to time, and we are not in a position to give the answers unless we get them here.

I was going to make a suggestion, Mr. Chairman. Those who contribute to charitable organizations get an exemption on their income taxes when they have a receipt. I was going to suggest that any reductions in

taxes tor charitable organizations-and I think there ought to be-should be levied against incomes. I think that would be the logical way to get it. They have to have taxes anyway.

I should like to support the hon. member for Cape Breton South in his plea to have something done about the present method of imposing the sales tax. I am not going to elaborate except to say I support him and the very fine explanation that he gave to the house of the pyramiding there is of that tax by the time the goods are bought by the consumer. The point I wish to make is not contained within the provisions of the present excise tax amendment. Rather, I want to bring to the attention of the committee a point of administration in connection with the act, and also a point concerning the tax itself.
In Canada the excise tax still applies to motor vehicles sold in this country. While this brings in a large amount of revenue to the federal government, I do feel that in this day and age, when it is recognized by all people that a motorcar is no longer a luxury, but that everyone should have the advantage of owning one, a somewhat different approach might be made to the problem.
On March 10 I received a return to a question I had asked the administration concerning the amount of excise and customs taxes collected by the federal government in connection with the sale of motor vehicles, and this return discloses a total amount of about $90,600,000. I realize that it is easy for a member in an opposition party to rise in the House of Commons and advocate certain tax cuts and changes, because we are not responsible for giving the service of government to our people. In the opposition groups we do make demands upon the government to give extended services; and when I say I think either that this tax should be discarded or that it should be greatly lowered, I do so with a full sense of responsibility.
Speaking for myself, I feel there are other ways the government could collect taxes-
Name them.

-without levying an excise tax on motor vehicles. It could get revenue from the imposition of an excess profits tax, through which of course it would get money from those corporations that are making excessive profits. In any case this is a tax to which consideration should be given by the taxation branch of the government, so that it may be made possible for more people in this country to buy cars, and to buy them cheaper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the debate yesterday and today has focused chiefly on the question of the remission of sales tax. In particular members in the opposition parties have suggested that it would be a comparatively easy thing to widen the opportunities for rebate or remission. Let me assure them we are not exaggerating the administrative difficulties of this form of rebate. As hon. members know, the federal tax on commodities is levied at the manufacturers' level; and after that article has passed through several hands it is very difficult to arrange a rebate.
The Leader of the Opposition suggested that in the case of municipalities it might be possible to have them organized as one entity under a provincial government, and that by virtue of that situation the number of units with which the federal government would have to deal would be reduced. It is true that at the moment provincial governments are exempt from federal taxation. This is not as a result of any concessions, or because these matters are easy to administer. It results from our constitution. That constitution, established more than eighty years ago, has stated that neither government could tax the other.
That particular constitutional requirement does not extend to municipalities. There are more than four thousand municipalities with which the federal government would have to deal in matters of this kind. I repeat that the administrative difficulties must not be minimized. And in support of that I would draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that in the last few days we have heard

a good deal about the closer association between the provinces and the municipalities than exists either legally or constitutionally between the federal government and those municipalities.
Notwithstanding that, and notwithstanding the fact that frequently we have heard the province described as the mother of the municipalities, while sales taxes are imposed by five of our provincial governments I know of none of the five that provides a rebate on purchases of municipalities. In addition to that, even when we get into the field of remission with respect to charitable institutions, it is true that the federal government has provided a certain and a considerable measure of remission to certain defined charitable institutions.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South asked that they be defined. As the hon. member for Eglinton said, we have had this provision since 1950, and the institutions that are free from federal sales tax are those bona fide institutions that care for children, the aged, the infirm, the incapacitated, if the institution qualifies and receives a grant either from a federal or from a provincial government. That means that all this class of institutions, in so far as federal sales tax is concerned, gets a rebate. On the other hand, hon. members will again recognize that there is a much closer relationship, in the field of health and welfare, between a provincial administration and hospitals than there is between the federal government and those hospitals. But I know of no provincial government-and there are many that are imposing sales tax-that provides similar remission on the purchases for hospitals.
The hon. member for Ontario referred, as a specific example, to the possibility that a school board in his city might save considerable sums were they not subject to a federal tax. I indicated to him that practically all building materials are among that wide class that are exempted from federal sales tax; but this is not true in the case of five of the provinces that impose sales taxes. In other words, if a school board in any of those five provinces had to pay out taxpayers' funds for the construction of new buildings, it would be exempt from federal tax in so far as practically all the materials that go into that building are concerned. But in the case of those provinces that impose a sales tax, they would have to pay to the provinces a sales tax, even though, as I say, we have heard frequently of the close relationship, of motherhood, of the municipalities to the nrovinces.
May I ask a question? In the case of how many of the provinces which do impose a sales tax is that sales tax applicable to construction materials entering into the building of schools?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Building materials as a
class are generally taxable under the sales tax provisions of the five taxing provinces; whereas the-

that similarly in the case of the federal government the purchases of those departments bear sales tax.
It is indirect; therefore it is much easier to pay.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I suggest to my hon. friend the very opposite. the other day made certain* assertions about the tax on automobiles, and he referred particularly to the weight of tax on school buses. It is true that there is a sales tax on school buses, but I would remind my hon. friend, if he is not already aware of this, that there is no excise tax on a bus or on a truck.
During his speech the hon. member made a reference to the tax on certain motor vehicles and I was a little surprised to find that in the figures he gave he was referring to an ordinary Chevrolet car and gave the factory price at some $2,200. I made some inquiries today in regard to a Chevrolet standard two-door sedan and I find that the retail price, not the factory price, of that vehicle was $2,190 and the tax was not in excess of $500 but amounted to $370.
That is the manufacturer's level. 1 referred, of course, to the retail level.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

certainly not over $500.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In this particular case the same point has been made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He made the suggestion that there should be some special marking of the taxes which are applied, but that is generally true in a large item such as an automobile, and in most cases the dealer indicates not only the sales tax but the excise tax. In my investigation this morning I found that that was done and both these taxes were spelled out on the tag attached to the car.
But may I point out that the motorcar industry is the one single exception in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think there are probably some others, but this is a conspicuous example. In this connection I made another small calculation which may be of interest to my hon. friend from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. In the case of the automobile, by the mere fact that they specify the 10 per cent sales

tax, it is very easy to determine the manufacturer's price of that vehicle. I checked on another low-priced car. The delivery or retail price was $2,245; I found that the sales tax was $137. With these particulars one can very easily calculate that the manufacturer's selling price is $1,377 and the total taxes amount to $343. Let us say, the tax and wages would amount to $680. But I have found that the dealer's mark-up accounts for some $525. Now, my hon. friend, as a retailer, can use his own judgment in regard to specifying and marking the 10 per cent sales tax on some of these articles, but I do not think he would do that in his own business.
I would be delighted to do that for the parliamentary assistant if others would do likewise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a good proviso.

It was the interruptions that were bellicose.
No. It was the tone of the parliamentary assistant's remarks that was bellicose. Apparently the hon. member for Ottawa West was not paying attention.
No; it was the tone of the interruptions.

The hon. member for Ottawa West may have lost interest in what was going on in the house.
I wish to refer briefly, Mr. Chairman, to several of the remarks that have fallen from the lips of the hon. gentleman. Let me speak first of all about the matter of the sales tax levied by the federal government and of which he spoke. He undertook to take issue with a figure used by the Leader of the Opposition in his remarks yesterday. The Leader of the Opposition referred to the collection by the federal government of sales tax at the expense of the municipal corporation of Montreal. The parliamentary assistant is asking the committee to believe today that that was a figure of combined federal and provincial sales tax. Mr. Chairman, it is no such thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It included contractors' expenditures.
No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, it did. Read
Hansard.

May I say to the hon. gentleman that the source of the figure is a publication of the city of Montreal. In that publication we have this statement:
The city of Montreal has paid in the year 1951-52 an estimated amount of $382,000 for the federal sales tax of 10 per cent on materials and equipment purchased either by the city itself or by contractors who carry out its works.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: By contractors; surely.

That is the direct expense of the city of Montreal. Is my hon. friend saying that, because the city of Montreal has certain work carried out on its behalf by contractors and therefore it is the contractors who have to pay the federal government, by some magic that is not a federal sales tax paid by the municipality? Surely in this chamber we have not reached the point where that kind of sophistry carries any conviction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Does the province
of Quebec exempt those contractors' expenditures?
[The Deputy Chairman.]
I do not happen to know the answer to that question; and from the way my hon. friend runs away from my question I can judge that he does not know either.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Sit down.
If he would permit a question, I would appreciate it.
The hon. member is not a minister.
Can the hon. gentleman tell the committee who retains ownership of the equipment on which that sales tax is paid? Is it the contractor or is it the city?
The city.

Evidently the city. We are not talking simply about purchases of equipment that the contractor used in his own business apart from the city. This is put forward by the city of Montreal as the payment by them of sales tax on materials and equipment purchased either by the city itself or by contractors who carry out its works. That is all passed on by the contractor to the city and, in that way, to the municipal taxpayer. That is the whole point.

I had understood quite differently the quotation read by the hon. member for Eglinton. I had understood it to imply that the contractor retained ownership of the equipment and that all the city of Montreal was saying in its statement was that the tax those contractors paid was a factor of cost to the city. But it did not go on to say that, as is now being argued, the whole of that tax was applicable to the city and a direct cost on the city as such.

If there was anything lacking in my observations, I must express my appreciation to the hon. member for Ottawa West for having clarified whatever was left in need of clarification in my remarks. We have the statement of the city of Montreal.
I made a statement yesterday in this chamber as to the payment of federal sales tax by the city of Toronto, and I said that amount had been calculated by the city treasurer or finance commissioner to be in the sum of $500,000 in a year. Those are incontestable facts. Let us not have any beating about the bush with regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any breakdown of the expenditure?

No; I have not a breakdown. However, that was the statement. I quoted it here yesterday. I quoted it in the house last year. At the same time I said

that no one knows how much is being collected by the federal government in sales and excise taxes at the expense of the municipalities because there is no segregation of the figures. In the two instances that are under discussion, we know what those two principal cities in this country are paying; and we can properly infer that substantial amounts of money are being collected by the federal government in sales tax and excise tax at the expense of municipal corporations. I believe a figure has been given for the city of Vancouver. Enough figures are available, Mr. Chairman, to leave no doubt in the mind of anyone who wants information on this subject that the federal government is collecting extremely large sums of money at the expense of the municipalities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They will likely find the exemptions for these costly items to be very beneficial.
The few that are being given; yes.

The parliamentary assistant keeps coming back and talking about some items. I have been talking about the actual imposition on the municipal taxpayers of these several cities of federal sales and excise taxes. Those figures are incontestable. I do not quite follow the purport and the purpose of the hon. gentleman's present interruption.
He does not know himself.

Let us turn for a moment to his interesting reference to the collection of sales and excise taxes some twenty years ago. It is an extremely poor answer to a strong case to delve back a generation ago and to say that no action was taken by the government of that day to meet the problem that is now under discussion. The fact of the matter is that whatever may have been done or left undone at that time, the needs of the situation are apparent to anyone today who is a realist. My hon. friend excuses the failure of the present government to bring any relief in the field of indirect taxation by saying that in 1935, when the Bennett government went out of office, the federal government was collecting 63 per cent of its total revenues in the form of indirect taxes. I have not the figures before me. I am not in a position to comment on the accuracy of the hon. gentleman's figure. I have no doubt that he is speaking from acceptable government records. However, I wish to look a little bit further into those figures. The budget of the federal government in that year was something between $400 million and $500 million. Actually, if my memory serves me
Excise Tax Act
correctly, it was less than $450 million. The budget with which we are dealing today is more than ten times the budget of 1935. My hon. friend's figures of percentages are not particularly eloquent in the light of the actual amounts. What was 63 per cent of $450 million? Mr. Chairman, it was something under $300 million, in round figures. But the federal government today is deriving 40 per cent of its revenues in indirect taxes. What is 40 per cent of a figure which is close to $5 billion? You have to take into consideration the other charges made by the federal government in reckoning up the total they take by these indirect taxes. That 40 per cent, Mr. Chairman- again taking a round figure-of $5 billion is something like $2 billion. Let my hon. friend give figures and not these misleading percentages. Let him compare the less than $300 million taken in indirect taxes in 1935 with the almost $2 billion taken today by this government in the form of indirect taxes. There you have a fair basis of comparison.
Again, Mr. Chairman, my friend speaks of the problem of 1935 as though it were more acute than the problem today. It is quite true that many municipalities were bearing a very heavy burden in 1935. There were many municipalities in default in this country. No one denies that. The fact of the matter is, however, that the federal government today is taking many times more from the municipalities in indirect taxes than it took in 1935.
Let it not be forgotten that when the Bennett government went out of office in 1935 the sales tax was levied at the rate of 6 per cent, and in that fateful year of 1935 the late Mr. Mackenzie King campaigned up and down the country denouncing the sales tax and referred to it as "that iniquitous tax".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Do not get bellicose.

Sir, my friend threw about so many figures that I do not know whether I have covered all that I intended to cover. I have this comment to make on what he said about the sales tax on American motor cars. He worked himself into quite a lather over what he said was the astounding figure of $90 that I had used in a radio address as being the federal tax on a standard type low-priced motor car in the United States. I took that figure from published figures of the American automobile industry and I have no doubt it is correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I assure my friend that it is not.

But I draw to the attention of the committee that what my friend worked himself into such a lather over was the difference between his figure of $125 tax on a motor car and mine of $90. Apparently there is such a world of difference between $90 and $125 that my friend is justified in fulminating in the manner in which he did this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Pretty nearly 40 per cent.

Yes, it is a figure of about 35 per cent more than the figure I used. I am quite prepared to take the figure published by the American automotive industry as an authentic figure. It is a figure that has been published in that country and in this country as well.
This is the first time the government has been so concerned about $35.

If the parliamentary assistant is looking for ways of saving $35, then I suggest to him that he might take another look at the excessive taxes on Canadian motor cars that are being collected by his government. The figure I quoted in my recent radio speech, to which he did me the honour of making reference in his remarks, was contained in this sentence:
For example, the federal tax on a standard type low-priced motor car without extras is $350 in Canada and only $90 in the United States.
He was only 40 per cent wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was the hon. member for Eglinton who was 40 per cent wrong.

The fact is that I should like to see the hon. gentleman, with his powers of subtraction, go to work on that figure of the Canadian tax and see what he can do to convince his minister and his government that the time is long past when a substantial reduction should be made in the heavy federal imposition on motor cars in this country. We hear people complaining about the high cost of motor cars in Canada. The fact is that

the Canadian federal government is contributing very substantially to the high cost of motor cars in this country and to the extent to which the cost of such motor cars in Canada exceeds that prevailing in the United States.
I shall not try to go over the ground further. We have had discussions in the house on the subject of indirect taxes. The reasons that the federal government chooses to levy its sales taxes at the manufacturer's level rather than at the retail level are that the taxes in that way are hidden and the consumer does not know what tax he pays, and, in the second place, that it is easier for the federal government to do it that way, regardless of the effect on the consumer, regardless of the fact that these taxes accumulate mark-ups as they pass from hand to hand, pyramiding as they go. But that has not given the government any degree of trouble or concern. What has concerned them is that they should find a way in which it will be easy for them to extract these taxes from the people so that the consumer who buys the goods shall not know exactly what he is paying in federal sales taxes.
Of course the provinces have no option in the matter. If they are going to collect a sales tax it must be at the consumer level because they have no power to levy indirect taxes. But in the United States the federal government has been a little fairer with the consumer and, where it finds it necessary to impose a sales tax, does not hesitate to levy it on the consumer rather than on the manufacturer or producer.
I commend that example to the consideration of the government. I have not said that the federal government in the United States collects all its excise and sales taxes in that way but I do say that the federal government in the United States has not found it impossible to collect its sales taxes at the consumer level rather than at the producer level. I commend that to the consideration of the government.

It is a little difficult to disentangle the customs tariff, excise taxes and sales taxes, particularly with respect to such a matter as I want to mention, the taxes that still remain on books. I was glad that the government mcved considerably in the matter of abolition of the sales tax. I am not of course alone in that opinion. The people who

use libraries are concerned, and may I say that we are woefully deficient in the matter of libraries.

I have just one point to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant in connection with books. I wish to draw his attention to the fact that I have two or three groups in my riding who are interested in historical events, who have published books in connection with jubilee celebrations held in small cities or towns. The Kaslo committee in my constituency provides an illustration of my point. Last year, without any knowledge of the advertising terms of the act, this committee published a very good history of the city in question for sale during the jubilee. speakerposition: subtopic
