speechtext:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Act and to provide, among other things:
1.	That the excise duty on malt be repealed and an excise duty of thirty-eight cents a gallon be imposed upon all beer or malt liquor subject to an allowance for wastage.
2.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution be deemed to have come into force on the seventh day of April, nineteen hundred and fifty-four.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. members would like an explanation of the purpose of this change. Paragraph 1 of the resolution proposes that the excise duty of 21 cents per pound on malt be repealed, and that all beer and malt liquor be subject to an excise duty of 38 cents per gallon. It is a change of method. The purpose of the change is to

Excise Act
introduce a more modern method of taxation rather than to substantially alter the general level of taxation in the industry.
At present the law also provides that where beer is brewed from a substance other than malt, for example from brewer's corn flakes or other corn adjuncts, an excise duty of 42 cents per gallon of beer will be levied in lieu of the duty on malt. This rate has been in effect since April 8, 1952, when this gallon-age duty was set at 42 cents per gallon. I am informed that approximately 2 pounds of malt were used in the production of one gallon of beer, thus making the gallonage duty about equal to the effective rate of duty on the beer brewed from malt.
However, due to changes in the brewing process the amount of malt used in the production of a gallon of beer has been steadily reduced. Consequently beer brewed from malt has been taxed at a lower rate than beer brewed from other substances. Representations have been received from farmers and others engaged in processing corn for use in the brewing of beer to the effect that brewers were reluctant to use corn adjuncts because of the differential in the two rates of duty. Adoption of this amendment will, of course, entirely remove the differential and brewers will have no reason to refrain from using corn products because of the excise duty.
Available information indicates that at present, on the average, about 1-8 pounds of malt is used in brewing one gallon of beer. I mentioned that when the tax was set it was assumed that two pounds of malt would be used in the production of a gallon of beer. This means that the previous duty levied on the malt content of beer was about 38 cents per gallon; that is the proposal in this amendment. Broadly speaking, the introduction of the new rate of 38 cents per gallon will not change the levy On malt beer. On other beer the duty will be reduced to 38 cents from 42 cents, but this class of beer constitutes only about 6 per cent of Canada's total beer production.

Can the parliamentary
assistant indicate what will be the position of the government so far as revenue is concerned when this change is made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I indicated there will be a slight reduction in the case of the 6 per cent of beer that is brewed from corn adjuncts, but in the case of the beer brewed from malt there should be no substantial change because of the ratio of malt now going into the brewing of beer which has worked out now roughly to 38 cents per gallon, and that is the proposal in the amendment.
I would think there would be some estimate in terms of dollars and cents as to what the position would be. Can the parliamentary assistant give us that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I said in my statement, we really do not expect much change in revenue, assuming the same quantities are produced. I might indicate that the revenue from the 21 cent per pound tax on malt for the last year for which I have figures, 1952-53, amounted to something in excess of $80 million.

speechtext:

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, for your consideration and the suggestions you have made. I wish to make a few comments on the question of income tax deductions with respect to individuals and corporations, because they are both mentioned in this Income Tax Act resolution as we have it before us. I wish to refer particularly to some suggestions that are not mentioned in the resolution.
I do not lightly suggest the granting of exemptions, just for the sake of pleasing everybody, because I know we have to collect taxes and to meet our responsibilities. But I do wish to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant what I consider to be three or four omissions in the present resolution.
The first of these concerns a number of my constituents, and has concerned them for a number of years. I refer to the fact that there is no exemption in respect of what I would

Income Tax Act
term unusual or abnormal travelling expenses. I refer to expenses incurred by workers and other people who have to proceed some distance to their places of employment. The need for this exemption is increasing because, more and more in order to obtain housing and other accommodation, working people, and those who are performing services, find that they must live at greater distances from their employment. For instance some of the workers of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company now live as far as thirty miles away from their employment. They have been forced to go that distance to obtain satisfactory sites for the building of their homes. Without doubt it is an exceptional expense for these workers. I am informed the same situation is found in other parts of the country. It is a constant cost over which these people have little or no control. We provide an exemption for a salesman who travels even a hundred miles to sell bubble gum. In contrast to that provision I do suggest there should be some consideration for the abnormal and unusual expenses of working people who are contributing to the production of this country.
I wish now to refer to another heavy expense experienced by those in my constituency who have to resort to the use of ambulances. Owing to the distances that must be travelled, ambulance charges sometimes run to as much as $50 or $100. Indeed, frequently people have to be taken 150 or 175 miles for treatment, I do think that under such circumstances ambulance charges should be deductible for income tax purposes. When a person requires an ambulance in an emergency he or she is ill or has suffered an accident, and most certainly is going to be unemployed for some time.
Then with respect to farm improvements I would point out that in the resolution the mining and oil companies are given exemptions for the development of their properties on the principle, as I understand it, that they are increasing the total productive capacity of the country. I make a plea for the farmers who are clearing land, or who may be draining or irrigating land. In this way they, too, are increasing our production. The costs incurred in these clearing, draining or irrigating operations should be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes.
There is one further point which is of particular interest to many of my constituents. It is also of interest to me, because I have been interested in the forest industry all my life. I believe those engaged in forestry are entitled to the same kind of exemption as those who are engaged in the mining or oil industries. Those in the forest industry 
should receive exemptions in respect of work undertaken to increase the conservation of timber on their properties, and in connection with replanting, the building of roads, the proper management of their properties and, in particular, for expenditure on fire protection.
I have brought this to the attention of the house on a half dozen occasions and, in this connection, wish to read from the report of the department of resources and development for the fiscal year ended March 31,
1953.	This makes reference to the activities of the forestry branch of the then department of resources and development, and states at page 97:
During the year, the interdepartmental committee on the relation of income tax deductions to forest management made its report. This committee, set up under the direction of the minister of resources and development was composed of representatives of the departments of finance, of national revenue (taxation division), and of resources and development. The committee, with the director of this branch as chairman, was particularly interested in corporation income tax deductions and their relation to sustained-yield forest operations.
It is interesting to note that they were interested only in corporation income tax deductions. What about the individuals who are also undertaking this kind of work in the forestry industry? The report continues:
Informal representations by the forest industries and discussions by the committee members resulted in two main changes with respect to income tax-deductions, both of which will encourage sustained-yield management.
I agree with that, and have spoken in favour of it on many occasions. The report continues:
Access roads and trails are now subject to a generous rate of depreciation, and forest management expenses designed to promote sustained yield are, generally speaking, recognized as current costs for income tax purposes.
That is the very thing several of us have been advocating in the house for a number of years. But according to this report it applies only to corporations. I wish to say that from my knowledge of the lumbering industry in my constituency I have not heard of any of the smaller companies or individual operators receiving any exemptions, or having knowledge of the policy designed as a result of this investigation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is an interesting point; but the act uses the word "taxpayer". So that it does not make any difference whether a taxpayer is a corporation or an individual, the same principle would apply. If an individual had an income from the business of logging or forestry he would have

exactly the same rights in the same circumstances as have been read out by the hon. member, although he referred to a "corporation".

I have practically completed my remarks, but I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant this question: What has been done to inform industry of this provision? I am confident, from my personal contact with quite a number of lumber operators who are attempting to carry on their operations along forest-management lines, that they are unaware of this provision. What is being done to inform industry, and would it be possible to obtain a copy of the regulations covering this type of exemption?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This right is not spelled out in the regulations. It would be the same type of deduction as an expense that people in many other types of business would be using. It is not usual to have to inform people of their rights under the Income Tax Act. It is usually the other way around. A request is made for a deduction. The ground is plowed by the taxpayer, when he finds something new, to see whether it will be treated as an exemption. Usually we do not have to advertise these things.
If an operator were to write to the department and ask for the regulations covering activities for which he could receive an exemption would he receive specific information?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The best procedure
would be for the taxpayer to inquire at the nearest district tax office. These are all based on regions, and he could communicate with his own regional director.
I am quite sure the majority of them know nothing about it. However I think the big companies are well informed about these exemptions.

While we are still in the midst of discussing the general provisions of the Income Tax Act there are a few points I should like to make apropos of some omissions, or to correct some inequities in the act that one would like to see. I merely put these suggestions forward. I should preface my remarks by saying that we are committed, and rightly so, to the principle that you cannot at the same time reduce sharply your taxation generally in a period when demands on government spending are not only very heavy but are likely to increase. I think it is sometimes a pity that that principle is not kept in mind by hon. members when we are discussing taxation. It would certainly help to put the discussion on a higher intellectual plane.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You are not against putting taxes on a fair basis, are you?

The point I want to raise particularly at this time is in respect of section 11 (1) (1). The sidenote of this paragraph is "alimony". I shall read the paragraph and then point out how the interpretation of it can be important. I might say here that no matter how well some of the statutes may be drawn in the beginning, obviously, as we put them into use, we shall find occasions when interpretations by the department and by the courts sometimes reveal inequities in the act itself. It is that kind of thing that I am concerned with here. The paragraph reads:
-an amount paid by the taxpayer in the year pursuant to a decree, order or judgment of a competent tribunal in an action or proceeding for divorce or judicial separation or pursuant to a written separation agreement as alimony or other allowance payable on a periodic basis for the maintenance of the recipient thereof, children of the marriage, or both the recipient and children of the marriage, if he is living apart from the spouse or former spouse to whom he is required to make the payment.
This sets out what requirement you must fill if you fall within the exception in the statute. The requirements of this paragraph are four. You must have an order for divorce or judicial separation. That is the first requirement. In Ontario, at least, and I think in several other provinces, there is no action for judicial separation, so that that exception is taken out of the picture. Therefore you must have an order for divorce or a written separation agreement under which the husband pays maintenance to the wife or, if you pay alimony, payments on a periodic basis, and under each of the three conditions, if the parties are living apart, such amounts may be deducted from your taxable income.
The problem is this. In Ontario, in a case where no divorce action can be obtained and in a case where the parties are separating and no separation agreement under the circumstances can be entered into, normally proceedings are taken through the family court. The family court handles all matters of domestic relations and, as hon. members can understand, by far the majority of domestic problems are heard in the family court, and by far the greatest majority of payments ordered by any court are by virtue of orders of the family court. There you will find the bulk of your cases. If you have a rich client you start alimony action in the supreme court, but that is not normally the case. We find then that family court orders represent the bulk of the cases where court orders are made for payment of money by the husband to the wife. That is what happens

Income Tax Act
in Ontario, and I am sure it applies in many of the other provinces. The problem is that such payments made by order of the family court are not deductible from the taxable income by interpretation of the income tax department. I would put forward as a suggestion to the department at this time that it would be well worth considering what I have termed an inequity in the act.
A curious by-product has arisen from this situation in that the judges of the family courts in the provinces of Ontario feel very badly. They feel that their courts are not considered as being competent courts of jurisdiction in such matters. Family court officials receive constant inquiries regarding this particular situation. This is one place where appropriate action could be taken to rectify what is an obvious misinterpretation by the department in regard to this particular point.
The other point I had was in regard to family allowances. We have new Canadians coming to this country. They have children but they do not qualify to receive family allowances until they have spent twelve months in the country. At the end of that time they can then get the family allowance, and their children qualify. But after the children qualify the allowable deduction is reduced from $400 to $150. If a child, for example, qualifies and the parent collects family allowance in the month of December they might receive one payment of $5 for family allowance, yet the allowance they are allowed as a deduction is reduced over the whole period of the year from $400 to $150. New Canadians find themselves rather at a loss to understand this situation. Of course it can be pointed out to them that when the children reach 16 they may have been receiving family allowance for eleven months of that year, but due to the fact that the child became 16 during the last month of the year they are allowed to go back to the $400 rate for the whole year. Hence what they lose in the roundabout they gain on the swings, or vice versa.
But they are lucky to be able to pay income tax the first year they are here. Ninety per cent of the farmers are never fortunate enough to pay income tax.

We hear a great deal about the farmers, although I did not think their problems would be injected into this present discussion. In the case of a child born in Canada it is quite true that it works out in the latter manner I have suggested, but in the case of new Canadians coming into the country they have to wait for a twelvemonth period before the child qualifies, and

when the child reaches the age of 16 they are not always in the position where they can make up what they lost at the beginning. I therefore think they have a very good point in bringing this matter forward and again, along with my suggestion regarding the family court payments, I would like to suggest this latter question regarding immigrants coming into the country be brought before the department for their consideration while we are discussing these resolutions.

Mr. Chairman, could I just intervene at this point, because I would like to reply at the first opportunity to the hon. member for York-Scarborough.
He mentioned two matters in connection with an order issued by the family court and I wish to assure him that some consideration was given to this problem prior to the bringing down of this budget. It is true that it is very difficult for these people to understand why we have these regulations,

particularly so when they first come into this country. I do not know that I can go along one hundred per cent with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We feel we can correct that in the bill.

The only thing I would like to suggest this time is that the department consider doing the same thing for them as it did for Canadian children born in this country, and that is to make the exemption applicable according to the actual payments, rather than according to the date of qualification or eligibility.
I would like to say a word also on the other point brought up by the hon. member for York-Scarborough. The matter he raised creates a very real problem for a good many taxpayers, particularly when a man may be contributing to the support of his family from which he is separated, and he can still be paying a large part of his earnings to them and still be taxed as a single man by reason of the fact that the wife has obtained employment which puts her in the taxable bracket also.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while we are on the subject of omissions, may I take just a moment to remind the parliamentary assistant, the government and the Minister of Finance of a very serious omission. I refer to the absence in the minister's budget proposals of any reference to the floor under medical expenses so far as income tax deductions are concerned. I need not take the time of the house to relate the history of this question. It is one that is well known to all hon. members of the house and well known throughout the country. But I do think that it is most unfortunate that the job the minister started a year ago of reducing that floor from 4 per cent to 3 per cent has not been continued.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was originally 5 per cent, of course.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well I can go back and give the history of this matter though I did not intend to, even though the parliamentary
Income Tax Act
assistant has asked for it. He is perfectly correct. In 1944, or possibly in 1943, the rate was reduced from 5 per cent to 4 per cent; in 1953 it was reduced from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. I hope we are not going to have to wait until 1963 to get it down to 2 per cent, and 1973 to get it down to one per cent, and 1983 to get rid of it altogether. That would really be a long, long story, considering the fact that members of this house showed considerable interest in the idea of abolishing that floor by allowing a certain motion to go through a couple of years ago. Again, I am not seeking to revive that debate because we might very well get off into the procedural aspects of the matter.- But I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the feeling of the people of this country is valid in that many of them have expressed the view that if medical expenses are to be allowed as deductions they should foe allowed right from the first dollar as is the case with charitable donations.
Speaking for myself I have no objection to there being a ceiling as to the amount that could be deducted. There are some who think there should be no ceiling, but it is true that a case can be made for a ceiling and the government two years ago raised that ceiling from what it was before. But there is no excuse for not allowing income tax deductibility for the first dollars one has to pay out as medical expenses, in the same way that the first dollars given to approved charities are allowed income tax deductibility.
I might point out once again that the Windsor chamber of commerce has been carrying on a considerable campaign in respect of this matter. The proposal that body makes is, I suggest, a second-best. But if the government is not prepared to go the whole way and to remove altogether the 3 per cent floor, they might give consideration to the suggestion made by the Windsor chamber of commerce and other bodies. That suggestion is that the 3 per cent floor should relate not to the net income, as is the case at the present time, but rather to the taxable income after the statutory deductions have been made. That procedure would make quite a considerable difference, and certainly it would seem to be more reasonable. The way the matter now stands, Mr. Chairman, a great many medical expenses are not allowed at all. That statement applies, I might point out, in particular to moneys paid out for expensive medicines such as insulin, ACTH, cortisone and some of these other modern drugs about which the minister had so much to say when he added them to the list. He was proud of the fact that he

Income Tax Act
was making those items deductible under the heading of medical expenses. Yet many people who thought they were going to get relief because of that change have discovered that what was the 4 per cent floor but is now the 3 per cent floor denies to them the advantage of those drug items being included as deductible, because heavy though their expenses are they do not happen to exceed 3 per cent of their total income.
Since you were good enough, Mr. Chairman, to allow this brief period when members might express their regrets over some of the omissions from the budget presented by the minister this year, I take this opportunity to express once again my great regret that nothing was done this year to remove the 3 per cent floor under medical expenses deductible for income tax purposes. I trust this floor will yet be abolished, and that medical expenses will be allowed as deductible right from the first dollar.

Mr. Chairman, I do not always find myself in complete accord with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. However, this is an occasion on which I must say that I find myself in complete accord with him. The matter of the health and welfare of the people is one of the great problems of today. There is no one who feels the heavy burden caused by ill health more than does the person in the lower income brackets. It seems to me to be almost absurd that, when any allowance is made as a deduction for income tax purposes, the whole amount of hospital expenses or medical expenses is not allowed as an income tax exemption.
I am not going to repeat what the hon. member has just said, but I should like to add one other thing that I think might be given consideration by the department or rather one other exemption that might be further extended. I refer to charitable donations or donations in that category by those who wish to help others in the matter of hospital care. Throughout this country there are many people who are helping those who cannot afford to meet their expenses for sickness and those of their families and are helping them to pay their hospital bills. Surely when hospitalization and medical care is as expensive as it is today, an exemption should be allowed to those who are thus contributing, even for nursing assistance and assistance in small hospitals, as is being done by people who feel they can afford to help someone else who is less fortunate. It seems to me that such an exemption would be just as justifiable as that which is given if one were to write out a cheque as a donation towards the building of a hospital. I think the exemption allowed for charitable donations is limited to a percentage of one's

income. These exemptions include grants to hospitals and assistance for other charitable services. Surely the department might give consideration to exempting for income tax purposes donations and assistance that are given by those who feel they can afford to do so.
There are many people in this country who have no children but who are financially able to assist those who have. There are many people who are growing older, who have small families or no family at all, who have been extremely fortunate and have estates who feel that they want to help those who are less privileged. I think that is a feeling that should be encouraged. In the older days when we did not have such assistance as that afforded by family allowances and other social benefits it was the common practice for those who could afford it to help those who were not able to look after themselves; that was a more common practice then than it is today. However, I submit that there are still many instances where people who have sufficient means are assisting in the hospital care of incurables and others who are less fortunate. I would urge the parliamentary assistant to the minister to give some consideration, not only to the point suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-and again I say that I am in complete accord with him on the matter- but also to extending the exemptions to those who are assisting in the hospitalization of what we might call the underprivileged or the less privileged people, and to put such assistance in the same category as a contribution to a hospital.

There is another matter that has not been raised yet which involves another of these exceptions. It is a question that I have discussed at some length with the department and it has to do with servicemen. In the case of the serviceman who is discharged from the service at some time during the year and marries after his discharge, I understand that he is then treated by the income tax department as though he were two men. For that part of the year during which he was in the service and for which he paid his income tax, although he may have paid income tax as a single man for ten months of the year and was married in the last month of the year, he is not entitled, having withdrawn from the forces, to any return or refund on the amount he has paid, as a civilian would be in similar circumstances. That looks to me as though we have developed for administrative purposes a set of regulations which discriminate against the serviceman. I realize that there may be some administrative difficulties in permitting the serviceman who is married in the latter part of the year after his discharge to get a refund on the taxes he paid as a single man, but surely there are not so many of these cases as to render it necessary for us to perpetuate that discriminatory action.

There are many things which one might mention in dealing with this resolution on the Income Tax Act and the legislation which it proposes to introduce. I suppose one could deal with the fact that the income tax policies of this government seem to be overwhelmingly weighted in favour of the coupon clippers of Canada. I do not intend to go into that because these matters have been covered by other speakers from this group during the course of the budget debate, and in any event I suppose they are matters of high government policy about which we cannot expect the government to do very much at this time. As I indicated when I rose before the dinner recess, I do intend to attempt to deal with some of the more elementary matters of justice and injustice in the application of the Income Tax Act as it affects the people of Canada.
As I said previously, as a citizen of Canada I have never felt that one should object to the paying of legitimate taxes, and by and large that goes for the great majority of the people of Canada. But it is in those instances where people feel that there is some injustice in the way in which the Income Tax Act applies to them that they are apt to be most concerned. I suggest that one of the instances where an injustice does exist is in the case of a great many of the workers of Canada who have to spend a good portion of their yearly income in travelling to and from the job which they are required to do. I intend to use as an illustration of this situation the manner in which the present working of the Income Tax Act applies to the loggers in the coastal area of British Columbia, because I feel that the situation in which they find themselves does offer a very clear-cut illustration of where an injustice exists.
Many of the loggers of British Columbia who have their homes in cities such as Vancouver and other places are required in the course of their normal employment to travel distances up to several hundred miles in some instances to the remoter logging camps. They have to pay their board and lodging in the logging camps and also to maintain a home where their family is. But in addition to this, they have to pay fares to and from their employment ranging from $30, $40 to $50 in each direction. This is not something which they have to do only once a year; it is something they have to do each time that the camp opens up and closes down. When the camp closes because of snow in the winter the cookhouses and the bunkhouses are closed down and those workers have no alternative but to return to their homes. When
Income Tax Act
they open up in the spring and the loggers go back to work they find themselves confronted with a situation where the camps are closed down because of fire hazards, and once again they have the expensive trip back to the city, and then in the fall when the camps reopen they again have to pay that fare.
Probably those people would grumble about having to pay taxes in any event, but they can clearly see that in many instances they are paying quite large sums for travelling expenses which people in other categories do not have to pay. They realize perfectly well that when any of the executives of those logging corporations travel to and from those camps they travel on company expense accounts, and those expense accounts are deductible as part of the expense of the operation of that company; whereas in their case they have to dig out that amount from their own pockets, and when they make up their income tax return at the end of the year no consideration whatever is given to that as an allowable deduction.
Hon. members may or may not be aware of the fact that the loggers union over a number of years has been attempting to secure as part of their agreement with the companies the concession that these fares to the remote logging camps should be paid. They realize perfectly well that if that arrangement could be written into their collective agreement the cost of those fares would then become part of the operating expenses of those logging companies and would be deductible for income tax purposes. Therefore, on the one hand they feel that the companies should pay those fares, and certainly on the other they cannot see any justice in the situation where, as long as they have to pay them themselves, the fares are not deductible for income tax purposes.
As a matter of fact, under the pressure of some shortage of skilled logging labour during the war years there was introduced what is known in the coastal area as the Queen Charlotte islands differential, which meant that the loggers were reimbursed in part at least for the fare to the more distant logging camps. They realize full well again that the amounts which the companies were paying under those conditions were considered to be part of the operating expenses of the companies for income tax purposes. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, here is a clear-cut instance of what is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander, and that as long as travelling expenses are allowable to corporations or to individuals in business, then they should be allowable when they are the necessary part of an individual worker's means of earning his livelihood.

Income Tax Act
Some may be inclined to suggest that it is a good idea, but it is impracticable from an administrative point of view. I must confess I have heard that argument advanced, and I cannot see that that is any valid reason why this arrangement should not be made. It seems to me it would be a very simple requirement that the individual concerned would have to attach a receipt for his travel vouchers to his income tax return, and if necessary in addition the travel voucher could have to have the verification of the employer that in fact that expense had been incurred in the course of going to and from his employment. I cannot see how there could be any insurmountable difficulties in the way of putting such a provision into the Income Tax Act and the regulations.
There is another example I would like to give which I think is parallel, and I refer to the case where business firms can deduct certain things as expenses for income tax purposes, whereas the working people are not allowed to do that. I have in mind the case of the skilled workers, technicians, and tradesmen who, in order to carry on their employment, have to make very substantial investment in tools and equipment, and men such as loggers and miners who have to spend considerable amounts on clothing for heavy duty wear. In these cases we find a situation where these things are not deductible for income tax purposes and it is my belief that in such instances the act should be so drawn that it will apply right around the book and these men will be able to make deductions for such expenditures.
I notice in one of the forms put out by the Department of National Revenue, namely the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide, 1953, there is a statement on page 3 to the effect that people who are covered by this guide are allowed to deduct certain things for income tax purposes. For example, on that page it states that small tools having a normal life of five years or less and costing not more than $50 may be claimed as expenses during the year. I cannot see why it is fair and just that certain people should be allowed to deduct such items when the ordinary tradesman who has to make an investment running into hundreds of dollars on articles which are subject to constant depreciation and replacement should not be allowed some reasonable deduction for income tax purposes.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter to which I would like to draw the attention of the committee. Some hon. members may recall that trade union dues are now deductible for income tax purposes. But there are certain funds which unions require from time to time

which are not deductible for income tax purposes. In certain instances the situation arises where the unions feel that they have to adopt some special means to protect themselves, and in the trade union movement we occasionally have such things as an assessment fund. In large measure these funds are collected by the union in an attempt to accumulate, if you like, a bit of a war chest. I would like to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that here is an instance where, due to the necessity of having to protect themselves from unscrupulous action on the part of the employers, the working people of this country have to accumulate funds which should be allowed to be deducted for income tax purposes.
As long as the employing interests in this country are able to deduct certain funds for income tax purposes which they apply for the very self-same purpose, then the working people of Canada should be able to do so too. Anyone who has had any experience with a strike realizes that strikes cost money to operate and I cannot see any reason why such deduction should not be allowed. For example, I have in my hand here a copy of the Gazette for Monday, March 15 and this issue contains an advertisement inserted by Noranda Mines Limited. Such things as that enter into the advertising expense accounts of corporations; and when unions find it necessary and desirable to levy an assessment of one dollar per month or something like that on their membership in order that the union may be in a position to protect itself I do not see why there should be any quibbling about allowing such amounts to be deducted under a trade union heading for income tax purposes.

It is one that has consistently escaped the notice, I might say, of the Minister of Finance and also that of the Minister of National Revenue. I refer to the taxation which is paid by individuals on owner-occupied premises in the municipalities. In my estimation, Mr. Chairman, the taxes which are paid by individual taxpayers within the municipalities on the premises which they themselves occupy should be deductible from taxable income for purposes of income tax. I should like to elucidate a little bit.
Those who are familiar with income tax realize full well that the only type of municipal taxation which is not deductible from income for purposes of income tax is the tax which is paid by the individual on the premises which he himself occupies. First of all, we should consider the case of the industrialist. On the premises which he occupies for business purposes he pays a tax or possibly two different types of taxes; he pays possibly

a real estate tax and a business occupancy tax. The business occupancy tax, of course, varies according to the various provinces in Canada. He may pay one or two types of tax on those premises. Sometimes he pays both. But those taxes are deductible from the revenue of his business for purposes of assessing the income tax which he as an individual or which the corporation which he represents shall pay to this government.
There is also to be considered the case of the person who owns municipal property and who rents it to various tenants for various purposes. In turn he may deduct from the revenue which he receives from that property the taxes which he pays to a municipality. Whether those taxes be for purposes of school rates or ordinary services, or even if they are for local improvements, he can deduct those taxes from the revenue which he receives from the property before calculating his revenue for tax purposes.
Then let us take the case of the farmer. The farmer is permitted to deduct from the revenue he receives from his farm the amount he pays to his municipality for municipal taxes. But the man who lives in his own home, who has made an investment in his own property and who occupies that property and rents no portion of it to anyone, is debarred from any exemption whatever from his income for income tax purposes.
Mr. Chairman, this is not a matter which I have approached lightly. It is something that I have thought about for a great many years. The more I think about it, the more am I convinced that the man who occupies his own premises-premises which he owns himself and in which he has invested a sizeable sum of money-definitely gets the short end of the stick. It is my opinion that the income tax department could probably do more than could any other department of government to encourage home ownership. It could certainly remove a terrific burden from the shoulders of the owner of small premises, the wage earners within our country, if it would permit such wage earners or owners of any property whatever to deduct from their incomes for income tax purposes the taxes which they pay upon the premises they occupy.
In making this proposal I realize that I have embarked upon a controversial subject. I know of its many ramifications. I know that a small businessman who runs a little store and who lives upstairs over that store in an apartment is not permitted to deduct the portion of taxes which apply to the premises which he personally occupies, but he can deduct those which apply to the portion of

the premises which he occupies solely for business purposes. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that this is an oversight on the part of the department. No doubt they have thought of it. I am sure that they have had consultations on the subject. However, for some inexplicable reason they have consistently turned it down. Hence I am prompted to raise the matter at this stage on the resolution in connection with the Income Tax Act and to suggest that the department should take the matter seriously under consideration and should at the first available opportunity bring down an amendment to the act which would permit the deduction from income for tax purposes of those real estate taxes which are paid on owner-occupied premises.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think probably at this point I should say something in answer to the hon. member for Hamilton West. Actually I know of no capital ownership by anybody that is as free from taxation as is the ownership of one's private residence. A tenant of course pays his rent out of income after paying his taxes, but in the case of one who lives in a house of his own ownership there is no assessment under income tax for the value of living in that house. I am informed that in the case of Great Britain they do assess a certain value, from the point of view of income taxation, for the fact that the person is living in a capital asset of his own ownership.

True enough, that is the case in Great Britain, but I do not think you can take a specific item from any country's income tax regulations and apply it to ours without examining the ramifications of the whole act. It is true that the tenant pays his rent, but just let us ask ourselves what his rent would be if the landlord were not permitted to deduct the taxes he pays from his revenue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In that case it is a business. The landlord is in business, and he pays tax because he has an income from a premises other than those in which he lives. Like any other businessman he can deduct the expenses that are incurred before he earns that income.

Very true, but if he were not permitted to deduct the real estate taxes he pays do you mean to tell me that the tenant would pay exactly the same rent? Certainly not. If the landlord had to pay another $500 the tenant in turn would pay another $40 a month rent. There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I now understand that the general discussion is through?

I want to present a problem to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance mainly for the purpose of clarification. There is a section in the Income Tax Act which allows a special exemption up to $500 in the case of persons physically handicapped. I believe it is possible to deduct expenses arising from the handicap up to a limit of $500. A case has come to my attention in which the exemption was granted in 1951 and was denied in 1952. There was no explanation as to why it was disallowed in 1952. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether there has been an amendment to the act which has changed the circumstances surrounding this special exemption.
The particular case I have in mind is that of a young woman who works as a stenographer. She is physically handicapped to such an extent that she uses crutches. She is crippled in both limbs and as a result has to incur special expenses in getting to and from work because of the necessity of hiring taxis. It is not possible for her to use public transportation facilities. We have been emphasizing in the house in recent months the need for successful rehabilitation of the physically handicapped. This being so, it would be my impression that every effort would be extended under the special provision in the Income Tax Act to take care of this difficulty in order to assist this person, and others like her, to make her living, even though under difficult circumstances.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the general discussion now been completed? The hon. member for Calgary South on paragraph 1.

Having listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion of the omissions from the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act, I should like to deal briefly now with the first four amendments proposed by the government and then follow with two or three points dealing with omissions because of government policy in so far as they affect these first four items.
The first four items of the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act are designed to maintain a stimulus to development of Canada's mineral resources, particularly petroleum and natural gas, gold, base metals and other industrial minerals. The first three amendments simply extend for one additional year, the calendar year 1957, policies which are already in effect, and no change of course is involved. The fourth amendment, that covering deep-test wells, involves a one-year extension covering the 83276-307J
Income Tax Act
calendar year 1955 but with one important restriction to the scope of its application.
In his budget address the Minister of Finance stated, as found at page 3733 of Hansard:
The incentive legislation for the oil, gas and mining industries will be extended for a further year. In the case of deep-test wells, however, this special concession will in future be restricted to more complicated structures such as occur in the foothills.
With the extension of this legislation the Conservative group in the house has no quarrel. In fact we believe that the real question is: Is mere extension of the prevailing policy enough? We strongly endorse the position of adequate incentives to ensure large-scale development of Canada's subsurface mineral resources in order that the nation's economy may be further strengthened, that production may be expanded for both peacetime and emergency needs, that new industries, both primary and secondary, and many thousands of new jobs may be created in Canada and, finally, that the feedbag of income from which governments in Canada secure their sustenance may be progressively enlarged.
Taxation policies of government must do more than simply gouge out from the always unwilling and unhappy taxpayer enough income to meet the apparent needs of government. They must also look ahead to the tax needs of the future by leaving the taxpayer enough incentive to continue working towards enlarged income and expanded production. They must also recognize the nature of problems peculiar to individual kinds of enterprises and take those special problems into account.
Among the industries with special problems peculiar to themselves are of course the metalliferous, industrial mineral and petroleum and natural gas industries. Each mine or well draws upon a strictly limited quantity or volume of solid, liquid or gaseous mineral. The owner of each mine or well literally produces himself out of business as he draws on his patch of subsurface resources or else he keeps himself in business, and thus continues to be an employer, producer and taxpayer, by continuously exploring for new source-beds of minerals into which he can tap with new mines and wells.
The fact that a mine or well is a depleting asset is recognized in Canada and in practically all other nations which have income taxes by provision of depletion allowances providing for some portion of income of a mine or well to be exempt from taxation. I will deal further with depletion allowances

Income Tax Act
after examining the four income tax amendments now before us which relate to minerals. The first amendment provides:
That the exemption of income from metalliferous or industrial mineral mines for the first three years of production be extended to mines coming into production during the calendar year 1957.
This, Mr. Chairman, is an indirect subsidy incentive designed to accelerate the opening up of new mines in Canada.
Item 5 amends section 83 of the provisions of the present Income Tax Act under which mines coming into commercial production prior to the end of the 1956 calendar year are exempted from tax for the first 36 months of that production. It applies to all metalliferous and to most industrial and mineral mines. It does not apply either to petroleum or natural gas wells. The stimulating effect of this tax concession subsidy has already been evidenced by the opening of many new mines across Canada. Without such freedom from taxation during initial difficult years, against the background of high costs and initial low income, it is extremely doubtful that Canada would be experiencing the mining booms of Bathurst, Ungava, Mani-touwadge, Sudbury, Lynn Lake and others now under way across the nation.
I might say, sir, the immediate net cost to Canada's treasury for the loss of corporate tax revenue from new mines is largely offset by the increased personal income and other tax revenue that would not exist without the new mining development spurred by the tax concession. In balance over the long-term, the nation and its tax collector will gain heavily from the new industry, production, jobs and revenue created.
I will skip now, sir, to the fourth amendment because it is in the same category as the first, that is, it is an indirect subsidy incentive. This one provides, and I quote:
That the special deduction from income and taxes allowed to taxpayers whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum or drilling for petroleum and to taxpayers whose principal business is mining or exploring for minerals, for expenses incurred in respect of deep-test oil wells be allowed for expenses incurred in respect of deep-test oil wells spudded in during 1955.
This extends, sir, by one calendar year, 1955, the provisions in 5 (a) of section 53 of chapter 25 of the statutes of 1949, as amended. I might say that I have been having a good deal of fun going through the various sections of the statutes on income tax law and the regulations dealing with this particular industry. I find items in a great many different places. Now, this particular amendment permits deduction from income -I should say deduction from income tax payable-of 35 per cent of the drilling costs
[Mr. Nickle.l
of exploratory wells that have been qualified in advance by the government as deep-test wells. The tax concession applies only if the wells are failures, that is dry holes.
In effect, the government pays indirectly through a reduction in tax received for 35 per cent of the deep-test dry hole drilling costs. The oil or mining company pays the other 65 per cent of drilling costs plus 100 per cent of the geological and geophysical exploration costs, which in some cases will amount to more than the drilling costs of the deep-test well. If the deep-test well finds oil or gas, that is a discovery, the tax concession does not apply. This concession was designed specifically to encourage the drilling of test wells at least 7,000 feet deep and costing at least $150,000, in areas where the dominion geological survey and Dr. George S. Hume, director general of scientific services, believe significant and valuable geological data can be gained.
I perhaps should point out that, in the act itself, no reference is made to the geological survey by Dr. Hume. To qualify as a deep test requires an actual order in council issued following a recommendation from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I mention the geological survey and Dr. Hume, sir, to ensure that the committee may not be under the misapprehension that before approving a deep-test purely scientific knowledge is not applied by the government department in passing on this particular feature.
Now, sir, only a very small fraction of exploratory wells have been qualified for this deep-test concession. From now on the percentage will likely be no more than one per cent of all wildcat or exploratory wells because of the limiting of the plan to the complicated deep structures such as those in the Alberta foothills. In 1951 there were only four wildcat wells qualified as deep-test. Of those, two were discoveries of oil or gas and thus lost the concession in taxes but opened up important new revenue sources for the government and for the companies which drilled them. In 1952 seven wells were qualified as deep-tests. Of those, six wells were dry and the government lost in taxes 35 per cent of their drilling costs. The seventh well was a discovery, so no concession was given. In 1953, twelve wells were qualified, and of those three were discoveries. So far in 1954, sixteen wells have been qualified as deep-tests, and the results of course will be determined in the months ahead.
During the three and one-third years covered by this deep-test concession a total of 39 wells have been qualified. During the same period some 3.000 exploratory wells

have been drilled or are now under way. This does not include an even larger number of development wells, in areas where oil or gas has been discovered. Thus the deep-test concession has applied only to about one and one-third per cent of exploratory wells.
It can be correctly concluded that the subsidy cost of the deep-test concession to the Canadian treasury has been less than one-half of one per cent of the total sums spent in the past three and a third years by the oil industry on exploration in Canada. Because the concession has ensured drilling of certain exploratory wells valuable to Canada that would not otherwise have been drilled, the deep-test provision has been, and is, important. However, the small cost in lost taxes should be viewed against a background of valuable geological information, discovery, personal income and other tax revenue deriving from drilling of the deep-tests, and of course against a background, too, of the tremendous exploration program in which the deep-test provision plays no part.
I come back now to the second and third amendments to the Income Tax Act affecting the mining and oil industry. One of these provides that:
That the special deduction from income allowed to taxpayers whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum, petroleum products or natural gas or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas, for expenses of exploring or drilling for oil or natural gas in Canada, be allowed for expenses incurred in the calendar year 1957, and that in addition a similar deduction be allowed to corporations whose principal business is mining or exploring for minerals, for expenses of exploring or drilling for oil or natural gas in Canada incurred in the calendar year 1957.
Paragraph No. 3 is almost the same, with the exception that it relates to the expenses incurred in searching for minerals in Canada, undertaken by both mining and oil companies.
Now, these, sir, are the most misunderstood by the Canadian public and by many members in this parliament, including some members of the cabinet, of the incentive provisions of the Income Tax Act. These two amendments simply extend by one year, the calendar year 1957, the provisions of section 53 (1A) of chapter 25 of the statutes of 1949 as amended, under which mining and oil companies are permitted to deduct from income before taxes the costs of exploration and development of oil, gas, and minerals. Under these provisions a mining or oil company expenses of exploration and development costs are charged off against income, if it has enough income, or are set up as a charge against hoped-for future income now or has income smaller than the expenses for exploration and development.
Income Tax Act
As many who have invested or gambled money in oil or mining companies know, there is no guarantee that sufficient income to recover exploration and development costs will ever be obtained, for exploration risks are high, and there are even numerous cases where companies have spent all their capital on exploration without success, and have folded up without ever enjoying production income. In these cases, of course, the provision permitting expensing of exploration or development costs has only a paper value.
By no stretch of the imagination is the right to expense exploration and development costs a subsidy or a tax concession, in the sense that the three-year freedom from taxes of new metal and industrial mineral mines and the deep-test well concessions are subsidies.
I regard, and I believe the government and public should also regard, the expensing of exploration and development costs in exactly the same way we all regard the normal operating expenses of normal businesses.
Costs of exploring for and developing mines and wells are just as much a necessary, normal operating expense of an oil or mining company, if it wants to stay in business, as are the costs of advertising to a merchant, the costs of a plant to a manufacturer, the costs of seeding and harvesting to a farmer, and all the other costs which must be taken into account by anyone in any kind of business if he hopes to make a success of it.
I recall that last summer a member of the cabinet of this government spoke in Alberta and was quoted by the press as stating that "the Liberal government of Canada has contributed half the cost of oil and gas exploration and development in the west" in its great desire to assist in getting a maximum development. This was presumably a reference to the so-called tax concessions or incentive legislation whose extension we are now considering.
Without in any way disparaging the legislation, the government which put it into effect, or the minister who made the statement-I must point out that his comment in Alberta indicated an all-too-widely accepted misconception of what this legislation is and does, and to what extent legislation of other nations-particularly the United States-affects exploration and development spendings in Canada.
The first question that arises is this: Are exploration and development costs a normal operating expense which properly should be chargeable against any income before making a split of the net income between the federal tax collector and the company that spent the money to create the income?

Income Tax Act
If such expenditures are not normal operating expense, then it might be correct to say that the government indirectly contributes half of these costs by permitting their deduction from income under this incentive legislation, in the light of prevailing rates of corporate taxation.
If the expenditures are normal operating expense, then it would be just as correct to say that the Canadian government pays half the cost of a merchant's advertising bill because it permits the deduction of such normal business costs from that merchant's income, before taxes are calculated and collected.
The second question that arises is this: Do other nations, particularly the United States, from which country comes over half of the moneys for minerals exploration and development in Canada, contribute to Canadian development in the same general manner as does the Canadian government? The answer is Yes. The United States for many years has encouraged American companies to risk their capital in natural resources exploration and development in other nations, by permitting deduction of these costs from American income before calculation of American taxes. This policy has brought hundreds of millions of United States dollars to Canada in the past eight years.
If we were to concede that the special deductions from income of exploration and development costs are in the nature of a handout from the government-something which I do not concede-then only one logical conclusion could be made: the taxpayers of the United States are contributing a big slice of the funds for Canadian resources development.
Actually, in so far as deduction of exploration and development costs from taxable income is concerned, I do not believe that the taxpayers of either Canada or the United States are paying a single dollar. What the governments are doing is recognizing that exploration and development are normal expenses undertaken by the companies concerned in an effort to find and develop new revenue, in which the government will share as soon as costs have been recovered.
Of course there is no assurance that exploration spendings will bring discoveries and profit-making production. If they do not, the losers are the companies who have footed the bill. Many of the companies, both domestic and foreign, carrying out Canadian exploration, have yet to make discoveries adequate to pull them out of the red. Many others have made discoveries that will assure an ultimate profit, both for
[Mr. Nickle.l
themselves and government. Many, many more discoveries will undoubtedly be made in Canada if the economic climate is favourable.
In fact, the Canadian government has already been assured by discoveries to date of many hundreds of millions of dollars of additional tax revenue in years ahead, as oil, gas, metal and industrial mineral discoveries of recent years advance from the return of capital stage to the stage of paying profits. The Canadian government will draw the same share of those profits, whether the discovering and producing companies are Canadian or foreign.
Since American companies play such a major role in Canadian resources development it might be well to look briefly at how United States and Canadian tax policies function in relation to them. Some operate here as a division of the American parent; others operate through Canadian subsidiary companies.
An American company doing business in Canada may include its Canadian exploration and development expenditures in its parent company's consolidated United States tax returns, deducting these expenditures from this United States income. When and if it develops Canadian income that income will also go into its consolidated tax returns. For Canadian tax purposes the expenditures may be carried forward and charged off against future income in Canada, when and if it is obtained. In order to invoice international double taxation in profit years, tax payments made in Canada may be used as a credit against the United States tax liability.
In effect United States income foots the bills for United States companies' explorations and pays any losses if adequate Canadian income is not obtained. If sufficient Canadian income to leave a profit after recovery of exploration costs is obtained, the profit is shared with the Canadian government.
The second method of operation of United States companies in Canada is through Canadian incorporations as subsidiaries to the parent. In the case of Canadian subsidiary companies, of course, they pay taxes in Canada, after the write-off of prior years' expenditures, the same as for an American subsidiary. The United States taxes at current rates would be paid on dividends transferred to the American parent company.
Sir, I now come to some suggested recommendations which I feel the minister and his aides might well take under consideration in trying to arrive at perhaps an even better program, from the viewpoint of Canada, in

so far as the income tax program is concerned, in stimulating or accelerating the development of resources in Canada.
My first recommendation is this: That the provisions under section 53 of chapter 25 of the statutes of 1949 as amended, for the charging off as expense of exploration and development costs associated with oil, gas and minerals search in Canada, should be incorporated in the Income Tax Act on a permanent basis; in contrast with the present practice of dealing with these annually as a special tax concession subject to extension each year.
In contrast with the present practice of dealing with this annually as a special tax concession subject to extension each year, this recommendation refers specifically to paragraphs 2 and 3 of the resolution to amend the Income Tax Act because the special deductions they refer to are designed simply to recover from income the actual costs of exploration and development which are simply normal operating expenses of the oil and mining industries, and they are not a subsidy. This recommendation specifically excludes paragraphs 1 and 4 of the resolution to amend the Income Tax Act on the grounds that these items are in the nature of incentive subsidies.
The first paragraph exempts from taxation the first three years' income from new metalliferous or industrial mineral mines. The other provides for deduction from taxes of 35 per cent of drilling costs of certain deep-test wells drilled in search of oil and gas but which fail to get production. This special concession applies to only about 1 per cent of exploratory wells.
Quite properly, sir, incentive subsidies should be subject to annual review and annual extension, revision or cancellation, dependent upon conditions prevailing at the time of review. I might add, sir, that depletion allowance changes, which I shall suggest in a few moments, could do much to reduce or eliminate the need of these incentive subsidies set up in items 1 and 4 of this Income Tax Act amendment.
The second recommendation is that the definition of exploration costs for oil and gas should be broadened to include all, instead of just part, of the costs incurred in land acquisition. This is the standard practice under the United States tax laws and its adoption in Canada would give Canadian companies closer to an even break with United States firms in the competition for rights to explore potential oil and gas lands in Canada.
Canada has already accepted in part the principle that cash paid for the acquisition
Income Tax Act
of the rights to enter upon lands for the purpose of exploration spendings and drilling are necessary and thus properly deductible in the same manner as drilling and exploration costs. Section 53 (3A) of chapter 25 of the statutes of 1949 as amended provides for deductions of amounts paid to the federal or provincial governments in the acquisition of a legal lease of oil and gas rights, provided the lease is surrendered without production being obtained.
The same principle, I submit, should apply with equal force and similar deductions should be allowed for bonus payments for the rights to do the same exploring and drilling granted under freehold leases and government permits, licences and reservations, items which in total represent many millions of dollars of costs which cannot now be deducted as an expense.
The final recommendation, sir, is this: Depletion allowances, as provided for in part 12 of the income tax regulations, should be revised, particularly in regard to oil and gas wells, to provide for their full application to gross income rather than net. This recommendation is based on two facts: The first fact is that the present depletion allowance policy in Canada encourages Canadian companies to rest on their laurels, drawing production from current wells, and cutting down on exploration; for the depletion allowance is only effective when a profit position has been reached and all exploration and development costs have been recovered.
The second fact is that the present Canadian depletion policy gives the United States company a competitive advantage over the Canadian firm in Canada, because the United States tax law permits deduction of depletion from gross income, prior to recovery of exploration and development costs.
Depletion allowances, basically, are recognition that a well or mine is a wasting asset, strictly limited as to the ultimate production it can yield. To stay permanently in business the owner must continuously explore to replace with new wells or mines the reserves that are produced. In principle, depletion allowances provide natural resources production industries with a lower rate of taxation than applies to industries which do not have the same problem of replacing by exploration the basic products they process. I might say, sir, that depletion does not apply of course to the normal business phases of such an industry as oil; in other words, profits from refining and marketing are taxed at the full corporate tax rate without benefit of depreciation allowance.
Under present Canadian policy the operators of oil and gas wells are permitted a

Income Tax Act
depletion allowance deduction of 33J per cent of the net profits until all the costs of exploration and development have been recovered. In recent years the oil and gas industry has poured into exploration and development many hundreds of millions of dollars in excess of production income. I believe that since the Leduc discovery in 1947 the total expenses in exploration and development have been over $1| billion in western Canada. The gross value of production before any deduction of costs has been just over $600 million. In other words, to date less than half the total expenses have been recovered. One result is that only about one-tenth of the companies who are actively exploring and producing in Canada are in the position of having net production income against which to apply depletion allowance. The actual depletion allowance benefit to active exploration companies therefore has only amounted to a fraction of 1 per cent of the spendings designed to replace and increase proved reserves of oil and gas. The purpose of the depletion allowance provisions therefore has been largely defeated.
Under present regulations a company could discover an oil or gas pool and if it were carrying on an active exploration program could produce all the oil or gas therefrom and receive very little, if any, depletion allowance. On the other hand, if the company reduced or halted exploration it could derive a very substantial depletion allowance and ultimate profit from the operation of the pool. As the regulations now apply, there is a penalty imposed on the company willing to continue large-scale exploration and that, sir, is an undesirable state in a nation like Canada where our national future depends in no small measure upon the continued risking of large amounts of capital on natural resource exploration and development.
The odds against discovery, in other words, the tremendous risk factor, must be kept in mind when considering depletion allowances as related to the oil and gas industry. To the investor and speculator considering putting his cash into oil the obvious attraction must be that there will be at least as much money left after taxes as would otherwise be available in less hazardous enterprises. With that incentive larger sums of money will be available from Canadian sources and the search to provide oil and gas requirements of the nation will be expanded.
In contrast to the very limited application of depletion provisions to the companies who pay the cost of Canadian exploration and development, we have a depletion allowance of 25 per cent of gross income extended to recipients of gross royalties and similar 
interests in oil and gas wells; in other words, the groups who do not pay the costs of exploration and development.
I would strongly urge that the government amend its current regulations to provide that the depletion allowance of 25 per cent of gross income be extended to those who provide the costs of exploration and development in place of the current allowance of 33J per cent of any ultimate net profits.
Such a step would go a long way towards providing the continuing incentive for Canadian capital to maintain a large-scale exploration program in Canada and would in addition put the Canadian in a nearer-to-equal position with his friendly and essential competitor, the American, in the drive to develop to the full Canadian resources.
I may say, sir, that United States companies have a choice when it comes to depletion in oil and gas wells. That choice is between the greater of two calculations: (1) percentage depletion 27i per cent of gross income not to exceed 50 per cent of net income. You will notice, sir, that this division in the United States is substantially greater than the present division under the Canadian act, and also greater in terms of gross income depletion than the proposal I have made.
The second point in the United States is cost depletion method which means a recovery of acquisition costs such as bonuses, et cetera, for the year on a unit of production basis. I do not understand that program myself so I will not attempt to interpret cost depletion.
I believe the existing regulations and policies in regard to encouraging the development of Canada's industrial mineral and metalliferous resources are adequate to accomplish the nationally desirable objective.
So far as oil and gas resources are concerned, government policy has undergone a considerable change for the better in recent years as the government's knowledge of the potentialities and problems of this comparatively new oil and gas industry increase. But present policies and regulations cannot yet be considered to have reached the final form in which they could achieve the maximum benefit for Canada.
I trust the government will give further serious consideration to the amendments I have suggested, preferably now before the legislation is passed or, if not now, at least long before the house again considers these matters a year hence.
In conclusion, sir, may I say briefly that there are four groups in Canada which may be said to be concerned with her natural resources development.

The first group comprises those who pay the shot for exploration and development, the oil and mining companies and those who invest their cash in them.
The second group consists of those who own the mineral rights, mainly the provincial and federal governments so far as the territories are concerned, plus a minority of rights owned by private companies and individuals.
The third group is the federal government which, on behalf of all Canadians, collects a share on the profits of all resource production in Canada, plus a goodly share of the moneys spent on exploration and development.
The fourth group, sir, is the Canadian people themselves who, as workers in the resources industry or in industries which are built up around resources development, and as citizens of a nation to whom the supply of oil and gas and other resources plays a vital part in their future development.
Now, under our existing mineral rights policies and tax policies in Canada, at least so far as oil and gas are concerned, we can reach one conclusion as far as the benefits are concerned. These benefits are spread between the groups I have mentioned and we can say this, that the ultimate net profit so far as oil and gas are concerned under existing regulations, the net profit of which will be realized by the companies who risk all the capital for exploration and development, will be about equal to the ultimate tax take by the federal government resulting from the capital spending and the production income.
This take or net profit to those who risk all the capital will also be about equal to the cash revenue derived by the government and private owners of mineral rights whose minerals are being appraised and developed by the members of the resource industries. Since those who risk all the capital wind up with a cash profit return of roughly equal to one-third of the total cash benefits to be derived in the development of these resources then I believe, sir, it behooves both the provincial governments and the mineral rights owners, as well as the federal government as the principal taxing authority, to do all in their power not to use the public's money for the development of these resources but to ensure that these private companies who actually finance and take the risks of resources development are given a fair deal in terms of tax policy.

speechtext:
The hon. member, of course, very properly drew attention to the expansion of the number of deep-test wells which have been recognized in a progressive way from 1951 up to the present time, but generally speaking we are very conscious of the fact that the deduction in this case for deep-test wells is rather an unusual one, particularly in that it is not only the deduction of the expenses incurred in this drilling, but is the aggregate of the expenses incurred in drilling the test wells and a 35 per cent of cost deduction from the actual tax. The Minister of Finance announced in his budget speech that this has always been an order in council recommendation, and that there is a likelihood from now on that the territory which may be considered as justifying this form of tax consideration may be somewhat narrowed.
