speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we pass on to paragraph 5?

Mr. Chairman, I hope the parliamentary assistant's suggestion that my proposition be deferred to this point indicates a willingness to consider a revision of paragraph 5. It seems to me there is an almost unanswerable case in this regard, and I shall be very interested to hear what reasons can be advanced against the extension of the principle of deducting pension payments from taxable income in the case of the selfemployed. The resolution provides for an increase in the deductions allowed to an employer or employee in respect of the amounts paid or contributed to or under an approved superannuation fund or plan.
My concern is with that great group in the community who are not now privileged to share in those deductions. As I began to say earlier, these deductions commend themselves to everyone as a means by which, in this era of high taxation, a person can lay up some part of his income in the form of a pension and can make some saving to provide for his retirement and old age. As I say, that principle commends itself to everyone because it is extremely difficult for anyone, after providing for the income tax that is at present payable, to save anything from his earnings. So much is that so that I believe that the normal self-employed person, unless he makes some capital appreciation which is not taxable, is unable in these days to build up any estate. I am not so much concerned about the problem of building up an estate as I am about the prospect which is open to employed persons but not to the self-employed, to acquire for themselves the equivalent of an estate in the form of a pension which is payable to them When they retire.
As matters now stand under the law, a man who is employed is not required to pay taxes on $900 of his income which he puts aside in the purchase of a superannuation pension. In fact, that amount can be increased, in the payment up of arrears, to $1,800 and his employer can make a like contribution. The employer's contribution is, in effect, part of the employee's salary; that is a fact which everyone recognizes, because the employer regards the employee as being worth not only his salary but the contribution which the employer makes. Hence today you have the possibility of normal savings of $1,800 of income, by putting it into a pension plan, on which no tax is levied.
That is the situation with regard to the employed. My question is this. Why is the self-employed person in any different position from that of the employed person? Who
[Mr. Benidickson.l
are the self-employed? My description of them may not be complete, but obviously they comprise a large section of the community. First you have the small businessman. No one will deny that the man who carries on business in an unincorporated way as an individual proprietor usually has a small business and has great difficulty not only in meeting his current expenses but in providing for his future. Then you have the fisherman who is working for himself and you have the farmer who is working on his own. Then you have the professions, that great group which comprises many of the members of the House of Commons and which includes doctors, dentists, lawyers, nurses and accountants. All those people normally work on their own account and have no employer from whom they receive a salary. In addition to them, you have artists. Then if you move on to the trades, you have people who work as plumbers, painters and artisans of one kind and another. A great many people in this country are not employed by anyone but rather exercise their right, their intelligence and their enterprise to provide for themselves in their own way.
Those people are not entitled to the benefits which accrue to the employed. Those people are not privileged to lay up $1,800 of their income each year, tax free, in the purchase of an annuity, a pension or other means of providing for themselves when the inevitable time of retirement comes along. It seems to me that that disability is one which should not be allowed to continue, Mr. Chairman.
I know that this point has been raised before in this chamber. I know that answers have been given to the effect that technically it is not easy to extend to those who are not on payrolls the right to save money in this way as can their associates who are employed. It seems to me that the technical difficulties are not hard to remove if the spirit to do so is present. By way of illustration I should like to put to the committee the simple case of two people, both working in the nursing profession, one employed by a hospital-say the Toronto Western hospital of which I happen to have some knowledge- which has an approved superannuation scheme. She can provide each year for her superannuation by a deduction from her salary, and a similar amount is contributed by the hospital.
In the next room to her may be working a nurse who is not employed by the hospital or is not on the staff, but who is employed by the patient in that particular room on a per diem fee. She has no such privilege

as that which is enjoyed by the other nurse. Yet they are both doing identical work. They both have to retire in due course. They are both entitled to save and to provide for their retirement by this method which has been so well recognized in the past for the employed. If there is any good reason for this disability-in fact I would use a stronger term than that; I say it is discrimination against the self-employed-to be continued, I shall be glad to hear what it is.
I know there are thousands of people in this country who would be extremely glad to be put in the same position as that of their fellow citizens whose only difference is that their income comes from a pay envelope instead of through their own earnings but who have exactly the same needs and pay exactly the same rate of taxation on their earnings. It seems to me that an approved annuity, which is payable as a retirement annuity, or an approved pension should be granted recognition. We have pensions purchasable from the federal government; we have retirement annuities supplied by the insurance companies. It seems to me that those provisions for one's retirement, which may not be anticipated, can in every sense be approved and be regarded as the equivalent to the approved pension plans. I therefore suggest that this matter be given immediate attention.

Mr. Chairman, resolution
No. 5 invites comment both for what it contains and for what it omits. It proposes:
That for the 1954 and subsequent taxation years the deduction allowed to an employer or employee in respect of amounts paid or contributed to or under an approved superannuation fund or plan shall be increased from $900 to $1,500.
That resolution, if approved, will involve amendment of two subsections of section 11 of the Income Tax Act. On the one hand it will permit an increase in the permissible deduction of the employer from $900 to $1,500 per annum in respect of any employee under such an approved superannuation or retirement scheme, and on the other hand it will permit, in the case of every employee under any such approved scheme, an increase in his permissible deduction from $900 to $1,500 without at the same time making any change in the right given to him under the section to deduct as well in respect of contributions to such a scheme for previous years' service.
First of all, as to what this resolution proposes, may I say this. It is evident that it involves a vertical extension of the provisions of section 11 of the act in this regard. What the reasons for this vertical extension are have not been indicated in any way to the committee as yet. We shall await with 83276-308i
Income Tax Act
interest what the parliamentary assistant has to say about that matter. So far as at least some of us in this chamber are concerned, we have not heard any public demand for this vertical extension. It will be interesting to know from what quarter have come the requests for it.
In at least one newspaper I have seen an editorial suggesting that this extension was being introduced for the benefit of members of parliament. This seems to me, Mr. Chairman, about as far-fetched an observation as anyone could well imagine, and I think the parliamentary assistant owes it to the house to say something about this. I think the public ought to be made to realize that the maximum that a member of parliament can contribute in respect of current indemnity is $240 a year. He falls far short of the $900 deduction allowed to him under the law at present, so that he is not going to derive any benefit from the extension of this amount to $1,500. I mention that in passing because it seems that members of parliament are always fair game in these matters for anyone who feels a little jaundiced. But, sir, it will be interesting to know what is the genesis and origin of this particular vertical extension.
So much, sir, for what the resolution proposes. I have more to say about what the resolution fails to do that should have been done. There should have been an extension proposed in the resolution of a horizontal nature rather than a vertical one. This is not a new matter. It was discussed in the house on April 10, 1953, very fully. That was when the house was in committee of the whole on the bill to amend the Income Tax Act. At pages 3702 to 3708 of Hansard is contained what I think was a useful and comprehensive discussion of this question.
The Minister of Finance is not in the house at present. I know his parliamentary assistant will not misunderstand me when I say I wish the minister were here to add to what he said last year because, while he then put forward certain objections and indicated certain difficulties in the way, he did leave us with the impression that he was not dismissing the subject finally, that he was prepared to keep an open mind on it and would review the subject further. Many of us hoped that by this year he would have been ready to propose some remedial legislation. At page 3704 he summed up his view in this way;
I have not taken a final position but the difficulties, the inequities, still appal me.
The minister is not here to explain what his thinking on this subject has been since we discussed the matter thirteen months ago.
The principle is incontestable in this house that the Canadian people should be encouraged to provide for their old age. We do give

Income Tax Act
recognition to that principle in various ways. The principle is recognized in the Income Tax Act in various respects. For the purpose of the present discussion, the principle is already extensively recognized in the subsections of section 11 of the act which I have mentioned. If these provisions in favour of employers and employees with respect to contributions to approved superannuation funds are allowed to stand and the principle upon which they stand is not to be further recognized then I must say that there is discrimination which must be subjected to close examination.
In the discussion a year ago the minister ventured to suggest that to extend the principle in the manner then proposed by some of us would in effect constitute a discrimination. I absolutely reject the minister's argument. The fact of the matter is that the principle is already recognized. The discrimination, if any exists, has been written into the act now, and the way to meet this situation is not to put an end to all remedial legislative efforts but rather to apply our best efforts to extend the principle and in that way abate any existing discrimination. The principle has been recognized and the statute in this respect is working quite satisfactorily.
So far as any of us have heard in discussion in the house, there has been no criticism of these provisions in section 11 of the act and there has been no complaint of difficulty on the part of the government in administering them. I do not doubt that in the ordinary course problems are presented in the process of administration but, Mr. Chairman, that is what we have administrative machinery for, and it is evident that this legislation has been operating satisfactorily. That cannot be gainsaid.
Those who are excluded, as has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Paul's, are, broadly speaking, the self-employed. Those concerned can be grouped into many categories but generally speaking -and it is for such groups that it seems to me the principle should be extended-they are bona fide agricultural, labour, business, industrial or professional associations or similar organizations. In proposing the extension to bona fide organizations of that kind I am proposing, it seems to me, nothing that is open to attack in principle and nothing that will present administrative difficulty that cannot be readily overcome.
There have been many submissions made to the Minister of Finance on this subject. Probably the most notable was the one made a year ago. It was a joint submission put before him on behalf of the following organizations: the Associated Dentists' Co-operative, the Association of Professional Engineers
[Mr. Fleming.!
of the Province of Ontario, the Canadian Dental Association, the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Canadian Medical Association, the Certified Public Accountants Association of Ontario, the Commercial Travellers Association of Canada, the Law Society of Upper Canada, the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada and the Toronto stock exchange. It was a very impressive brief that was submitted to the minister in the name of these organizations. The minister must have been impressed with that presentation.
Now, sir, there was some suggestion from the minister last year about administrative difficulties. I submit that there is no administrative difficulty offered in this respect that cannot be overcome in the same way that any administrative difficulties have been overcome in reference to the operation of the existing subsections (f) and (g) of section 11 of the act.
The minister promised to give consideration to this subject during the past year. He has made no reference to it whatever even in introducing his resolution for a vertical extension of the provisions of the present act in this regard. I am afraid that the minister, contemplating his retirement from the office which he now holds, has probably lacked the interest to press these matters to a conclusion. It is evident that in this and in other respects which have come under debate in the house during the past two days he is leaving many problems on the doorstep of his successor, whoever he may be.
There was one difficulty raised by the minister last year that I think warrants special mention. He suggested that what would be involved in the case of the selfemployed of the groups to whom I have alluded would be virtually a double deduction. He said in effect: Today we allow the employer a deduction of $900 from his taxable income and we allow the employee a deduction of $900 from his taxable income, so that there is a total deduction of $1,800 in the case of the contributions to a retirement allowance for any one employee. In the case of the self-employed, the minister contended that to put them on a similar footing we would have to allow a similar total deduction of $1,800, and in the case of the self-employed that would accrue entirely to the benefit of one person and not two as at present. My answer is that whatever limitations are necessary to assure equitable application can certainly be devised. That kind of objection is no excuse for doing nothing to meet a situation of this nature where a very serious discrimination now exists.

Looking abroad, sir, there has been since this matter was under discussion on April 10, 1953, one very notable development in the United Kingdom. It is the submission to the chancellor of the exchequer of what is known as the Millard Tucker report. This report was submitted recently to the chancellor of the exchequer by a royal commission which takes its name from the chairman, Mr. James Millard Tucker, K.C., J.P. The committee was appointed in August, 1950, by Sir Stafford Cripps when he was chancellor of the exchequer, and is composed of very eminent men. It has surveyed this whole question of the taxation treatment of superannuation and retirement provisions under the law of the United Kingdom. I am told that the same committee is now extending its investigations into other aspects of taxation law and administration.
This report deals specifically, among other subjects, with the subject of the tax position of the self-employed in relation to provisions being made by them in various forms for their maintenance on retirement. I do not propose to weary the committee by referring to the details of this report. It is a document embracing some 156 pages of very fine type, a report that has about it every mark of learning and of thorough investigation into this subject. The reference to the committee calls for investigation into this and a number of other related subjects. The committee has among its extensive recommendations included one in favour of a scheme for putting self-employed persons on a comparable basis in regard to taxation with employees who enjoy the benefits of a superannuation scheme provided by their employers.
There is a minority report submitted by two members of this committee, which makes certain observations upon the report of the majority, but as I read that it does not attack the basic recommendation to which I have just made reference. The committee covers this particular subject of the tax position of superannuation provision made by the selfemployed in chapter 6, and has embodied some 30 recommendations in detail dealing with almost every aspect of the subject and certainly providing every type of safeguard that is required to ensure equitable treatment of those in the self-employed field and to avoid any form of discrimination with respect to that class.
Now that report came only recently before the chancellor of the exchequer. When asked whether he would be prepared to introduce legislation to implement its recommendations at the present session of the parliament of the United Kingdom I am informed he said that the session was so far advanced he did
Income Tax Act .
not feel he had time to give this subject the study it required before introducing legislation based upon the recommendations of the Millard Tucker committee. But he did give assurance that before another session of the parliament of the United Kingdom was convened he would give to this subject and to the recommendations of the Millard Tucker committee exhaustive study and consideration.
Exhaustive study and consideration of this subject are long overdue in Canada. At a time when the government has seen fit to propose this vertical extension of the provisions of the present act, it seems to me the government has failed in its duty in coming before the house without any proposal for a horizontal extension of the same provisions. A horizontal extension is unquestionably much more urgently required in the interests of fair play, in the interests of the removal of existing discrimination, than is any vertical extension. The time to deal with a vertical extension, if there is a case for one, is after a horizontal extension has been written into the law of this land to remove the existing discrimination and to give fair play and justice to the self-employed in this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the parliamentary assistant replies to the statements that have been made by the hon. member for St. Paul's and the hon. member for Eglinton I should like to urge that he give the committee a clear statement as to why the changes set out in this part of the resolution are being made. Without necessarily agreeing to all the specific suggestions that have been made by the last two speakers, I certainly agree with the general statement that a horizontal extension is more important than a vertical one.
What does strike me about these figures is the practical result. It is now possible for an employee to get a deduction for $900 in the course of a year as a current payment into a superannuation fund. What employee can pay even that much into a pension fund? The payments that employees make into pension funds are at varying rates, but 6 per cent of one's salary is a fairly good rate, indeed, shall I say, a fairly high rate. This $900 is 6 per cent of a $15,000 annual salary. It does seem to me if provision has been made for a person on a salary as high as $15,000 a year to get income tax deductibility for 6 per cent of that, that is about as far as we need to go.
If this amount that can be deducted is to be raised to $1,500, that is 6 per cent of an annual salary of $25,000. It seems to me that the government is getting the cart before

Income Tax Act
the horse in being concerned about people up in those brackets before it does something to encourage the broadening of pension plans to cover our people generally. One could look at a lot of different tables and get different results, but speaking very generally and bearing in mind the fact that these contributions are in turn usually matched by the employers, when you are talking about a $900 annual contribution from employees, that usually means a total of $1,800, $900 from the employee and $900 from the employer. Over 25 years that could buy a pension of between $4,000 and $5,000, depending upon when the contract starts and the age at which the person goes on pension.
The proposal to raise the amount that can be deducted to $1,500, according to this very rough calculation I have made, results in allowing income tax deductibility to people who are purchasing pensions of $8,000 or $9,000 a year. It does seem to me we should be concerned about broadening the base of the exemption and encouraging the development of plans that will help those who are now not covered at all before we should be concerned about income tax deductibility for the purchase of pensions of these high orders.
I stress the further point that when you raise the amount that you can deduct from $900 to $1,500, not only does that take you up into the higher income brackets before a pension of that kind can be afforded, but when you get up into those upper brackets it means that the income tax saving that arises from the greater deductibility is that much greater, because you are in the higher income tax brackets.
Perhaps the parliamentary assistant has an explanation for this. He may think it is a good one, and we will be glad to hear it as soon as he is given the opportunity to speak. But I do want to say that this is hardly the sort of thing the government should be bringing in, bearing in mind the fact that we are still waiting for the government to go ahead with the plan that it had before us a few years ago, which was to raise the amount that can be bought under a government annuity.
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to get out of order by discussing that question, but I do lay this before the committee as an example. There was an occasion when something was being done to make it possible for people who could buy annuities at $1,200 to have them increased to $2,400. That is down within reasonable brackets. But it was not carried out, for some reason which has not yet been made known to us. But here is

this move, which is a help to people in brackets which to most Canadians seems rather high and fanciful.
I think something should be done to encourage the establishment of the kind of pension plans that would enable employees to carry their pension rights with them when they move from one employment to another. And one of the ways that can be encouraged is through income tax provisions providing income tax deductibility where plans are funded, and employees are given the right to move about.
It is one of the things that happens with some pension plans, that sometimes employees seem to be frozen on the job because they cannot lose such pension rights as they have earned. It seems to me that that is the sort of problem, the need for broadening the base, to which the government should be directing its attention, instead of raising these figures to levels which produce the results I suggest they produce- and which, so far as I know, have not been requested. I hope the parliamentary assistant will explain why this resolution was brought in at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
One of the questions raised and described by the hon. member for Eglinton was the reason for what he described as a vertical rise in the pension ceiling. This legislation I think was generally approved in 1946, when it was introduced. A ceiling of $900 was established at that time. I think hon. members will recognize that wages and salaries have increased between 1946 and the present time roughly in the proportion of the increase in the ceiling proposed here.
My hon. friend from Eglinton, too, was asking from what quarters the suggestion was made that brought about this legislation. I certainly want to assure him, as he said, that it did not come from members of parliament; because under their pension scheme this change in the act would be of no benefit. The hon. member himself outlined that our maximum contribution is in the nature of $240.
That is per annum.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, per annum. The hon. member for St. Paul's of course was not with us in the last session, and I do not know whether he has read the very full statement that was given by the Minister of Finance at the last session explaining why he felt that this could not or should not be extended to the self-employed.

The hon. member for Eglinton emphasized, and I felt wrongly, the minister's explanation of last year, in that he suggests that he presented administrative difficulties as being the important difficulties in his rejection last year. Then and now, on this suggestion that the self-employed should have a provision in a horizontal way, similar to what is provided for employees, I suggest to the hon, member for Eglinton-

The minister did not confine his objection to the matter of administrative difficulty. He argued on the basis of discrimination and that is why I spent as much time as I did in my remarks in dealing with the subject of discrimination.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Certainly the preponderance of the minister's argument was on principle. I wish to assure my hon. friend that not only this year but last year the representations that came in from certain groups were very carefully considered. But I am quite satisfied that after a re-examination of the problem the minister came to the same conclusion that he did last year, which the hon. member for Eglinton quoted:
I have not taken a final position but the difficulties, the inequities, still appal me.
The hon. member referred to the report in the United Kingdom of a commission which was giving consideration to this problem. I believe the commission brought in a report about two months ago. Perhaps it was too early to have it considered by the chancellor in his budget, which was brought down the same night as our Canadian budget. I do wish to point out-

speechtext:
I see it is about ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I was going to conclude by saying that there is a very striking difference in the take-home pay, shall we say, after taxes of the self-employed, in the United Kingdom, as compared with the same group in Canada. I have some figures here showing the tax of a married taxpayer with no dependents receiving an income of $10,000 a year. In Canada that person would be paying a tax of $1,660, plus $60 as the old age security tax. The same individual with
Income Tax Act
that income in the United Kingdom would pay a tax of $4,086, plus a social security tax of $39. I think that is the distinguishing point between the situation in this country and that in the country from which this commission report has been received.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.
